Otherwise it always passes `config["credentials"]` -- a real (possibly empty `{}`) dict -- into `_build_client`, which then does `credentials.get(field)` per-field with no fallback to `Settings`/.env at all (service.py:73-150).

2. `seed_from_env_if_empty()` (runtime_config.py:501-551) runs on every startup (app/main.py) but only acts once, when the `provider_runtime_configs` table is completely empty. When it fires, it creates a row for EVERY one of the 11 `AI_BACKENDS` in one pass -- including backends with zero matching .env vars, which get `encrypted_credentials=""` (decrypts to `{}` via `_decrypt_credentials`, runtime_config.py:91-93). It also sets `is_active=(backend == settings.ai_backend)` for exactly one row.

3. `set_active_ai_backend()` (runtime_config.py:331-349) only flips `is_active` flags; it never touches or re-seeds credentials.

4. Consequence: after the very first boot of this feature (true for essentially every real, already-running deployment), `get_active_ai_config()` is non-None as long as some row is active, which is guaranteed after seeding. So for any backend other than whichever one happened to be `settings.ai_backend` at the moment of that one-time seed, switching to it via "Set Active" hands `_build_client` an empty-but-non-None credentials dict, never consulting .env again -- even though the RuntimeError text (service.py:192-195) explicitly tells the operator "...or check .env" as a remedy, which is dead advice in this state.

5. This is exactly the same bug shape the codebase already found and fixed for IOC providers: providers/base.py:162-164's `effective_configured = (override.get("configured") or self.configured) if override else self.configured`, whose adjacent comment (base.py:144-161) describes verbatim the same failure mode ("a provider with a perfectly valid .env credential... got permanently short-circuited... by an unrelated blank DB row") and states the intended semantics are "DB value OR env fallback," mirroring `get_credential()`'s "for as long as no runtime config has been seeded/configured" contract. No equivalent per-field OR-with-env fallback exists for AI backends in service.py or runtime_config.py, so `_get_ai_client`'s own docstring (lines 153-163, "only if no runtime config has been seeded yet at all") is inconsistent with the seed-everything-at-once, all-or-nothing implementation.

This is a real, reachable gap, not a hypothetical or an intentional pattern from the provided allow-list (none of the 8 listed intentional designs cover this). Severity: P3 is appropriate -- real, config-time-only, wastes an admin's time and produces a misleading error remedy, but there is a working alternative (the "AI Providers panel" upsert path, which correctly merges new credentials into the DB row) so it is not a hard outage, has no security or data-integrity impact, and only manifests when adding/switching to a backend that wasn't the active one at the single historical seed moment.

details.title: No per-investigation snapshot of the active AI backend -- summarize_provider() and generate_final_assessment() can silently use different backends within one lookup, with zero traceability
details.actual_behavior: _get_ai_client() (service.py:153-196) re-reads app/core/runtime_config.get_active_ai_config() (a fresh DB query) every single time it is called whenever backend_override is None. app/api/routes/lookup.py's stream_lookup() calls summarize_provider(..., backend_override=payload.ai_backend) once per successful provider result, sequentially inside its `async for result in run_all_providers(...)` loop (lookup.py:168-176), and calls generate_final_assessment(..., backend_override=payload.ai_backend) once at the end (lookup.py:238-246) -- both pass through payload.ai_backend, which for an ordinary (non-comparison) investigation is None, so both resolve the backend independently via the currently-active runtime config at the moment each call happens. The pipeline's own comments describe this as a genuinely long-running (~25-40s), multi-provider, sequential-await flow. ProviderSummary (app/ai/schemas.py:58-68) and its persisted row AISummaryRecord have no ai_backend/ai_model field at all (unlike FinalAssessment, which does and gets it force-set at service.py:708-710) -- so if two different summarize_provider() calls within the same lookup used two different backends, or the final assessment used yet a third, there is no persisted signal of that ever having happened.
details.failure_scenario: An analyst starts an investigation while Ollama is the active backend. Provider 1-3 results stream back and get AI-summarized against Ollama. Partway through the same still-running investigation, the same or another admin uses AiQuickSwitch.tsx (whose own docstring promises this "takes effect on the very next investigation, anywhere in the app, immediately") to switch the active backend to Anthropic. Providers 4-6 in the SAME lookup then get their per-provider summaries generated by Anthropic, and generate_final_assessment() -- called once after every provider finishes -- picks up whichever backend is active at that instant. The resulting investigation record silently blends judgments from two different AI vendors under one seamless-looking report, and there is no field anywhere in the persisted AISummaryRecord rows that would let anyone reconstruct which backend authored which provider summary after the fact.
details.reasoning:
Verified against the actual code, not just the reviewer's description.

Confirmed facts:
1. `_get_ai_client()` (service.py:153-196) calls `get_active_ai_config()` (runtime_config.py:226-241) whenever `backend_override is None`, and that function opens a fresh DB session and queries `is_active == True` on every single invocation -- no caching, no snapshot.
2. In `lookup.py`'s `stream_lookup()`, `summarize_provider(..., backend_override=payload.ai_backend)` is called once per successful provider result *inside* the `async for result in run_all_providers(...)` loop (lines 168-171), and `generate_final_assessment(..., backend_override=payload.ai_backend)` is called once afterward (lines 238-246). `LookupCreateRequest.ai_backend` (schemas/lookup.py:26) defaults to `None` for an ordinary investigation ("None = whichever AI backend is currently active platform-wide"), so both calls resolve the backend independently via whatever is active *at the instant each call executes* -- confirmed by reading `_get_ai_client`'s own docstring, which states this is deliberate for "switch AI, no restart."
3. `ProviderSummary` (ai/schemas.py:58-68) and its persisted row `AISummaryRecord` (models/lookup.py:105-116) have no `ai_backend`/`ai_model` column at all -- confirmed by reading the model definition directly (only `lookup_id`, `provider_id`, `summary` JSONB). `FinalAssessment`/`FinalAssessmentRecord` do carry `ai_backend`/`ai_model`, force-set per-call at service.py:708-710 to `used_backend`/`used_model` -- but that is only a snapshot of the single final-assessment call, not of the whole investigation's earlier per-provider calls.
4. Critically, `AiQuickSwitch.tsx`'s own docstring (lines 9-11) explicitly promises switching "takes effect on the very next investigation, anywhere in the app, immediately" -- implying an *already-running* investigation should NOT be affected. The actual per-call DB re-read in `_get_ai_client()` violates that stated contract: an admin switching the active backend mid-flight during a still-streaming lookup WILL cause later provider summaries (and/or the final assessment) in that same lookup to silently use the new backend, with zero persisted signal that a split occurred.

This is a genuine architectural gap (no per-investigation snapshot/pinning of the resolved backend, no backend field on per-provider summary records), not one of the eight listed intentional patterns.

Severity correction (P1 -> P2): The deterministic risk score/severity/verdict-consistency is never affected (design pattern #3 -- AI backends only narrate, and `generate_final_assessment` mechanically overwrites risk numbers with the scoring engine's values regardless of which backend ran), so this cannot corrupt the actual security determination of an investigation. The blast radius is limited to AI-narrative provenance/audit-trail: a mixed-vendor prose report with no way to reconstruct which backend wrote which provider summary. Real and worth fixing (it also breaks an explicit UX promise), but it requires a fairly specific trigger (an admin/analyst actively switching the global backend while another lookup is still mid-flight in its ~25-40s window) and the resulting harm is traceability/trust-in-narrative, not data corruption or a wrong security verdict -- which places it below P1 (broad-impact/core-functionality-broken or correctness-critical) and squarely at P2 (real, moderately impactful, narrower trigger and consequence).

titles: AI-generation-failure fallback silently rescales a legitimate 0<score<1 deterministic risk value by 100x

details.title: AI-generation-failure fallback silently rescales a legitimate 0<score<1 deterministic risk value by 100x
details.actual_behavior: When generate_final_assessment() falls through to its ai_outcome="failed" return (every retry attempt raised), it builds `risk=RiskAssessment(overall_risk_score=scoring.overall_risk_score, malicious_probability=scoring.malicious_probability, severity=scoring.severity, ...)` via RiskAssessment's normal constructor with plain floats. RiskAssessment.overall_risk_score/malicious_probability/confidence_score all carry the field_validator `_reject_0_to_1_scale` (app/ai/schemas.py:140-152), which multiplies by 100 any value strictly between 0 and 1 -- a guard meant to catch an AI emitting "0.5" for 50%. app/scoring/engine.py's score_investigation() can legitimately produce a real, correct score in that exact (0,1) range for a weak single-provider signal (this file's own comment at lines 670-688 explicitly names "a real, tiny, correct score like 0.4" as the motivating case, and states the fix -- passing an already-constructed RiskAssessment INSTANCE through model_copy() so Pydantic v2's default revalidate_instances="never" skips re-running that validator -- but that fix is applied ONLY to the ai_outcome="success" path (lines 689-699). The "failed" fallback (736-745) and the "skipped_no_evidence" fallback (528-537) still construct RiskAssessment fresh from plain scoring.* floats, so the exact same field_validator DOES fire there and silently mangles the real value by 100x. severity (not one of the three floats) stays correct, so the resulting object is internally self-contradictory (e.g. severity="none" with malicious_probability=40.0-90.0).
details.failure_scenario: A lookup has exactly one provider return OK status with a VirusTotal-style detection ratio (data={"total_engines": 70, "malicious_count": 1}), zero correlation edges, zero Security Assessment findings. score_investigation() (app/scoring/engine.py) computes overall_risk_score=malicious_probability≈0.4 (mean_vote=1/70≈0.0143, corroboration_factor(n=1)=0.4, 65*0.0143*0.4≈0.37, rounds to 0.4) and severity="none" (0.4 < the 10.0 'low' threshold) -- an accurate near-benign read. The configured AI backend then fails both retry attempts (e.g. this file's own lines 612-619 describe a Groq HTTP 429 rate-limit as a real, reproduced case that breaks immediately with NO retry). generate_final_assessment() returns the ai_outcome="failed" FinalAssessment with risk.malicious_probability and risk.overall_risk_score both rescaled from 0.4 to 40.0 by _reject_0_to_1_scale, while risk.severity stays "none". app/api/routes/lookup.py:250-252 persists `stream_lookup_row.risk_score = final.risk.overall_risk_score` (40.0) and stores the same contradictory object in final_assessment/DB with no further correction -- an analyst sees a 40% (or, with a slightly larger but still <1 threat_intel_score, up to ~90%) malicious-probability score with severity 'none' for an indicator that was actually flagged by only 1 of 70 AV engines.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading backend/app/ai/service.py, backend/app/ai/schemas.py, and backend/app/scoring/engine.py, plus a direct pydantic 2.13.4 reproduction.

Mechanism confirmed:
- RiskAssessment.overall_risk_score/confidence_score/malicious_probability all carry `_reject_0_to_1_scale` (schemas.py:140-152), a field_validator that multiplies any value strictly between 0 and 1 by 100.
- The "success" path (service.py:689-699) builds the persisted risk via `assessment.risk.model_copy(update={...})` on an already-constructed instance, then feeds that instance (not a re-validated dict) back through `FinalAssessment.model_validate`. My repro shows `model_copy(update=...)` performs NO field validation at all on the updated fields, so a legit 0.4 stays 0.4.
- The "skipped_no_evidence" path (service.py:528-537) and the "failed" fallback path (service.py:736-745) both instead call `RiskAssessment(overall_risk_score=scoring.overall_risk_score, malicious_probability=scoring.malicious_probability, ...)` — a plain constructor call with bare floats. My repro confirms this DOES run `_reject_0_to_1_scale`, turning 0.4 into 40.0.
- score_investigation() (engine.py) can legitimately emit such a value: with one provider vote of 1/70 (`_PROVIDER_VERDICT_WEIGHT=65.0`, `_corroboration_factor(1)=0.40`), `threat_intel_score = 65 * (1/70) * 0.4 ≈ 0.371`, rounded to `overall_risk_score=malicious_probability=0.4`, while `_severity_band(0.371)` falls through every threshold in `_SEVERITY_THRESHOLDS` (10.0 for "low") to `severity="none"`. This exactly matches the claimed scenario.
- The mangled value is what's actually persisted: `app/api/routes/lookup.py:250` sets `stream_lookup_row.risk_score = final.risk.overall_risk_score` with no correction, and `final.model_dump()` (containing the contradictory severity="none" alongside malicious_probability=40.0) is stored in `final_assessment` and streamed/exported (lines 252, 290, 599, 708).

This is a genuine asymmetry bug, not one of the listed intentional patterns — patterns (3)/(8) don't cover this, since the issue isn't "AI output not validated" or "a status is wrong," it's that the platform's OWN deterministic-fallback code path re-triggers a validator meant only to catch AI mis-scaling, corrupting a value the code never should have touched.

Severity: I disagree with the claimed P1 and downgrade to P2. Reasons: (1) it only fires when the AI backend has already exhausted both retries (an already-degraded, non-default scenario) AND the deterministic score legitimately lands in the narrow (0,1) pre-rounding band — a fairly specific combination, not the common/happy path (which is unaffected, since that path correctly uses model_copy). (2) The corruption is a 100x *overestimate* (0.4 → 40, or higher), i.e. it biases toward false positives/over-caution rather than masking a real threat as benign — the more dangerous direction for a security tool. (3) The resulting object is internally self-contradictory (severity="none" next to malicious_probability=40-90), which is itself a visible tell likely to prompt an analyst to distrust/double check that specific assessment rather than act on it blindly. These mitigating factors keep it from P1/P0 territory, but it's still a real, reproducible data-integrity defect worth fixing (P2).

titles: Self-registration admin-bootstrap check is not transaction-safe (TOCTOU)
register() has an unguarded check-then-act race on the email-unique constraint, unlike its sibling create_user()
register() has no IntegrityError handling for a concurrent duplicate-email race, unlike admin.py's create_user()

details.title: Self-registration admin-bootstrap check is not transaction-safe (TOCTOU)
details.actual_behavior: register() decides whether self-registration is 'open' with a plain SELECT (`select(User.id)`, line 55-56) and decides whether an email is already taken with a second plain SELECT (line 71-72), with no row/table lock and no serializable transaction around the subsequent INSERT+COMMIT. Under Postgres's default READ COMMITTED isolation (no isolation_level override anywhere in app/core/db.py), two concurrent POST /auth/register calls that each arrive before either has committed will both see an empty `users` table and both pass the 'registration closed' check, so both requests successfully create an ADMIN account -- even though the code's own comment states self-registration 'only bootstraps the very first admin'.
details.failure_scenario: An attacker with network access to a freshly-deployed, not-yet-configured HORIZON GRID instance sends a POST /auth/register with a candidate email at (or fractionally before) the moment the legitimate operator submits their own first-admin registration. Both requests race through the empty-table check before either commits, so both succeed and the attacker walks away with a second, fully independent ADMIN account with no credentials shared with or known to the legitimate operator -- the 'registration is closed after the first admin' invariant the comment claims is not actually enforced.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the bootstrap check and the insert in one transaction using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a sentinel row (or a unique partial index / advisory lock keyed on 'first-admin-bootstrap') so only one concurrent register() call can win the empty-table race; alternatively use SERIALIZABLE isolation for this specific transaction.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading backend/app/api/routes/auth.py (lines 55-84), backend/app/core/db.py, backend/app/models/user.py, and the integration test backend/app/tests/integration/test_auth_registration.py.

The register() handler does exactly what the finding claims: it runs `select(User.id)` (line 55) to decide whether self-registration is still "open," and if the table is empty it proceeds to a second plain SELECT for the duplicate-email check (line 71-72), then INSERT+commit (lines 75-82) with role hardcoded to Role.ADMIN (line 79). There is no `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, no advisory lock, no unique sentinel/partial-unique-index on "an admin already exists," and no explicit transaction isolation override anywhere -- app/core/db.py's create_async_engine call (lines 16-22) sets only pool_pre_ping/pool_size/max_overflow, nothing about isolation_level, so the engine runs at Postgres's default READ COMMITTED. The only uniqueness constraint on User (models/user.py line 22) is on `email`, which does nothing to stop two different emails from both slipping through the empty-table check concurrently. RateLimiter (core/cache.py) is keyed per-email (`register:{email}`), so it doesn't serialize an attacker's request against the legitimate operator's request either.

The integration test file's own docstring independently corroborates that this register() path is the actual live "first user becomes admin" bootstrap mechanism relied on by the real Setup Wizard/first-run flow (not some dead/legacy branch), and that it's deliberately not exercised via a real concurrent HTTP test because it runs against a real dev/prod database.

So the mechanics of the claim hold up: under READ COMMITTED, two concurrent register() calls that each execute their `select(User.id)` before either has committed its INSERT will both see an empty table, both pass the "closed" check, and (since they use different emails) both commit successfully as ADMIN. This is a genuine, unmitigated TOCTOU race in a security-critical bootstrap check, not one of the documented intentional patterns.

On severity: impact is severe (unauthenticated attacker walks away with a full, independent admin account), but exploitability is bounded by a narrow, self-closing window that only exists between fresh deployment and the legitimate operator's first successful commit -- once any row exists, the door closes permanently. That combination of high impact / high attack complexity (precise timing + network access during a brief bootstrap phase) is consistent with the original reviewer's P2 rating; I don't see grounds to raise it to P0/P1 (no persistent exploitable window, single-use race) or lower it to P3 (impact is a full admin takeover, not cosmetic). Keeping P2.

details.title: register() has an unguarded check-then-act race on the email-unique constraint, unlike its sibling create_user()
details.actual_behavior: register() does `existing = await db.execute(select(User).where(User.email == normalized_email)); if existing.scalar_one_or_none(): raise HTTPException(400, ...)` and then unconditionally does `db.add(user); await db.commit()` at lines 81-82 with no try/except around the commit. If two requests for the same not-yet-registered email race (e.g. a double-submit/network-retry, or two people racing to become the bootstrap admin while the users table is still empty), both can pass the SELECT check before either commits; the second commit then violates the DB-level `unique=True` constraint on User.email (app/models/user.py:22) and raises an uncaught sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError, producing an unhandled 500 instead of the intended 400.
details.failure_scenario: Two POST /auth/register calls for the same email arrive concurrently while the users table is empty (this is the only window reachable, since the 'registration closed' 403 check happens first once any user exists). Both pass `user_count.first() is None` and both pass the duplicate-email SELECT (neither has committed yet). The second db.commit() raises IntegrityError, which propagates out of the route as an unhandled 500 Internal Server Error instead of a 400.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the db.add(user)/await db.commit() in a try/except IntegrityError block that raises HTTPException(400, 'Email already registered'), mirroring core/users.py's create_user().
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading. auth.py lines 70-83 exactly match the claim: normalized_email = payload.email.lower(); a SELECT-based duplicate check (raise 400 if found); then unconditional user = User(...); db.add(user); await db.commit(); await db.refresh(user) with no try/except anywhere around the commit. app/models/user.py:22 confirms `email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), unique=True, ...)`, so a second concurrent commit for the same not-yet-committed email genuinely raises sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError. The sibling app/core/users.py:create_user() (used by admin.py's POST /admin/users, which maps DuplicateEmailError to a clean 409 -- not literally 400 as the reviewer assumed, a minor inaccuracy that doesn't affect the core finding) does the identical check-then-act SELECT but wraps its db.commit() in try/except IntegrityError -> DuplicateEmailError (users.py lines 176-184), proving the asymmetry claim. I also checked app/main.py for a global exception handler that might rescue this: there is one (@app.exception_handler(DBAPIError) at line 205), but it explicitly narrows to `isinstance(exc.orig, AsyncpgDataError)` (Postgres SQLSTATE class 22, data exceptions) and does `raise exc` for anything else -- a unique-violation IntegrityError is SQLSTATE class 23, so it is NOT caught there and does propagate as an unhandled 500. The race window is real: the 'registration closed' 403 check (lines 55-60) runs before the duplicate-email check and fires unconditionally once any row exists, so the duplicate-email race is only reachable while the users table is still empty (the one-time bootstrap-admin step), exactly as the reviewer stated (e.g. a double-submit/network-retry of the same registration form). This doesn't match any of the 8 listed intentional-design exceptions. Severity: downgrading P2 to P3. This codebase's own BUG_AND_REPAIR_HISTORY.md shows the team's own calibration: an unhandled-500-from-bad-input bug trivially reachable on any single request by any caller (BUG-QA-009, raw uuid.UUID() crash) was rated P1, and a trivially-reachable oversized-field crash (BUG-QA-012, also on this same register endpoint) was rated P2. This bug, by contrast, requires precise concurrent-request timing AND is only reachable during a single one-time bootstrap window before any user exists in the entire deployment's lifetime, AND is self-healing with no data-integrity impact (the unique constraint still guarantees exactly one row is ever created; only the losing request's HTTP response is wrong -- 500 instead of 400 -- and any retry behaves correctly). That combination of narrow reachability, one-time-only window, and zero lasting impact places it below the P1/P2 input-crash bugs already catalogued in this repo's history, closer to the P3 tier (e.g. BUG-QA-017 login case-sensitivity, BUG-QA-019 missing max_length) rather than P2.

details.title: register() has no IntegrityError handling for a concurrent duplicate-email race, unlike admin.py's create_user()
details.actual_behavior: The duplicate-email check at lines 71-73 is a plain SELECT-then-INSERT with no `try/except IntegrityError` around `await db.commit()` (line 82). backend/app/core/users.py's create_user() (lines 181-184) explicitly catches `IntegrityError` for the exact same duplicate-email race and converts it into a clean `DuplicateEmailError` -> HTTP 409; register() has no equivalent handling.
details.failure_scenario: Two concurrent POST /auth/register calls with the identical email arrive during the bootstrap window (table still empty) before either commits. Both pass the 'no existing user with this email' SELECT check, both attempt to INSERT; the second INSERT violates the unique constraint on users.email and raises an unhandled `IntegrityError`. main.py's only DBAPIError handler (`_database_data_error_handler`) explicitly re-raises anything that isn't an asyncpg `DataError`, so this propagates as a bare, unhandled 500 instead of the intended clean 400 'Email already registered' response.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the commit in register() with the same try/except IntegrityError -> HTTPException(400, 'Email already registered') pattern already used in app/core/users.py's create_user().
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code reading. auth.py's register() (lines 71-73) does `existing = await db.execute(select(User).where(User.email == normalized_email)); if existing.scalar_one_or_none(): raise HTTPException(400, ...)` and then unconditionally does `db.add(user); await db.commit()` at line 82 with no try/except around the commit. By contrast, app/core/users.py's create_user() (lines 176-184) performs the identical SELECT-then-check pattern but wraps `await db.commit()` in `try/except IntegrityError as exc: raise DuplicateEmailError(...) from exc`, proving the codebase already has and uses this exact defensive pattern elsewhere for the same race. The users table has `email` declared `unique=True` (app/models/user.py line 22), so a genuine DB-level unique constraint backs this. main.py's only DBAPIError handler (`_database_data_error_handler`, lines 205-228) explicitly narrows to `isinstance(exc.orig, AsyncpgDataError)` and does `raise exc` for everything else, so an IntegrityError from a UniqueViolation would not be caught there and would propagate as a bare unhandled 500. The race window is real but narrow: register()'s own preceding check (lines 55-60) means self-registration is only reachable at all while the users table is completely empty (pre-bootstrap), so this is exploitable only during that one-time window before any account exists, and only degrades the response (500 instead of a clean 400) -- it does not create a duplicate row, bypass auth, or corrupt data, since the unique constraint still enforces correctness underneath. That combination (a real, reproducible, narrow-window, cosmetic-severity bug matching an established in-codebase remediation pattern) supports the P3 severity the original reviewer assigned; I see no basis to raise it higher (no security bypass or data integrity loss) or to drop it to P4 (it's a concretely reproducible functional defect, not a style nit).

titles: login() has a timing side-channel that lets an attacker enumerate valid account emails

details.title: login() has a timing side-channel that lets an attacker enumerate valid account emails
details.actual_behavior: `if not user or not verify_password(payload.password, user.hashed_password):` short-circuits on `not user`: when no account matches the submitted email, `verify_password()` (passlib/bcrypt, deliberately slow, ~tens to hundreds of ms) is never invoked at all, so the 401 response returns almost immediately. When the account exists but the password is wrong, the full bcrypt verification runs before the same 401 is returned. The two 401 responses are functionally identical in body/status but measurably different in latency.
details.failure_scenario: An attacker sends repeated POST /auth/login requests (bounded only by the per-email rate limiter, which still allows several samples per window and resets afterward) for a candidate email and measures response time. Emails with no account respond fast (no bcrypt call); emails with a real account respond consistently slower (bcrypt runs). Averaging a handful of timing samples per candidate lets the attacker reliably distinguish 'account exists' from 'account does not exist', defeating the same enumeration protection this file explicitly implemented for the registration endpoint.
details.proposed_fix: Always perform a constant-cost password check regardless of whether the user was found -- e.g. call verify_password() against a fixed dummy hash when `user is None` before returning 401, so both branches take comparable time.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading auth.py and security.py: `if not user or not verify_password(...)` short-circuits, so bcrypt (passlib CryptContext, deliberately slow) is skipped entirely when the email doesn't exist but runs fully when it does, before both cases converge on an identical 401 response. This produces a measurable latency difference between 'no such account' and 'wrong password' responses. The per-email rate limiter (10 attempts/60s, confirmed in core/config.py) slows but does not prevent an attacker from collecting enough timing samples over time, since bcrypt's cost (tens-hundreds of ms) is large relative to normal network jitter. This directly parallels the email-enumeration oracle the same file's author explicitly patched in register() (lines 25-38), showing the project's own threat model treats this class of leak as worth preventing, yet login() reintroduces it via a different channel. Not covered by any of the 8 listed intentional-design exceptions. Severity: real but constrained information disclosure (account-existence enumeration, not direct credential/account compromise), so P2 (Medium) as originally claimed is appropriate -- not P0/P1 (no auth bypass) and not P3/P4 (it's a reliably exploitable oracle, not merely theoretical). Proposed fix (constant-time dummy-hash verify when user is None) is a standard, correct mitigation.

titles: add_to_basket has a check-then-insert TOCTOU race on the (owner_id, ioc_value) unique constraint
Re-adding an already-basketed IOC returns 201 and silently drops the new note

details.title: add_to_basket has a check-then-insert TOCTOU race on the (owner_id, ioc_value) unique constraint
details.actual_behavior: The endpoint SELECTs for an existing BasketItem (lines 56-62) and only INSERTs if none is found (lines 76-86), with no locking or upsert between the two. Two concurrent identical requests from the same user can both pass the SELECT before either commits; the second INSERT then violates `uq_basket_owner_ioc` (models/basket.py), raising a SQLAlchemy IntegrityError. That IS routed through the global `@app.exception_handler(DBAPIError)` in main.py, but the handler only converts `isinstance(exc.orig, AsyncpgDataError)` (Postgres SQLSTATE class 22) to a 422 and does `raise exc` for everything else -- a unique-violation is SQLSTATE 23505 (class 23, IntegrityConstraintViolationError), which is not a DataError, so it is re-raised and surfaces as an unhandled 500.
details.failure_scenario: A user double-clicks 'add to basket' (or the frontend retries a slow request) for the same ioc_value within the same race window; one of the two concurrent POST /basket requests gets an unhandled 500 instead of the expected idempotent 201/200 with the existing item.
details.reasoning: Read basket.py (lines 45-86), models/basket.py (unique constraint on owner_id+ioc_value), and main.py's DBAPIError handler. Confirmed the endpoint does SELECT-then-INSERT with no locking, upsert, or exception handling around the commit. Confirmed the global DBAPIError handler only special-cases asyncpg DataError (SQLSTATE class 22) and re-raises everything else via `raise exc`, so a unique-constraint violation (SQLSTATE 23505, IntegrityConstraintViolationError, class 23) is not caught and surfaces as an unhandled 500. This exact race pattern is independently corroborated: core/users.py's create_user and core/runtime_config.py's upsert_ai_provider both explicitly identify and fix the identical SELECT-then-INSERT-vs-unique-constraint race (one via try/except IntegrityError -> clean domain error, the other via with_for_update()+retry, with an inline comment calling the unmitigated version 'a real bug, not an acceptable tradeoff'). basket.py has neither mitigation, making this look like a genuine gap rather than an intentional design choice. None of the 8 listed known-intentional-pattern exemptions apply to this finding. The failure scenario (double-click / retried POST /basket for the same IOC racing) is plausible and consistent with the code as written. Severity: no data corruption, first request still succeeds; only the duplicate/loser request gets a spurious 500 instead of an idempotent 200. This matches P2 (moderate correctness bug, narrow trigger window, no security/data-integrity impact) -- consistent with the original reviewer's rating and with how the codebase's own authors treated analogous instances.

details.title: Re-adding an already-basketed IOC returns 201 and silently drops the new note
details.actual_behavior: When a BasketItem for (owner_id, ioc_value) already exists, add_to_basket returns the existing, unmodified item at line 62 -- but the route's status_code is still fixed at 201 (line 45 decorator), and any new `note`/refreshed `latest_lookup_id` the caller submitted in this call is discarded rather than applied to the existing row.
details.failure_scenario: An analyst adds an IOC to their basket with note 'seen in phishing campaign', later re-adds the same IOC with note 'confirmed C2' expecting the note to update -- the second call returns HTTP 201 (implying success) but the basket item still shows the original note.
details.reasoning:
Read backend/app/api/routes/basket.py lines 45-86 directly. Confirmed exactly as claimed:
- Line 45: `@router.post("", status_code=201)` fixes the status code for the whole handler regardless of branch taken.
- Lines 56-62: when a BasketItem already exists for (owner_id, ioc_value), the handler returns `_serialize(existing)` immediately — it never looks at `payload.note` or re-queries for a newer `latest_lookup_id`, and never updates the `existing` row. So a repeat POST with a different `note` is a true no-op that still reports HTTP 201.
- Confirmed via app/schemas/basket.py that `note` is a legitimate, documented request field (not a leftover/unused param), and via grep across backend/app that `note` is purely a display field (never read by scoring/case/compare logic) and `latest_lookup_id` is not re-derived from the basket item in compare_basket_iocs (that endpoint takes lookup_ids directly from payload).
- Checked the current frontend (InvestigationActions.tsx, lib/api.ts, basket/page.tsx): `addToBasket()` is only ever called with just `iocValue` in the shipped UI — there is no UI affordance to enter/edit a note at all, so the exact "analyst types note A, then note B" scenario cannot currently be triggered through the product's own UI. It is, however, live and reachable via direct API calls (curl/Swagger/any integration), since the schema and code path fully support passing `note` on every POST.
- Also confirmed a workaround exists: DELETE /{item_id} followed by a fresh POST fully replaces the item including note/latest_lookup_id, so this is not a dead end for a determined caller.

This is not one of the listed intentional design patterns (RBAC role re-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED, AI-narration-only scoring, basket privacy, toolkit/suite duplication, nmap flag safety, provider status semantics) — it's a genuine logic gap in idempotent-add handling: real state change requested by the caller is silently discarded, and the response status doesn't distinguish "created" from "already existed unchanged."

Severity: agree with the original reviewer's P4. Real-world impact is low — it's a per-analyst, display-only annotation field (not used in scoring, correlation, or case logic), the failure is currently unreachable through the shipped frontend (no note-input UI exists yet), and a full workaround already exists (delete then re-add). This is a minor API-correctness/idempotency polish item, not a functional break or security/data-integrity issue, so P4 remains appropriate.

titles: update_case's generic field-setter lets 'case:write' set status=CLOSED, bypassing the dedicated 'case:close' permission gate
add_case_ioc crashes with unhandled 500 on malformed or nonexistent lookup_id

details.title: update_case's generic field-setter lets 'case:write' set status=CLOSED, bypassing the dedicated 'case:close' permission gate
details.actual_behavior: update_case (gated on "case:write") does `for field_name, value in payload.model_dump(exclude_unset=True).items(): setattr(case, field_name, value)`, and CaseUpdateRequest.status accepts any CaseStatus including CLOSED. This fully duplicates what the separate close_case endpoint does, except close_case is deliberately gated behind the stricter "case:close" permission while update_case only checks "case:write" and never re-derives/blocks the CLOSED transition.
details.failure_scenario: Currently not exploitable: in ROLE_PERMISSIONS (models/user.py) every role holding 'case:write' (ADMIN, ANALYST) also holds 'case:close', so no live account can leverage this today. It becomes a real privilege-escalation path (PATCH /cases/{id} with {"status": "closed"} using only case:write) the moment a role is introduced with case:write but not case:close -- exactly the separation the two distinct permissions were designed to allow.
details.reasoning:
Verified directly against backend/app/api/routes/cases.py (lines 133-159) and cross-checked app/schemas/case.py, app/models/case.py, app/models/user.py, and app/auth/rbac.py.

Confirmed facts:
1. update_case (line 138) is gated by require_permission("case:write") only.
2. Its body (lines 140-144) does `updates = payload.model_dump(exclude_unset=True); for field_name, value in updates.items(): setattr(case, field_name, value)` -- a fully generic setter with no field allow/deny list and no re-check of any finer-grained permission.
3. CaseUpdateRequest (app/schemas/case.py lines 24-29) includes `status: Optional[CaseStatus] = None`, and CaseStatus (app/models/case.py) includes CLOSED among its members -- nothing in the schema restricts which status values update_case's caller may set.
4. close_case (lines 148-159) is a separate endpoint gated by require_permission("case:close") whose entire effect is `case.status = CaseStatus.CLOSED`. update_case can achieve the exact same state mutation via `{"status": "closed"}` while only holding case:write.
5. require_permission (app/auth/rbac.py lines 74-86) does exact-string set membership against ROLE_PERMISSIONS with no implication logic between permissions -- so case:write and case:close are genuinely independent gates in the code; any relationship between them exists only incidentally in the current data (ROLE_PERMISSIONS in app/models/user.py), not structurally.
6. Current ROLE_PERMISSIONS (models/user.py lines 48-76): ADMIN and ANALYST both hold case:write AND case:close together; VIEWER holds neither. So today no role can exploit the gap -- this matches the original reviewer's own caveat.

This is a genuine authorization-design flaw (a dedicated, more-privileged permission gate that a co-existing generic field-setter endpoint silently bypasses), not a false positive and not one of the eight documented intentional patterns in this codebase (it doesn't match the JWT-role-recheck, provider-status, AI-narration, basket-visibility, security-assessment/pentest-overlap, nmap-flag, or provider-status patterns). It is a legitimate CWE-863-style incorrect-authorization gap: the separation of case:write vs. case:close is meaningless as currently implemented, since update_case's generic setter re-derives the exact same privileged transition without checking the stricter permission.

Severity: I concur with the original reviewer's P3. It is not currently exploitable by any real account (every role with case:write also has case:close today), so it is not an active P0/P1 vulnerability -- but it is a real latent privilege-escalation trap that would silently activate the instant a new role is introduced with case:write but not case:close (a plausible future change given the two permissions clearly exist to be separable), and the fix is cheap (exclude 'status' from the generic setter, or re-check case:close when status==CLOSED). P3 (low/moderate, fix proactively, no live exploit path) is well-calibrated; I would not lower it to P4 because the existence of a dedicated close_case endpoint/permission signals deliberate intent to separate this privilege, making the silent bypass a real design defect worth tracking, nor would I raise it since there is no current exploit path and the impact (case status field) is not highly sensitive.

details.title: add_case_ioc crashes with unhandled 500 on malformed or nonexistent lookup_id
details.actual_behavior: Line 174 does `lookup_id=uuid.UUID(payload.lookup_id) if payload.lookup_id else None` with no try/except. `CaseIOCAddRequest.lookup_id` (app/schemas/case.py) is typed as a plain `Optional[str]`, not a UUID, so FastAPI/Pydantic never validates its format before it reaches this line. A non-UUID string raises a bare `ValueError` from `uuid.UUID(...)`, which is not a DBAPIError/SQLAlchemyError of any kind and is not caught by the app's global `@app.exception_handler(DBAPIError)` (main.py), so it becomes an unhandled 500. Separately, even a syntactically-valid UUID that doesn't correspond to any real IOCLookup row will fail the FK constraint on commit with an asyncpg ForeignKeyViolationError wrapped in a SQLAlchemy IntegrityError; that IS a DBAPIError so the handler runs, but its body only special-cases `isinstance(exc.orig, AsyncpgDataError)` (class-22 errors) and does `raise exc` for anything else, so a ForeignKeyViolationError (class 23) still ends up re-raised as an unhandled 500.
details.failure_scenario: POST /cases/{case_id}/iocs with body {"ioc_value": "1.2.3.4", "ioc_type": "ipv4", "lookup_id": "not-a-uuid"} raises ValueError -> unhandled 500. POST with a well-formed but non-existent lookup_id (e.g. a random uuid4 string) raises a ForeignKeyViolation IntegrityError on commit -> also unhandled 500.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading cases.py, schemas/case.py, models/case.py, and main.py. CaseIOCAddRequest.lookup_id (schemas/case.py:35) is a plain Optional[str] with no UUID validation. add_case_ioc (cases.py:174) calls uuid.UUID(payload.lookup_id) with no try/except -- a non-UUID string raises a bare ValueError that no handler catches, producing an unhandled 500. Separately, CaseIOC.lookup_id (models/case.py:53-55) has ForeignKey('ioc_lookups.id'); a syntactically valid but non-existent lookup_id UUID fails that FK constraint on commit as an asyncpg ForeignKeyViolationError wrapped in SQLAlchemy IntegrityError (a DBAPIError subclass). The sole global handler for DBAPIError in main.py (lines 205-228) only special-cases isinstance(exc.orig, AsyncpgDataError) (Postgres class-22 data errors) and does `raise exc` for everything else, so the class-23 FK violation re-raises unhandled -> 500. This is exactly the same bug pattern already identified and fixed in basket.py's compare_basket_iocs (verified: lines 133-137 wrap uuid.UUID(raw_id) in try/except (ValueError, AttributeError, TypeError), with an inline comment explicitly describing this exact prior bug -- 'this raw uuid.UUID() call had no try/except, so any non-UUID string ... crashed the whole request with an unhandled 500'). cases.py's add_case_ioc has the identical unguarded call and was simply never patched to match. Not one of the documented intentional design patterns. Severity: client-triggerable by any user with case:write via one malformed/stale optional field in a routine workflow (attaching an IOC with an optional lookup reference to a case), producing a 500 instead of a clean 4xx -- a real but non-security, non-data-loss correctness/error-handling gap, directly analogous to the already-fixed basket.py issue. P2 is an appropriate severity; not P0/P1 (no security or integrity impact) and not P3/P4 (it's a straightforward, reachable, unhandled-crash bug on a real endpoint, not cosmetic).

titles: Persisted correlation edges silently lowercase related IOC/entity values

details.title: Persisted correlation edges silently lowercase related IOC/entity values
details.actual_behavior: source_type/source_value/target_type/target_value are derived by splitting edge.source/edge.target (GraphEdge.source/.target, which ARE the correlation engine's node_id strings built by app/correlation/engine.py::_node_id() as f'{type}:{value.strip().lower()}') on the first colon. Because the node_id was already lowercased before this split, the 'value' half persisted into CorrelationEdgeRecord.source_value/target_value is always lowercase -- unlike GraphNode.value (used directly, un-lowered, by the live SSE `correlation` event built at lines 193-199 from the same correlation.nodes), which preserves the provider's original casing.
details.failure_scenario: An OTX pulse (or any provider) reports threat_actor 'APT29' or malware_family 'WannaCry' for an IOC. During the live investigation, the SSE `correlation` event streams the node with value: 'APT29'. After the lookup completes and the analyst reloads the page (GET /lookup/{id} -> _correlation_payload(), which rebuilds nodes purely from the persisted CorrelationEdgeRecord rows), the same node now renders as value: 'apt29', a visible, unexplained discrepancy from what was shown live.
details.proposed_fix: Build the CorrelationEdgeRecord's *_value columns from the corresponding GraphNode.value (looked up via correlation.nodes by node_id) instead of re-deriving it by parsing the already-lowercased combined node_id string.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the actual code end-to-end. app/correlation/engine.py:_node_id() builds GraphEdge.source/.target as f'{type}:{value.strip().lower()}' (engine.py line 58), while the corresponding GraphNode.value (engine.py line 129: value=str(raw_value)) keeps the provider's original casing. The live SSE `correlation` event in lookup.py (lines 193-199) serializes `correlation.nodes` directly via `n.__dict__`, so it shows the original-case value (e.g. 'APT29'). But lookup.py lines 183-186 build the persisted CorrelationEdgeRecord's source_value/target_value by `edge.source.split(':', 1)[1]` / `edge.target.split(':', 1)[1]` -- i.e. by re-parsing the already-lowercased combined node_id string instead of looking up the corresponding GraphNode.value. This mechanically forces source_value/target_value to always be lowercase in the DB. app/evidence/loaders.py::correlation_from_records() (used by GET /lookup/{id} via _correlation_payload, plus analysis.py, hunting.py, security_assessment.py) then rebuilds GraphNode.value directly from these lowercased persisted columns, so any later reload of the same investigation shows 'apt29' where the live view showed 'APT29'. This is a genuine, deterministic, 100%-reproducible discrepancy for any mixed-case correlation value (threat_actor/malware_family/campaign names are almost always mixed-case in real provider data, e.g. OTX pulses), not an edge case. It does not match any of the 8 documented intentional patterns, and the CorrelationEdgeRecord docstring ('so a lookup's graph can be rebuilt from Postgres alone') establishes that exact rebuildability was the actual intent, with no comment anywhere excusing case-normalization on this path -- confirming this is an oversight (accidentally reusing the identity-normalized node_id string instead of the display-preserving GraphNode.value), not a deliberate simplification. The same anti-pattern (splitting the lowercased node_id instead of using GraphNode.value) also appears in app/core/security_assessment.py:617-620 and app/evidence/builder.py:125-126, reinforcing that this is a real, unintentional bug class in this codebase rather than a one-off. Severity: this is display/data-fidelity only -- it does not affect scoring, verdicts, or deduplication/matching (which already key off the lowercased node_id everywhere, e.g. evidence/pivot.py, evidence/loaders.py), and there's no crash or true data loss (the original case is simply not persisted). Given it's a systematic, always-visible, permanently-baked-in correctness defect in a component the codebase explicitly frames as a durable evidentiary record for a security-analyst-facing product, but with impact confined to cosmetic/display fidelity, P2 (as originally claimed) is an accurate rating -- not P0/P1 (no security or functional-correctness impact) and not P3/P4 (it's not a rare corner case; it's the default outcome for the most common threat-intel field types like threat actors/malware families).

titles: Preformatted detection-rule blocks do not wrap long single-line rule text, risking off-page overflow in the exported PDF

details.title: Preformatted detection-rule blocks do not wrap long single-line rule text, risking off-page overflow in the exported PDF
details.actual_behavior: Line 765 passes `rule.get("rule", "")` straight into `Preformatted(..., styles["Code"])`, which (per ReportLab's own implementation, confirmed against reportlab==4.2.5 pinned in backend/requirements.txt) only breaks lines on literal '\n' characters and does not word-wrap long lines -- unlike Paragraph, which this file otherwise uses everywhere for AI-authored free text specifically to get wrapping/escaping.
details.failure_scenario: An AI-generated detection rule in a single-line-oriented format (e.g. a long splunk_spl or elastic query with no internal newlines) exceeds the printable page width; that line renders running past the right margin of the PDF rather than wrapping, making part of the rule illegible/cut off in the exported report.
details.proposed_fix: Either hard-wrap long lines (e.g. textwrap.fill at a fixed column count) before passing to Preformatted, or render detection rules via a monospace-styled Paragraph (with escaping) so ReportLab's normal word-wrap logic applies.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading both lookup.py:755-765 and reportlab's actual Preformatted implementation (flowables.py, matching the pinned reportlab==4.2.5 in the venv). Preformatted's own docstring/behavior is explicit: by default it does NOT wrap lines, only breaks on literal '\n', and no maxLineLength/splitChars is passed at this call site -- unlike every other dynamic string in this function, which goes through Paragraph()+_pdf_esc for proper wrapping/escaping. I computed the actual page budget: styles['Code'] is Courier 8pt with leftIndent=36pt inside a SimpleDocTemplate using default 1-inch margins, giving roughly ~90 characters before text runs into the blank right margin and ~105-110 characters before it is drawn past the physical page edge (where PDF viewers clip to the MediaBox, i.e. genuinely invisible, not just cramped). I then checked app/ai/schemas.py and confirmed detection_rules[].format explicitly includes splunk_spl, sentinel_kql, elastic, qradar_aql, suricata, snort, zeek -- formats that are conventionally written as a single long physical line with no embedded newlines and routinely exceed 100+ characters in real-world use. So the failure scenario isn't a contrived edge case: it's centered on exactly the rule formats this feature is built to support. This doesn't match any of the 8 documented intentional-design-pattern exclusions. I'm raising severity from the claimed P3 to P2: this isn't a crash or security issue and is confined to one PDF export section, but it causes silent, unindicated content loss (part of a security detection rule literally missing from the exported report) in an artifact meant to be handed to a SOC/SIEM team to implement -- a real correctness problem more consequential than a cosmetic P3, but still bounded enough that P0/P1 would overstate it.

titles: update_scope's /16 cap is enforced per-CIDR-entry, not aggregated across the declared scope

details.title: update_scope's /16 cap is enforced per-CIDR-entry, not aggregated across the declared scope
details.actual_behavior: The loop at lines 209-219 checks each CIDR string in payload.scope_definition['cidrs'] independently against the 65536-address cap and never sums num_addresses across the list. The route's own error message (line 217-218) even says 'limited to ... addresses (/16) or smaller per CIDR', confirming the check is per-entry, not scope-wide.
details.failure_scenario: A caller submits a cidrs list containing many separate CIDRs, each individually <= a /16 (e.g. dozens or, in the extreme, all 65536 distinct /16 blocks that partition all of IPv4), all of which pass this check individually. The resulting declared scope can cover far more address space than a single /16 -- up to the entire IPv4 Internet the comment explicitly says this control prevents.
details.proposed_fix: Sum network.num_addresses across every CIDR in the list (deduplicating overlaps if desired) and compare the total against the cap, not each entry independently.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code reading: the loop in update_scope (pentest.py:208-219) checks each CIDR string's num_addresses independently against the 65536 cap and never sums across payload.scope_definition['cidrs'], despite the immediately preceding comment (lines 194-199) explicitly framing this as 'a single scope-wide ceiling' meant to stop 'the whole IPv4 Internet' from being a valid declared scope. The route's own error text ('... or smaller per CIDR') corroborates the per-entry (not aggregate) nature of the check. Traced scope_definition.cidrs downstream to orchestrator.py's _is_in_scope(), which gates add_target and exploit.py's exploit-validation authorization -- so this is a real, security-relevant control, not cosmetic. Confirmed via user.py that Role.ANALYST (not just ADMIN) holds 'pentest:create', the permission gating this route, so the bug is reachable by non-admin users with a single API call containing many individually-compliant /16 CIDRs. Does not match any of the 8 documented intentional design patterns. Kept severity at P2 (matching original): real and easily triggered by a low-privilege authenticated role, but blast radius is partially bounded by independent downstream layers (nmap's hardcoded/flag-restricted invocations, and the separate ADMIN-only per-finding confirmation gate required for actual Metasploit exploitation), so it doesn't rise to P0/P1 RCE-equivalent impact, but does fully defeat a named safety ceiling, ruling out P3/P4.

titles: set_ioc_provider_enabled never validates provider_id against the known registry, unlike its configure sibling

details.title: set_ioc_provider_enabled never validates provider_id against the known registry, unlike its configure sibling
details.actual_behavior: set_ioc_provider_enabled (lines 162-172) skips that check entirely and calls `await svc.set_ioc_provider_enabled(provider_id, payload.enabled, ...)` directly with the raw path parameter. app/core/runtime_config.py's set_ioc_provider_enabled (lines 452-474) silently INSERTs a brand-new ProviderRuntimeConfig row (kind=IOC, provider_name=provider_id) whenever no existing row matches, then unconditionally records an audit entry ("Enabled/Disabled IOC provider '<id>'"). The route returns 200 with `{"provider_id": provider_id, "enabled": payload.enabled}` regardless of whether that id refers to anything real.
details.failure_scenario: An admin responding to a compromised/leaked VirusTotal key calls POST /runtime/ioc-providers/virus_total/enabled with {"enabled": false} (typo: the real registered id is "virustotal"). The call returns 200 and writes an audit-log line reading "Disabled IOC provider 'virus_total'." -- appearing to be a successful, audited security action. In reality the real `virustotal` config row is untouched and remains enabled/active with the compromised key, while an inert, meaningless `virus_total` row is created instead. The admin has no signal (no 404, no warning) that the disable never took effect.
details.proposed_fix: Validate provider_id against get_all_providers() (the same `known` map configure_ioc_provider already builds) before calling svc.set_ioc_provider_enabled, and 404 on an unrecognized id.
details.reasoning: Read backend/app/api/routes/runtime.py directly: configure_ioc_provider (138-155) validates provider_id against known = {p.provider_id: p for p in get_all_providers()} and 404s on unknown id; set_ioc_provider_enabled (162-172) has no such check and passes the raw path param straight to svc.set_ioc_provider_enabled. Read backend/app/core/runtime_config.py's set_ioc_provider_enabled (452-474): it queries ProviderRuntimeConfig by exact provider_id, and if no row is found it silently INSERTs a brand-new row keyed by the caller-supplied id (provider_name set to the same unvalidated string) rather than raising, then unconditionally calls record_audit with a message like \"Disabled IOC provider '<id>'.\" Also confirmed get_ioc_provider_snapshot() (383-401), which actually drives per-investigation provider enable/disable state, keys strictly by exact provider_id with no fuzzy/normalized matching, so a mistyped or unregistered id truly never affects the real provider's config and there is no signal to the caller (200 OK, plausible-looking audit entry, no 404/warning). This is a genuine inconsistency versus the sibling endpoint that clearly implements the intended validation pattern, and does not match any of the 8 listed intentional-design exceptions. Severity: requires admin-level access and a human-caused bad id (not attacker-controlled), but produces a silent, convincingly-audited no-op in a security-sensitive action (credential/provider disablement) with zero error feedback -- this fits P2 as originally claimed rather than P0/P1 (no direct compromise or attacker-reachable bypass) or P3/P4 (more than cosmetic given the false-security-signal consequence).

titles: hash_password/verify_password are synchronous, CPU-bound bcrypt calls invoked directly inside async request handlers -- block the whole event loop

details.title: hash_password/verify_password are synchronous, CPU-bound bcrypt calls invoked directly inside async request handlers -- block the whole event loop
details.actual_behavior: `hash_password` and `verify_password` are plain synchronous functions wrapping passlib's bcrypt backend, which is deliberately slow (real per-call cost on the order of hundreds of ms at bcrypt's default work factor). Every call site in the codebase (api/routes/auth.py login()/register(), core/users.py create_user()/reset_password()) calls them as plain synchronous function calls directly inside `async def` route/service functions -- never via `asyncio.to_thread`/`run_in_executor`. A synchronous CPU-bound call made this way runs on, and blocks, the single asyncio event-loop thread for its entire duration.
details.failure_scenario: A burst of concurrent POST /auth/login requests against any existing account (verify_password is reached whenever `user` is found, regardless of whether the password is correct, since `not user or not verify_password(...)` short-circuits only on missing users) each stall the event loop for ~200-300ms apiece and serialize. With even a modest number of concurrent login attempts (an attacker rotating across a handful of known/guessed valid emails, each independently under the per-email rate limiter's 10-requests/60s ceiling), the aggregate blocked time is enough to visibly stall every other concurrent request on that worker -- lookups, dashboard polling, other users' sessions -- not just auth traffic, since it's all one event loop.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the passlib calls in `await asyncio.to_thread(hash_password, ...)` / `await asyncio.to_thread(verify_password, ...)` at each call site, or make hash_password/verify_password themselves async wrappers around to_thread so every caller gets non-blocking behavior automatically.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading backend/app/auth/security.py: hash_password() and verify_password() (lines 13-18) are plain `def` (not `async def`) functions that call passlib's CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"]) synchronously, with no rounds override so it uses bcrypt's default work factor (realistically ~200-300ms/call). Verified every call site is a direct synchronous call inside an `async def` function with no asyncio.to_thread/run_in_executor anywhere in the codebase: api/routes/auth.py's async register() (hash_password, line 77) and async login() (verify_password, line 120 -- reached whenever `user` is found, i.e. any guessed/known valid email, since `not user or not verify_password(...)` only short-circuits on missing users), and core/users.py's create_user() (hash_password, line 179) and reset_password() (hash_password, line 269). Also confirmed the deployment is single-worker: backend/Dockerfile's CMD and docker-compose.prod.yml's command both run plain `uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000` with no --workers flag -- one process, one asyncio event-loop thread. Confirmed the per-email rate limiter (app/core/config.py: login_rate_limit_max_attempts=10, window_seconds=60) throttles by count within a rolling window but does not pace/serialize timing, so a burst of concurrent requests against even a handful of known/guessed valid emails can pile up concurrently-blocking bcrypt calls before the limiter rejects further attempts. This is a real, verifiable event-loop-blocking bug and does not match any of the documented intentional design patterns. Severity: the original reviewer's P2 is well-calibrated -- it's a genuine, unauthenticated-reachable, whole-process-wide availability/performance degradation (not just self-DoS of the auth endpoint), but it requires a burst of concurrent traffic and only degrades responsiveness rather than compromising data or auth/authorization, so it doesn't rise to P0/P1; P2 (moderate) is appropriate and I would not adjust it.

titles: record_audit has no failure isolation, so a transient audit-log write failure can turn an already-completed primary action into a client-visible 500

details.title: record_audit has no failure isolation, so a transient audit-log write failure can turn an already-completed primary action into a client-visible 500
details.actual_behavior: record_audit opens a new session, adds a row, and awaits db.commit() with no try/except (lines 26-36); any exception (DB momentarily unavailable, pool exhaustion, deadlock) propagates straight out to the caller. Several callers invoke record_audit AFTER already committing the real state change in a separate session -- e.g. app/core/users.py's reset_password() commits the password change and closes its `async with new_session()` block (line ~276) and only THEN calls `await record_audit(...)` outside that block (line ~280) -- so a failure purely in the audit write raises out of reset_password/record_login_success/etc. and the FastAPI endpoint returns an unhandled 500, even though the underlying action (password already changed, login already recorded) has already durably succeeded.
details.failure_scenario: An admin calls the reset-password endpoint while Postgres is briefly saturated/unreachable for just the audit-log commit (e.g. a connection-pool exhaustion blip). The password is already changed and committed, but record_audit's commit throws; the client receives a 500 and has no way to know the reset actually took effect, and may retry believing it failed.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the commit in record_audit with a try/except that logs the error and does not re-raise (audit-log failures should degrade to a logged warning, not abort the caller's already-committed business action), consistent with how decrypt_secret in this same batch treats its own failures as non-fatal.
details.reasoning: Read backend/app/core/audit.py lines 20-36 directly: record_audit wraps db.add + await db.commit() with no try/except, so any exception from the commit (connection failure, pool exhaustion, deadlock) propagates to the caller. Verified the claimed call chain in app/core/users.py: reset_password (262-286), create_user (187), update_user (229), set_user_active (253), and record_login_success (289-295) all commit the real state change in one `async with new_session()` block and then call `await record_audit(...)` afterward, outside that session, unguarded — matching the finding exactly. Verified caller-side impact: admin.py's reset-password route only catches UserNotFoundError, so any other exception becomes an unhandled 500; auth.py's login() calls record_login_success (which updates last_login_at, commits, then calls record_audit) before building/returning the TokenResponse, so a failure purely in the audit write would make a user with valid credentials get a 500 with no tokens issued despite a successful login. Checked app/main.py's only exception handler (DBAPIError) and confirmed via its own docstring that it is scoped narrowly to Postgres data/encoding errors and explicitly does NOT swallow connection failures, which 'still surface as a real 500' — so there is no other safety net. This is a real, verified bug, not a described-but-nonexistent one, and not one of the documented intentional patterns. Severity: the trigger is a narrow transient condition (audit-session commit failing right after the primary session's commit already succeeded) rather than a routine failure, and it causes no data loss/security compromise, but when triggered it produces a hard unhandled 500 on core auth/admin paths (login, password reset, user management) despite the real action already having succeeded — this matches a P2/medium rating well, consistent with the original reviewer's assessment.

titles: RateLimiter.allow()'s INCR-then-EXPIRE is not atomic, so a crash between the two calls leaves a rate-limit key that never expires

details.title: RateLimiter.allow()'s INCR-then-EXPIRE is not atomic, so a crash between the two calls leaves a rate-limit key that never expires
details.actual_behavior: allow() does `current = await r.incr(self._key)` then, only `if current == 1`, does `await r.expire(self._key, self._window_seconds)` (lines 71-73). These are two separate round trips, not wrapped in a MULTI/EXEC transaction or Lua script. If the process is killed/crashes/OOMs between the incr() and the expire() (i.e. exactly when a key was just created with value 1), that key is left in Redis with no TTL at all -- it will never expire and will keep incrementing forever on every subsequent call, permanently exceeding max_calls.
details.failure_scenario: The backend process is killed (OOM, deploy restart, k8s eviction) in the narrow window right after `incr()` returns 1 for `rate_limit:login:someadmin@example.com` but before `expire()` runs. From then on that Redis key has no TTL, so every future login attempt for that email keeps incrementing a counter that never resets -- `allow()` returns False forever, permanently locking out that admin's login, which is exactly the 'hard lockout' the login-rate-limit comments in auth.py say this design was explicitly built to avoid.
details.proposed_fix: Use a single atomic operation, e.g. a Lua script (`INCR` + conditional `EXPIRE` in one EVAL) or `redis.asyncio.Redis.pipeline(transaction=True)` wrapping both calls, or set the key with `SET key 1 EX window NX` first and only fall back to `INCR` when it already exists.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading backend/app/core/cache.py lines 69-74 directly: RateLimiter.allow() does `current = await r.incr(self._key)` and then, only `if current == 1`, a separate `await r.expire(self._key, self._window_seconds)` call. These are two independent Redis round trips with no MULTI/EXEC pipeline, no Lua EVAL, and no SET NX EX pattern anywhere in this file or any caller. This is the textbook non-atomic INCR+EXPIRE rate-limiter race: if the process dies (or even just the expire() call itself times out / hits a transient Redis network error, which is arguably a more common trigger than a full process crash) between the incr() that creates the key (current==1) and the guarded expire() call, the key is left in Redis permanently without a TTL. On every subsequent call current increments again but the `if current == 1` guard is false, so expire() is never retried -- the key is now stuck forever with no TTL.

I verified the claimed cross-file design invariant by reading app/api/routes/auth.py: login() (lines 87-111) and register() (lines 23-50) both instantiate RateLimiter keyed on the attempted email and call allow() before any password check. login()'s own comment (lines 96-99) explicitly says: 'A fixed-window limit, not a hard lockout, so this can never itself become a way to lock a real admin out.' A stuck, TTL-less key does exactly what this comment says must never happen: once current exceeds max_calls (default 10 per config.py's login_rate_limit_max_attempts/window_seconds), allow() returns False forever for that email, since the counter never resets. The same RateLimiter class is also reused unmodified in lookup.py, so the same class of bug affects IOC-lookup rate limits too. I found no pipeline/transaction wrapper, no Lua script, and no compensating cleanup job anywhere in the codebase (grepped all RateLimiter/rate_limit/expire( call sites and the relevant test files) that would prevent or repair a TTL-less stuck key.

This is not one of the listed known-intentional patterns (JWT role re-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED status, AI-narration-only scoring, Basket privacy, security-toolkit/pentest-suite overlap, nmap flag restrictions, or per-call provider status) -- it's a genuine, previously undocumented atomicity gap in a shared caching/rate-limit utility.

Severity: the original P2 (low confidence) is a fair call and I'm keeping it as-is. Arguments for not raising it: the trigger is not attacker-controlled (an attacker cannot force a crash/timeout at the exact right instant), and the blast radius is scoped to a single rate-limit key (one email's login/register bucket or one lookup-limiter key), not a system-wide outage; recovery is a trivial `redis-cli DEL rate_limit:...` or a Redis restart (if Redis has no persistence enabled, a restart wipes the stuck key incidentally). Arguments against downgrading to P3: the failure mode is a genuine denial-of-service against a legitimate account that directly contradicts an explicit, load-bearing design comment in auth.py, requires out-of-band Redis access to fix (not exposed via any admin UI/API in this codebase), and the actual trigger surface is broader than 'process crash' alone -- any transient error/timeout on the specific expire() call permanently dooms that key, which is more plausible in real deployments (network blips, Redis failover, connection pool churn) than a precisely-timed SIGKILL. P2 correctly balances low-but-nonzero likelihood against a real, hard-to-self-recover, invariant-violating impact.

titles: decrypt_secret only catches InvalidToken, not the UnicodeEncodeError a corrupted/non-Fernet ciphertext can raise
decrypt_secret crashes (does not return "") on non-ASCII ciphertext, contradicting its documented never-raise contract

details.title: decrypt_secret only catches InvalidToken, not the UnicodeEncodeError a corrupted/non-Fernet ciphertext can raise
details.actual_behavior: Line 77 does `ciphertext.encode("ascii")` before ever calling Fernet.decrypt, and the try/except only wraps for `InvalidToken` (line 76-84). A genuine Fernet token is always ASCII (urlsafe-base64), so this path is silent for actual Fernet corruption (malformed base64 is itself converted to InvalidToken inside the cryptography library). An ordinary credential change that decrypts fine (e.g. rotating API key A -> B) does NOT hit that branch, so the previous test result for the old value is served as-is for the new, never-tested value.

- Confirmed the route layer (api/routes/runtime.py lines 47 and 148) calls upsert_ai_provider/upsert_ioc_provider directly for ordinary Save requests, so this is reachable via normal admin UI use, not just an edge case.
- Confirmed the frontend (ProviderConfigRow.tsx line 182-185) renders `Last test: {ok ? "OK" : "Failed"} -- {message}` directly from these fields with no "is this stale relative to the current credential" check.
- The repo's own BUG_TRIAGE.md documents BUG-008, same root cause ("upsert_ai_provider() ... never calls record_ai_test_result()"), for the mirror-image direction (stale FAILURE persisting on a now-healthy backend), rated P3, status "OPEN (disclosed, not fixed)". This corroborates the underlying code defect is real, current, and previously identified as unfixed -- not an intentional design choice and not something already patched elsewhere.
- This does not match any of the 8 documented intentional-design exceptions.

Severity: the finding under review describes the more dangerous direction of the same defect -- a stale SUCCESS ("Connected. Key is valid.") surviving a credential rotation, actively asserting a rotated/possibly-broken credential is validated when it has never been exercised. That's worse than BUG-008's stale-failure case (which merely under-reports health on a working backend) because it can cause an admin to trust a broken credential, and given the codebase's designed-in graceful degradation (ProviderStatus reporting rather than raising, per known pattern #8), a bad credential's failure may not surface loudly elsewhere either.
