titles: CVE-enrichment phase of run() is not wall-clock bounded, contradicting the module's own timeboxing guarantee
CVE-enrichment call is not defensively wrapped, despite depending on a callee whose 'never raises' contract isn't fully upheld

details.title: CVE-enrichment phase of run() is not wall-clock bounded, contradicting the module's own timeboxing guarantee
details.actual_behavior: The module docstring (lines 23-24) promises 'Every run is wall-clock timeboxed (_TIMEOUT_SECONDS); the subprocess is killed, not left running, on timeout.' In reality, `timeout_seconds` (from `_timeout_for`, line 160) is only applied to `asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=timeout_seconds)` (line 166), i.e. to the nmap subprocess itself. Once nmap exits, the code enters an unbounded loop (lines 198-249) that calls `await search_cves_by_service(client, product, version)` (line 207) once per open port with an identified product, sequentially, with no aggregate deadline. Each call has only its own internal 15s HTTP timeout (vuln_intel.py); nothing caps the total number of calls or their cumulative wall-clock time.
details.failure_scenario: An analyst runs the 'standard' profile (--top-ports 1000, -sV) against a /28 CIDR (16 hosts, the maximum permitted). If the hosts collectively expose e.g. 200 open ports with an identified product (plausible for a block of internal multi-service servers), the enrichment loop issues 200 sequential NVD lookups. Under NVD rate-limiting/latency (each call can take up to its full 15s timeout), total enrichment time can reach ~3000s (50 minutes) -- more than 3x the already-generous 960s (16 min) subprocess timeout budget for that same target -- while still holding the scan semaphore, delaying or starving other analysts' legitimate scan requests.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the enrichment loop (or the whole post-subprocess processing block) in its own asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=...) derived from the same _timeout_for budget (or a separate enrichment-specific budget), degrading gracefully (skip remaining CVE lookups, keep already-gathered findings) if exceeded.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of nmap_tool.py and vuln_intel.py, plus the semaphore usage in core/security_assessment.py.

1. nmap_tool.py:160-172 applies `timeout_seconds` (from `_timeout_for`) only to `asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=timeout_seconds)` -- i.e. only to the nmap subprocess. No wait_for/deadline exists anywhere else in the file or in `_execute_run` (core/security_assessment.py) wrapping the call to `tool.run()`.
2. After the subprocess exits and XML is parsed, lines 198-249 loop over every host/port and, for each open port with an identified product, sequentially `await search_cves_by_service(client, product, version)` (line 207) with no cap on iteration count and no aggregate deadline around the loop.
3. vuln_intel.py confirms each such call has its own independent 15.0s httpx timeout (line 50) and swallows httpx.HTTPError to return [] -- so each port's enrichment call can legitimately consume up to ~15s under NVD slowness/rate-limiting, and these seconds are purely additive across ports since calls are sequential, not concurrent (no asyncio.gather).
4. core/security_assessment.py line 399 (`async with _scan_semaphore:`) wraps the entire `await tool.run(...)` call per tool, i.e. the semaphore slot is held for the full duration including the unbounded enrichment loop, confirming the claimed resource-contention mechanism (`_MAX_CONCURRENT_SCANS = 4` at line 73).
5. The math checks out: `_timeout_for` scales up to min(num_addresses,8) = 8x for a /28 (16 addresses), giving a 960s subprocess budget (lines 69-70), while a plausible 200-open-port-with-product /28 scan could add up to ~3000s of sequential enrichment on top -- 3x+ the subprocess budget itself.
6. This is not one of the 8 documented intentional patterns (it isn't AI narration, provider-status graceful degradation, JWT role re-derivation, basket visibility, Security-Assessment-vs-Pentest overlap, exploit gating, or nmap flag restriction), and there is no comment anywhere in nmap_tool.py acknowledging the enrichment phase is deliberately excluded from the timebox -- the module docstring (lines 23-24) states the guarantee unconditionally and the code does not fully deliver it.

Severity: P2 is appropriate, matching the original reviewer. It's a genuine contradiction between documented behavior and actual behavior with a real (if scenario-dependent) availability impact -- a slow/rate-limited NVD can hold one of only 4 concurrent scan-semaphore slots for tens of minutes beyond the documented budget, delaying other analysts. It is not P0/P1 because each individual call is still bounded (15s), the loop is not literally infinite/unkillable, a manual cancel still works correctly during the enrichment phase (CancelledError propagates normally to _execute_run's handler), and the impact is confined to the security-assessment scan-concurrency subsystem rather than the whole app, data integrity, or a security boundary.

details.title: CVE-enrichment call is not defensively wrapped, despite depending on a callee whose 'never raises' contract isn't fully upheld
details.actual_behavior: cves = await search_cves_by_service(client, product, version) is called with no try/except. search_cves_by_service (app/security_assessment/vuln_intel.py) only catches httpx.HTTPError around the request/raise_for_status(); the subsequent payload = response.json() (vuln_intel.py line 56) is unguarded. If the HTTP call returns a 200 status with a non-JSON body (e.g. an intercepting proxy/captive-portal page, a malformed/degraded NVD response), response.json() raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError subclass), which is not an httpx.HTTPError and is therefore not caught by vuln_intel.py, and propagates straight through nmap_tool.py's run() uncaught.
details.failure_scenario: A self-hosted deployment sits behind a corporate egress proxy that returns an HTML error/captive-portal page with HTTP 200 for the NVD API host (common in locked-down enterprise networks, which is exactly this platform's stated self-hosted deployment target). The first open port with an identified product triggers this on the first CVE lookup; the resulting unhandled JSONDecodeError aborts the whole assessment run (marked FAILED), including discarding results from any other tools run alongside nmap in the same request, rather than degrading gracefully to 'no CVE match' for that one finding as the enrichment step is supposed to do.
details.proposed_fix: Either fix vuln_intel.py to catch ValueError/json.JSONDecodeError (and ideally validate payload is a dict before calling .get) alongside httpx.HTTPError, or wrap the call site here (line 207) in a defensive try/except that treats any enrichment failure as 'no CVEs found' rather than propagating.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of both files. vuln_intel.py's search_cves_by_service (lines 45-56): the try/except only wraps the client.get()/raise_for_status() call and catches httpx.HTTPError (lines 53-54); response.json() at line 56 sits OUTSIDE that try block. A 200-status response with a non-JSON body (e.g. a captive-portal/proxy interstitial page) makes raise_for_status() pass silently and response.json() raise json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError, not an httpx.HTTPError), which is not caught anywhere in the function -- directly contradicting the function's own docstring promise (lines 34-39) that it "Never raises for an ordinary no-results/network failure." nmap_tool.py's call site (lines 206-207, `cves = await search_cves_by_service(client, product, version)`) has no try/except, so the exception propagates straight out of run(), violating base.py's abstract contract (lines 87-93: "Must never raise... so one tool's failure never aborts the others in the same run").

I traced one level further than the original finding: in core/security_assessment.py's _execute_run, tool.run() calls happen inside a loop (lines 397-402) wrapped by a single `except Exception as exc` (line 431) that marks the whole SecurityAssessmentRun FAILED and returns -- and tool_results (successful findings from any other tools already run in that same request, e.g. dns/tls/http-headers tools) are only ever persisted in the block AFTER that loop completes (lines 454-482), so they are never written to the DB if nmap's enrichment call raises partway through. This exactly matches the claimed failure scenario: one bad CVE-lookup response destroys the entire multi-tool run's results, not just that one finding.

I also confirmed reachability is not a rare edge case: the "standard" and "web" nmap profiles both pass -sV (version detection, nmap_tool.py lines 91-93), so `product` is populated on essentially any normal scan of a host with identifiable services, meaning the vulnerable code path is hit routinely -- only the specific "200 status with non-JSON body" network condition is the narrower part of the trigger, and that is a real, known pattern for enterprise/self-hosted deployments behind SSL-inspecting or category-blocking proxies (this project's stated deployment target per the module's own safety-boundary docstring).

I'm upgrading severity from the reviewer's P3 to P2: the blast radius is not "one enrichment field missing" but total loss of an entire multi-tool assessment run's results, and the failure is deterministic/repeatable (every retry against the same target from the same network fails identically) until the code is fixed -- effectively breaking the nmap tool, and any run bundling it with other tools, for affected self-hosted/enterprise deployments rather than being a one-off transient glitch.

titles: asyncio.wait_for timeout does not stop the underlying blocking socket work in _connect_sync, leaking a thread + open socket
timedelta.days truncation overstates elapsed time for recently-expired certificates by up to a full day

details.title: asyncio.wait_for timeout does not stop the underlying blocking socket work in _connect_sync, leaking a thread + open socket
details.actual_behavior: `_connect_sync` runs two full sequential blocking socket/TLS operations (each with its own `_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`=15s socket timeout) inside a single `asyncio.to_thread` call, wrapped by `asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=_TIMEOUT_SECONDS + 5)` (20s total). `asyncio.to_thread` schedules the function on the default `ThreadPoolExecutor`; when `wait_for` times out it cancels the *awaiting* task, but a `run_in_executor` future backing a thread that has already started cannot actually be stopped -- the thread keeps running both blocking connect/handshake calls to completion in the background, regardless of the coroutine having already returned a TIMEOUT ProviderResult to the caller.
details.failure_scenario: Scanning a target whose TLS port accepts the TCP connection but then stalls during the handshake (or during the second 'strict' verification connection) for close to/over 15s on each of the two sequential connection attempts: the coroutine returns a TIMEOUT result to the API caller after ~20s as expected, but the background thread keeps both sockets open and keeps running for up to another ~10-30s past that, consuming a slot in Python's shared default thread-pool executor (default size ~`min(32, cpu_count+4)`) the whole time. Multiple concurrent scans against slow/hanging targets can exhaust that shared pool, silently delaying every other unrelated `asyncio.to_thread` call in the process (including other tools/routes that rely on the same default executor) until each abandoned thread eventually finishes or the OS-level socket timeout fires.
details.proposed_fix: Use a native asyncio TLS connection (`asyncio.open_connection(..., ssl=...)` / `loop.create_connection`) instead of a blocking socket in a thread, so cancellation actually closes the transport; or run `_connect_sync` in a dedicated, size-bounded executor and explicitly close the raw socket object from the calling coroutine on timeout so the blocked syscall unblocks promptly.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading tls_tool.py lines 52-94 directly. `_connect_sync` (lines 52-74) performs two sequential blocking `socket.create_connection(...)` + TLS `wrap_socket(...)` calls, each independently bounded only by its own 15s socket timeout (`_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), so the function's own worst-case runtime is not tightly capped -- a stalled connect and/or a stalled handshake read on each of the two sequential attempts can push real elapsed time well past the wrapper's 20s cutoff. This is dispatched via `asyncio.to_thread(_connect_sync, host, port)` (line 90), which under the hood is `loop.run_in_executor(None, ...)` on the default ThreadPoolExecutor, wrapped in `asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=_TIMEOUT_SECONDS + 5)`. This is a genuine, well-documented asyncio/executor limitation, not a misreading: `wait_for`'s timeout cancels the *awaiting* Task/Future, and that cancellation is forwarded to the backing `concurrent.futures.Future` via `.cancel()` -- but `Future.cancel()` only succeeds while the future is still PENDING (queued, not yet picked up by a worker thread). Once a worker thread has started executing `_connect_sync` (which happens almost immediately for any live target), `cancel()` returns False and the running thread cannot be interrupted from the coroutine side -- there is no cooperative check or socket close that would unblock the blocking syscall. The coroutine returns a TIMEOUT `ProviderResult` to the caller at ~20s while the thread and its open socket(s) keep running in the background until the socket's own timeout eventually fires. This is not one of the 8 documented intentional patterns (none concern role claims, provider statuses, AI narration, basket visibility, pentest/security-assessment overlap, or nmap flags). Cross-checking app/providers/whois_rdap.py shows this codebase's own authors are explicitly aware that `asyncio.to_thread` executor slots can only be bounded by an inner socket-level timeout, not by outer coroutine cancellation ('so this can't hang the to_thread executor slot indefinitely either way') -- yet tls_tool.py's inner timeout (up to roughly 30-60s worst case across two sequential blocking connections) is not tightly matched to its outer wait_for timeout (20s), leaving exactly the leak window that pattern is meant to avoid. I also confirmed via app/core/security_assessment.py that tools within one run execute sequentially, but `start_run` spawns each run as an unbounded background task via `_spawn_background` with no global concurrency limiter, so multiple concurrent runs against slow/hanging TLS targets is realistic, and leaked threads consume slots in the same default ThreadPoolExecutor shared by other to_thread users in the process (whois_rdap.py, bedrock_client.py), plausibly delaying unrelated features. Given the platform's purpose is investigating potentially-malicious IOCs, a target that accepts a TCP connection then stalls during the TLS handshake (a trivial tarpit listener) is an easy, realistic trigger. Impact is real but bounded/self-recovering (each leaked thread terminates once its own socket timeout eventually fires; no unbounded growth, no crash, no memory leak), and matters mainly under concurrent-scan load or an adversarial slow target -- consistent with the originally claimed P2 rather than a P0/P1 crash/compromise bug or a trivial P3/P4 cosmetic issue.

details.title: timedelta.days truncation overstates elapsed time for recently-expired certificates by up to a full day
details.actual_behavior: `days_until_expiry = (not_after - now).days` and the expired-cert message uses `-days_until_expiry` as the number of days ago the cert expired. Python's `timedelta` normalizes negative deltas so that `.days` is floored toward negative infinity (e.g. a delta of -5 minutes has `.days == -1`, confirmed by direct execution: `timedelta` for `now - 5min - now` prints '-1 day, 23:55:00', `.days == -1`).
details.failure_scenario: A certificate expired 5 minutes before the scan runs. `days_until_expiry` is `-1` (not `0`), so the finding description reads 'The certificate for {host} expired 1 day(s) ago', overstating the actual elapsed time (5 minutes) by nearly a full day. This misleads an analyst triaging how stale/urgent the expiry is, even though the `high` severity classification itself (based on `days_until_expiry < 0`) happens to still be correct.
details.proposed_fix: Compute elapsed/remaining time from `delta.total_seconds()` (e.g. `days_expired = int((-delta.total_seconds()) // 86400)` for the expired branch) instead of relying on `timedelta.days`, which floors toward negative infinity rather than truncating toward zero.
details.reasoning: Verified by reading tls_tool.py lines 99-116 and by direct execution of the exact Python semantics involved. Code: `days_until_expiry = (not_after - now).days` at line 102, and for the expired branch (lines 108-116) the description uses `-days_until_expiry` as the number of days ago the cert expired. Python's timedelta normalizes so 0 <= seconds < 86400, meaning .days floors toward negative infinity for negative deltas rather than truncating toward zero. Confirmed via `py -3`: a cert that expired 5 minutes ago produces `timedelta(-1 day, 23:55:00)`, `.days == -1`, so `-days_until_expiry == 1`, and the finding text reads 'expired 1 day(s) ago' when only 5 minutes have actually elapsed. Further confirmed the bug is broader than the 'recently-expired' framing suggests: a cert expired 10 days and 5 hours ago yields `.days == -11`, so the message says 'expired 11 day(s) ago' -- overstated by a full day whenever the elapsed time isn't an exact multiple of 24h from the current instant, which in practice is almost always the case for any expired cert. This is a genuine, verified logic error, and it is not one of the documented intentional design patterns (it doesn't touch role/JWT derivation, provider status semantics, AI narration guardrails, Basket visibility, Security-Assessment-vs-Pentest overlap, or Nmap flag safety). Impact is limited to a human-readable description string: it does not change the `severity="high"` classification (still correctly driven by `days_until_expiry < 0`), does not affect which findings are generated, and does not affect any downstream security decision -- it only makes the 'how many days ago' text in the report slightly misleading for triage/urgency framing, in the direction of overstating staleness. That matches a low-severity, cosmetic-but-real correctness bug, consistent with the original reviewer's P3 rating; the proposed fix (compute from total_seconds() and truncate toward zero) is a reasonable, minimal correction. I concur with P3.

titles: response.json() and payload parsing sit outside the try/except, contradicting the function's own 'never raises' guarantee

details.title: response.json() and payload parsing sit outside the try/except, contradicting the function's own 'never raises' guarantee
details.actual_behavior: The `try/except httpx.HTTPError` block (lines 45-54) only covers the network request and `raise_for_status()`. `response.json()` (line 56) and the subsequent `payload.get("vulnerabilities")` / iteration (lines 58-68) run unguarded afterward. `json.JSONDecodeError` (a `ValueError` subclass, not an `httpx.HTTPError`) or an `AttributeError` (if the parsed JSON is not a dict, e.g. a list or null) will propagate out of `search_cves_by_service` uncaught.
details.failure_scenario: NVD's REST API returns HTTP 200 with a non-JSON body (e.g. an HTML maintenance page, a transient CDN/WAF error page, or a truncated response during an outage) or an unexpected JSON shape (e.g. a bare list/null). `response.raise_for_status()` passes (status is 200), so the try block succeeds, but `response.json()` raises `JSONDecodeError`, which propagates unhandled into whatever tool (e.g. nmap_tool's enrichment step) called `search_cves_by_service`, aborting the enrichment (and potentially the whole scan) instead of gracefully degrading to an empty CVE list as documented.
details.proposed_fix: Move `response.json()` and the payload-shape handling inside the try block (or wrap them separately), catching `(ValueError, TypeError, AttributeError)` in addition to `httpx.HTTPError`, and return `[]` on any of them per the documented contract.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of backend/app/security_assessment/vuln_intel.py lines 45-69: the try/except at lines 45-54 catches only httpx.HTTPError around the request and raise_for_status(). response.json() (line 56) and the payload.get("vulnerabilities") iteration (lines 58-68) execute unguarded afterward. A 200 response with a non-JSON body raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError, not httpx.HTTPError) and a non-dict JSON payload raises AttributeError on .get() -- neither is caught, directly contradicting the docstring's explicit 'Never raises... returns an empty list' contract.

I also traced the actual caller chain, which the original reviewer only gestured at generically: nmap_tool.py's run() calls search_cves_by_service() at line 207 inside its port loop with no local try/except, and core/security_assessment.py's _execute_run() (line 402) has only asyncio.CancelledError and a generic except Exception (line 431) that marks the ENTIRE SecurityAssessmentRun as FAILED in the DB. So this isn't just a single enrichment call failing gracefully -- it can fail the whole multi-tool scan run because of a transient/malformed response from a third-party API (NVD outage, WAF/CDN HTML interstitial, truncated body, empty body), exactly the kind of network hiccup the docstring says this function is designed to shrug off.

Checked against all 8 documented intentional patterns in this codebase (ProviderStatus degradation, JWT role re-derivation, AI-narration-only, Basket/Case visibility, Security-Assessment-vs-Pentest duplication, nmap flag safety boundary, provider status semantics) -- none apply here; this is a plain list-returning helper with its own explicit no-raise contract, not a ProviderStatus-based component. Severity: real but contained failure mode (loud FAILED status, not silent corruption, no security impact, user can retry) triggered by an infrequent but realistic external-API edge case -- P2 as originally claimed is appropriate, not higher or lower.

titles: Cleanup ordering can raise a foreign-key IntegrityError that masks the real assertion failure and permanently leaks rows

details.title: Cleanup ordering can raise a foreign-key IntegrityError that masks the real assertion failure and permanently leaks rows
details.actual_behavior: The test creates `test_user` via a fixture (lines 145-161) whose teardown unconditionally runs `await db_session.delete(user); await db_session.commit()` (lines 160-161) regardless of test outcome. But the IOCLookup row created by the live POST /api/v1/lookup/stream call is persisted with `requested_by=user.id` (see app/api/routes/lookup.py line ~90), and the FinalAssessmentRecord created for it is persisted with `requested_by=user.id` too (app/api/routes/lookup.py line ~261). Both `ioc_lookups.requested_by` and `final_assessment_records.requested_by` are plain `ForeignKey("users.id")` columns with no `ondelete=` clause anywhere in app/models/lookup.py (confirmed: no `ondelete` string exists anywhere in backend/), so Postgres defaults to RESTRICT/NO ACTION. The only code that deletes the IOCLookup/FinalAssessmentRecord rows is `_delete_lookup_and_dependents(db_session, lookup)`, called as plain test-body code at line 313 -- i.e. only reached if every assertion from line 264 through line 311 passes. If any of those assertions fails (which is exactly what happens if the deterministic-scoring wiring this test exists to guard ever regresses), the AssertionError propagates immediately, line 313 never executes, and the still-referenced IOCLookup/FinalAssessmentRecord rows are left in the DB. pytest then runs the `test_user` fixture's teardown, whose `await db_session.delete(user)` now violates the FK constraint from the still-present ioc_lookups/final_assessment_records row(s), raising an IntegrityError.
details.failure_scenario: Suppose a future regression makes app/ai/service.py stop overwriting risk numbers (the exact bug this test exists to catch), so `lookup.risk_score` ends up 99 instead of the deterministic ~26.0. The assertion `assert lookup.risk_score == expected.overall_risk_score` at line 298 raises AssertionError. `_delete_lookup_and_dependents` at line 313 never runs. pytest then tears down `test_user` (lines 160-161): `await db_session.delete(user)` fails with `IntegrityError: update or delete on table "users" violates foreign key constraint "ioc_lookups_requested_by_fkey"` (and/or the final_assessment_records equivalent), which is reported as a teardown ERROR on top of the original assertion FAILURE, obscuring the real signal in CI output. Both the IOCLookup row (plus its cascaded provider_results/ai_summaries/correlation_edges/evidence_items rows), the FinalAssessmentRecord row, and the User row are left permanently in the shared docker-compose Postgres instance (the commit that would have deleted the user is rolled back by the IntegrityError), accumulating garbage on every failed run.
details.proposed_fix: Move `_delete_lookup_and_dependents(db_session, lookup)` into a try/finally around the test body (or into the test_user fixture's own teardown, deleting any IOCLookup/FinalAssessmentRecord rows referencing user.id before deleting the user), matching the guaranteed-cleanup pattern already used in test_lookup_export_permissions.py.
details.reasoning: Verified by reading the actual files. In test_deterministic_scoring.py, the `test_user` fixture (lines 145-161) unconditionally deletes the user in its teardown (`await db_session.delete(user); await db_session.commit()`) with no try/finally protecting it. The live POST /api/v1/lookup/stream call persists an IOCLookup with requested_by=user.id (confirmed in app/api/routes/lookup.py line 90) and a FinalAssessmentRecord with requested_by=user.id (line 261). Confirmed in app/models/lookup.py that both requested_by columns are plain ForeignKey("users.id") with no ondelete, and grepped the entire backend (including alembic/versions/*.py migrations that actually define the real DB constraints) for 'ondelete' -- none exists outside .venv_test site-packages (library internals, irrelevant). Postgres therefore defaults to NO ACTION/RESTRICT on that FK. There is also no relationship on the User model cascading deletes to IOCLookup/FinalAssessmentRecord, and app/core/db.py's new_session() is a plain session with no rollback-only wrapper, so the app's writes are genuinely persisted, not implicitly undone at test end. `_delete_lookup_and_dependents` (lines 225-233) is invoked only as the literal last line of the test body (line 313), after nine unprotected `assert` statements (lines 264-311) -- there is no try/finally around it. If any of those assertions fails (e.g. the exact deterministic-scoring regression this test exists to catch), the AssertionError propagates immediately, line 313 never executes, and the IOCLookup/FinalAssessmentRecord rows referencing user.id remain. Pytest then tears down the test_user fixture, whose unconditional delete of the user row raises IntegrityError against the still-referencing rows, producing a secondary teardown ERROR alongside the original assertion FAILURE and leaving the user/lookup/assessment rows permanently orphaned in the shared docker-compose Postgres instance. I also confirmed the sibling file test_lookup_export_permissions.py does use a guaranteed-cleanup pattern (try/finally around _make_user/_delete_user, plus fixture-teardown-based bare_lookup cleanup), supporting the reviewer's claim that this file deviates from an established safer pattern already in use in the same test suite. This is a genuine resource-lifecycle bug in test cleanup ordering, not one of the eight documented intentional design patterns. Severity: confined to integration-test infrastructure (no production code path), so P0/P1 would be too high, but it causes real, non-self-healing DB pollution in a long-lived shared Postgres plus confusing/noisy CI output exactly in the failure scenario the test exists to safeguard -- consistent with the originally claimed P2.

titles: Test only overrides REDIS_URL/checks Redis reachability, but the orchestrator it exercises unconditionally needs a real Postgres connection too, causing 5 of 6 tests to error out
clean_redis_cache fixture nulls out the shared Redis connection pool without ever closing it

details.title: Test only overrides REDIS_URL/checks Redis reachability, but the orchestrator it exercises unconditionally needs a real Postgres connection too, causing 5 of 6 tests to error out
details.actual_behavior: The module docstring (lines 1-16) and the skip marker (lines 48-51) claim 'The only real infrastructure dependency is Redis'. The autouse session fixture `_point_app_settings_at_host_redis` (lines 219-236) only overrides `REDIS_URL` / clears the `get_settings` cache; it never sets `DATABASE_URL` nor rebuilds `app.core.db`'s `_engine`/`_SessionLocal`, the way every sibling integration test that touches DB-backed code does (e.g. test_lookup_stream_persistence.py lines 57-97, test_dashboard_api.py, test_lookup_export_permissions.py, test_deterministic_scoring.py all explicitly set DATABASE_URL to the host-published Postgres port and recreate `db_module._engine`). However, `app.providers.orchestrator.run_all_providers()` (imported at line 30) now unconditionally calls `await get_ioc_provider_snapshot()` (orchestrator.py line 116) whenever the filtered `applicable` provider list is non-empty; that function (app/core/runtime_config.py get_ioc_provider_snapshot, lines 383-401) opens `app.core.db.new_session()`, whose engine was built at MODULE IMPORT time (app/core/db.py lines 15-23) from the default `database_url` = `postgresql+asyncpg://ioc:ioc@postgres:5432/ioc_intel` -- the in-network-only 'postgres' hostname, exactly analogous to the 'redis' hostname problem this file's own fixture docstring describes and fixes, but for Postgres instead. Since this test file never overrides that hostname/port and only starts Redis per its documented `docker compose up -d redis` instructions, any attempt to open that session fails (DNS/connection error) from the host test process.
details.failure_scenario: Run the suite exactly as documented (`docker compose up -d redis`, then `pytest app/tests/integration/test_lookup_flow.py` from the host). test_providers_run_concurrently_not_sequentially, test_partial_failure_does_not_block_other_providers, test_streaming_variant_yields_as_completed_and_isolates_failure, test_second_lookup_is_served_from_cache_and_skips_http_call, and test_not_configured_provider_short_circuits_without_http_call all pass at least one IPV4-supporting provider, so `applicable` is non-empty and `run_all_providers` calls `get_ioc_provider_snapshot()` before ever reaching the httpx.AsyncClient/task fan-out; that call raises an unhandled DB connection error (e.g. name-resolution failure on 'postgres') that propagates straight out of the async generator, so `await run_all_providers_collected(...)` / `async for result in run_all_providers(...)` raises inside the test body and every one of those 5 tests errors out rather than exercising the concurrency/cache/error-isolation behavior they claim to test. Only test_unsupported_ioc_type_is_filtered_before_dispatch survives, because its single provider doesn't support IPV4, so `applicable` is empty and `run_all_providers` returns before ever reaching the snapshot call (orchestrator.py lines 106-107).
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the actual code. test_lookup_flow.py's docstring (lines 11-16) and skip marker (48-51) claim Redis is the only real infra dependency, and its sole autouse session fixture _point_app_settings_at_host_redis (219-236) only overrides REDIS_URL / clears get_settings' cache -- it never touches DATABASE_URL or app.core.db's _engine/_SessionLocal, unlike the sibling test_lookup_stream_persistence.py (lines 57-97), which explicitly rebuilds db_module._engine/_SessionLocal for exactly this reason and documents why (db.py builds its engine at MODULE IMPORT time). I verified app/core/db.py: _engine = create_async_engine(_settings.database_url, ...) at module scope (lines 15-22), and Settings.database_url defaults to postgresql+asyncpg://ioc:ioc@postgres:5432/ioc_intel (config.py line 39) -- the in-network-only 'postgres' hostname; there is no .env in backend/ and no conftest.py anywhere under backend/app/tests (verified via find), so nothing rewrites DATABASE_URL before db.py is imported when this file is collected/run standalone. I then verified app/providers/orchestrator.py's run_all_providers: it filters `applicable = [p for p in candidates if p.supports(ioc_type)]` and returns early only if applicable is empty (lines 104-107); otherwise it unconditionally calls `snapshot = await get_ioc_provider_snapshot()` (line 116) BEFORE any cache check or httpx client work. get_ioc_provider_snapshot (runtime_config.py 383-401) does `async with new_session() as db: await db.execute(select(...))`, which opens a real connection via the wrongly-hostnamed engine. BaseProvider.supports() (base.py line 129-130) checks only ioc_type membership, not configured/requires_key -- confirmed by reading base.py -- so even the 'not configured' fake provider (which supports IPV4) lands in `applicable` and triggers the snapshot call before ever reaching its NOT_CONFIGURED short-circuit in run(). Walking through all six tests: the five that pass an IPV4-supporting provider (concurrency, partial-failure, streaming, cache, not-configured) all populate a non-empty `applicable` and thus call get_ioc_provider_snapshot() -> new_session() against the unreachable 'postgres' hostname before doing anything else, so they'd error with a DB connection/DNS failure exactly as claimed. Only test_unsupported_ioc_type_is_filtered_before_dispatch uses a DOMAIN-only provider against an IPV4 lookup, so `applicable` is empty and run_all_providers returns before line 116 -- it alone survives. This exactly matches the claimed 5-error/1-pass split, and the root-cause chain (module-import-time engine bound to an unresolvable in-network hostname, never overridden by this file's Redis-only fixture) is real and directly analogous to the Redis problem this same file explicitly fixes. I am downgrading severity from P1 to P2: this is a test-infrastructure defect confined to a non-production integration test file (it does not affect production behavior, user-facing functionality, security, or data), even though it is a significant defect within that scope (it silently invalidates 5/6 of the file's tests when run exactly per its own documented instructions, undermining confidence in the concurrency/cache/error-isolation guarantees it claims to verify).

details.title: clean_redis_cache fixture nulls out the shared Redis connection pool without ever closing it
details.actual_behavior: The fixture explicitly creates its own short-lived `client` for flushing keys and correctly calls `await client.aclose()` on it (line 267). But for the separate, module-global `cache_module._pool` object (the connection pool that `app.core.cache.get_redis()` lazily creates and that the code-under-test actually uses via `get_cached_result`/`set_cached_result` during the test body), the fixture only does `cache_module._pool = None` (lines 255 and 268) both before and after the test, dropping the Python reference without ever calling `.aclose()`/`.close()` on the underlying `aioredis.Redis` object that reference pointed to.
details.failure_scenario: Any test in this file that actually reaches provider dispatch (once the DB issue above is fixed) causes `get_redis()` to lazily create a new pooled `aioredis.Redis` client bound to that test's event loop; at teardown this fixture discards the reference via `cache_module._pool = None` without closing it, relying on GC to eventually tear down the underlying asyncio transport/sockets. Across a full test run (6 tests, each creating a fresh pool because `_pool is None` forces recreation) this leaves several un-gracefully-closed Redis connections per run, which typically surfaces as 'Unclosed connection'/'Task was destroyed but it is pending' warnings and, in a larger suite or CI run with many such files, can contribute to file-descriptor/connection exhaustion.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading both files. app/core/cache.py defines a module-global `_pool: Optional[aioredis.Redis]` created lazily inside get_redis() and used by get_cached_result()/set_cached_result(), which are in turn called from app/providers/orchestrator.py's _run_with_policy() on every provider dispatch (cache-check at the top, and cache-populate on OK results). test_lookup_flow.py's autouse `clean_redis_cache` fixture (lines 239-268) creates its own separate local `client` purely for flushing provider_cache:fake_* keys and correctly closes that local client via `await client.aclose()` (line 267). However, for the actual `cache_module._pool` object -- the one get_redis() lazily creates and that the code-under-test uses during the test body -- the fixture only does `cache_module._pool = None` (lines 255 and 268), dropping the reference without ever calling `.aclose()`/`.close()` on the underlying aioredis.Redis object. This is not hypothetical: several tests in the file (test_providers_run_concurrently_not_sequentially, test_partial_failure_does_not_block_other_providers, test_streaming_variant_yields_as_completed_and_isolates_failure, test_second_lookup_is_served_from_cache_and_skips_http_call) call run_all_providers_collected/run_all_providers directly, which unconditionally routes through _run_with_policy -> get_cached_result/set_cached_result -> get_redis(), so a real pooled client bound to that test's event loop is created and then discarded ungracefully at teardown. This matches a genuine resource-leak anti-pattern (undrained connection pool relying on GC/refcounting instead of an explicit graceful close), and is distinct from the get_redis()-internal loop-mismatch recreation logic in app/core/cache.py (which handles reuse across loops but has nothing to do with gracefully closing a discarded pool). That said, real-world impact is modest: this is test-only fixture code (not a production code path), the fixture teardown runs while the same test's event loop is still open so refcount-based cleanup of non-cyclic parts often reclaims the socket promptly, and the actual observable effect is at worst noisy 'Unclosed connection'/pending-task warnings across a handful of tests in one file rather than a production-facing leak or reliable CI failure. That impact profile is consistent with the claimed P3 (minor, non-blocking hygiene issue), so I'm keeping the severity as originally assessed rather than upgrading or downgrading it.

titles: test_ollama_connect_error_is_reported_cleanly relies on real OS socket behavior rather than mocking the transport failure, and the implementation only catches one of two plausible exception types
Bedrock has only one test (missing-credentials); the real boto3 call, its ClientError-code mapping, and the shared os.environ bearer-token mutation are completely untested

details.title: test_ollama_connect_error_is_reported_cleanly relies on real OS socket behavior rather than mocking the transport failure, and the implementation only catches one of two plausible exception types
details.actual_behavior: This test deliberately makes a real TCP connection attempt to http://localhost:1 with no respx mock installed (per its own comment), assuming that will raise httpx.ConnectError, which is what `_check_ollama`'s `except httpx.ConnectError` (connection_test.py line 355) specifically catches to produce the 'Could not reach Ollama...' message the test asserts on.
details.failure_scenario: On a host/container/sandbox where connecting to an unused loopback port stalls instead of immediately refusing (e.g. some restrictive network namespaces or virtualized loopback layers), httpx would raise ConnectTimeout (a TimeoutException) instead of ConnectError. `_check_ollama`'s except clause wouldn't catch that, so it would propagate to `_timed()`'s outer `except httpx.TimeoutException`, producing message 'Request timed out.' instead of 'Could not reach Ollama...', and the assertion `'reach ollama' in result.message.lower()` would fail. Empirically this test passed on the current Windows host, so this is a latent portability risk rather than an observed failure.
details.proposed_fix: Either mock the transport-level failure explicitly (respx side_effect=httpx.ConnectError(...)) instead of relying on real socket behavior, or widen the except clause in _check_ollama to also cover httpx.ConnectTimeout with the same friendly message.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct file inspection. test_ollama_connect_error_is_reported_cleanly (lines 532-539 of test_ai_connection_test.py) is the only error-path test in the file without @respx.mock -- every other ~40 tests use it (grep confirms @respx.mock decorators throughout, none on this test). It deliberately hits a real socket at http://localhost:1 per its own comment. In backend/app/ai/connection_test.py, _check_ollama (lines 333-371) only catches httpx.ConnectError (line 355) to emit the 'Could not reach Ollama...' message the test asserts on; the AsyncClient uses timeout=60 (line 341); the outer _timed() wrapper (lines 38-48) separately catches httpx.TimeoutException (line 42) and emits a different message 'Request timed out.' (line 43). httpx.ConnectTimeout is a TimeoutException, not a ConnectError, so on any host/sandbox where the loopback connect stalls rather than refusing immediately, the test would take the wrong exception path and produce the wrong message, failing the assertion. This exactly matches the reviewer's claimed call chain with no misreading. It is not one of the listed intentional design patterns. Impact is confined to test-suite reliability/flakiness in unusual network environments, not production behavior, and the reviewer's own 'low confidence'/'empirically passed on this host' framing is accurate -- so P4 is the right severity, not an under- or over-statement.

details.title: Bedrock has only one test (missing-credentials); the real boto3 call, its ClientError-code mapping, and the shared os.environ bearer-token mutation are completely untested
details.actual_behavior: test_bedrock_no_credentials_fails_before_any_request is the ONLY bedrock test in the file. No test exercises a successful converse() call, any ClientError code (UnrecognizedClientException/AccessDeniedException/ResourceNotFoundException/ThrottlingException), BotoCoreError handling, or -- most importantly -- the os.environ AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK set/restore logic at all.
details.failure_scenario: _check_bedrock mutates a process-wide global (os.environ) for the duration of a boto3 call and restores it in `finally`. If two 'Test Connection' calls for Bedrock with different bearer tokens run concurrently in the same backend process (e.g. two admins testing different Bedrock credentials at the same time, or a double-submit from one tab), the environment writes/restores from the two coroutines can interleave: request A's boto3.client().converse() call can end up authenticating with request B's bearer token (or vice versa), and the env var can be left restored to the wrong value afterward. This test suite gives no signal about this because no test ever calls _check_bedrock with valid-shaped credentials, let alone concurrently.
details.proposed_fix: Add tests that stub/monkeypatch boto3.client (or use a fake) to cover: a successful converse() response, each mapped ClientError code, and a concurrency test that runs two _check_bedrock(bearer_token=...) calls interleaved (e.g. via asyncio.gather with a synchronization point) to assert os.environ isn't corrupted or crossed between them.
details.reasoning: Verified directly against backend/app/tests/unit/test_ai_connection_test.py and app/ai/connection_test.py. The test file has exactly one Bedrock test (lines 542-547), which only checks the early no-credentials-provided path in _check_bedrock; it never reaches boto3.client(...).converse(). Every other backend (groq, openai, etc.) has multiple respx-mocked HTTP tests covering 200/401/404/429-style responses, but Bedrock's actual network call goes through boto3, not httpx, so respx can't intercept it -- and grepping the whole file confirms there is no boto3/moto/unittest.mock patching anywhere, so no test can exercise a successful converse() call, any of the four mapped ClientError codes (UnrecognizedClientException/AccessDeniedException/ResourceNotFoundException/ThrottlingException), BotoCoreError, or the os.environ['AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK'] set/restore in the try/finally (connection_test.py lines 390-425). That env-var mutation is a genuine process-wide global write guarded only by try/finally with no locking, so concurrent bearer-token-based test-connection calls could plausibly interleave and cross credentials or leave the wrong value restored -- a real, currently-unverified risk, not one of the documented intentional patterns (not NOT_CONFIGURED graceful degradation, not the AI-narration-only rule, not pentest exploit gating, etc.). Severity: this is a coverage gap on a risky code path rather than a demonstrated live failure -- it requires a specific concurrent-admin-testing trigger and is confined to an admin 'test connection' feature, not a hot path -- so P2 (as originally claimed) is appropriate; I don't see grounds to escalate to P0/P1 or downgrade to P3/P4.

titles: _fake_lookup's `provider_results or [default]` pattern silently discards an explicit empty list, making the "no provider results" test vacuous
_fake_lookup's `final_assessment or {defaults}` pattern silently discards an explicit final_assessment=None, making the dedicated crash-regression test a no-op

details.title: _fake_lookup's `provider_results or [default]` pattern silently discards an explicit empty list, making the "no provider results" test vacuous
details.actual_behavior: `provider_results=provider_results or [_fake_provider_result()]` at line 53 means that when a caller passes `provider_results=[]` (an empty list, which is falsy in Python), the expression evaluates to the default single-item list instead. Verified empirically: `_fake_lookup(provider_results=[]).provider_results` returns a one-element list containing the default NVD provider result, not `[]`.
details.failure_scenario: The test never actually runs `_render_csv` against a truly empty provider_results list -- it silently runs the exact same one-provider path as the default fixture (identical to test_render_csv_includes_metadata_and_provider_rows). If a future change to _render_csv broke on an empty provider list (e.g. code assuming at least one row exists, or an off-by-one in the blank-separator-row logic), this dedicated test would not catch it, since the empty-list code path is never actually invoked.
details.proposed_fix: Same fix as the final_assessment issue: use a sentinel default instead of None/or, so an explicitly-passed empty list is honored as-is.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading backend/app/tests/unit/test_lookup_export.py directly.

Line 53: `provider_results=provider_results or [_fake_provider_result()]`. This is the classic Python "falsy sentinel" gotcha: an explicitly-passed empty list `[]` is falsy, so `[] or [default]` evaluates to `[default]`, not `[]`. There is no way for a caller of `_fake_lookup` to actually produce an empty `provider_results` list through this helper.

test_render_csv_handles_no_provider_results (lines 96-99) does exactly that: `lookup = _fake_lookup(provider_results=[])`, intending (per its own inline comment "metadata section still renders") to exercise `_render_csv`'s `for p in lookup.provider_results:` loop (confirmed at line 604 of app/api/routes/lookup.py) with zero iterations. Because of the `or` pattern, `lookup.provider_results` is actually `[_fake_provider_result()]` — a one-element list — so the loop runs once, identically to the default-fixture path already covered by test_render_csv_includes_metadata_and_provider_rows. The test's only assertion, `"CVE-2021-44228" in csv_text`, passes regardless (that string appears in the metadata section written before the provider loop even starts), so the test gives no signal either way about the empty-list code path. This is a genuine vacuous-test bug, not one of the eight documented intentional patterns.

Severity: I agree it's real but consider P2 an overstatement. This defect lives entirely in test code and gates a very simple, low-risk code path — a bare `for p in lookup.provider_results:` loop with no indexing, no off-by-one arithmetic, and no special-casing of the empty case that would plausibly regress silently. The production code being under-tested is trivial enough that the realistic risk of an undetected regression is low. This is a legitimate test-quality/coverage gap worth fixing (e.g., via a sentinel default), but it does not rise to P2-level real-world impact — it's better characterized as P3.

details.title: _fake_lookup's `final_assessment or {defaults}` pattern silently discards an explicit final_assessment=None, making the dedicated crash-regression test a no-op
details.actual_behavior: `_fake_lookup(final_assessment=None, ...)` builds the returned SimpleNamespace with `final_assessment=final_assessment or {<full default assessment dict>}`. Because `None` is falsy, `final_assessment or {...}` evaluates to the default dict whenever the caller passes `final_assessment=None` (there is no way to distinguish "not supplied" from "explicitly None" with this pattern). Verified empirically: `_fake_lookup(final_assessment=None).final_assessment is None` returns `False` -- the resulting object actually carries the full default assessment dict (executive_summary, mitre_mappings, etc.), never `None`.
details.failure_scenario: Because `lookup.final_assessment` is never actually `None` in this test, the test always executes the normal full-assessment PDF-building code path (identical to test_render_pdf_produces_a_real_pdf) instead of the `if not fa` early-return path. If a future change broke the real early-return branch -- e.g. someone changed the guard or introduced a `None.get()` call before it -- this test would keep passing (green in CI) while the documented regression ("HTTP 500 from a None.get() somewhere" for an in-progress investigation) reappears in production, completely undetected.
details.proposed_fix: In _fake_lookup, distinguish 'argument not supplied' from 'explicitly falsy' via a sentinel default instead of None, e.g. `_UNSET = object()` as the parameter default, so `final_assessment=None` is honored as a real None and only the sentinel triggers the default dict.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading both files. In test_lookup_export.py, _fake_lookup(final_assessment=None, ...) (line 42) builds the SimpleNamespace with `final_assessment=final_assessment or {<full default dict>}` (lines 54-70). Since `None` is falsy, `None or {...}` always evaluates to the default dict -- there is no way to make this helper actually return an object whose final_assessment attribute is None. In app/api/routes/lookup.py, _render_pdf's early-return branch is `fa = lookup.final_assessment; if not fa: ... return` (lines 697-702), exactly the branch the docstring of test_render_pdf_handles_missing_final_assessment_gracefully (lines 110-117) says it targets ('not a 500 from a None.get() somewhere'). Because _fake_lookup(final_assessment=None) actually hands back the full default assessment dict, `fa` is truthy in that test, so the test silently runs the same full-assessment code path as test_render_pdf_produces_a_real_pdf and never exercises the `if not fa` guard. This is a genuine, verifiable test-coverage gap: nothing else in the file can produce a lookup with final_assessment=None either (every other call site either omits the arg, getting the same fallback, or passes an explicit non-empty dict), so the `if not fa` branch in production code has zero test coverage despite a dedicated test appearing to cover it. The proposed sentinel-default fix (_UNSET = object()) is a correct, standard remedy.

On severity: this is a test-only defect, not an active production bug -- the production early-return branch itself works fine today; the risk is purely that a future regression to that specific branch would go undetected by this suite. That tempers the P1 claim: P1 typically implies current high customer impact, but here the impact is contingent (a hypothetical future regression) and confined to one PDF-export edge case (in-progress/failed investigations), not a live user-facing failure. P2 (moderate, real, worth fixing promptly) better reflects a concrete false-sense-of-coverage gap around a documented prior 500-crash bug, without overstating it as equivalent to an active production-impacting defect.

titles: Audit Log tab never renders actor_email, so no entry shows who performed the action

details.title: Audit Log tab never renders actor_email, so no entry shows who performed the action
details.actual_behavior: The Audit Log tab renders only entry.timestamp, entry.action, and entry.detail. It never references entry.actor_email, even though AuditLogEntry (lib/types.ts) carries actor_email as a distinct field, and the backend (backend/app/core/audit.py record_audit, and every call site in backend/app/core/users.py, runtime_config.py, security_assessment.py, pentest/orchestrator.py) deliberately keeps `detail` as an actor-agnostic human-readable description (per audit.py's own docstring: 'detail must be human-readable description text ONLY') while passing the actor separately as actor_user_id/actor_email.
details.failure_scenario: Admin-A disables user bob@x.com and Admin-B disables user alice@x.com. Both produce rows with action="user.disable" and detail text like "Disabled user 'bob@x.com'."/"Disabled user 'alice@x.com'." -- an administrator reviewing the Audit Log tab to answer 'who disabled this account / who last touched this AI provider config' cannot determine the actor from anything rendered on screen, despite that data being fetched over the wire in every getAuditLog() response and being the entire point of an audit trail (accountability).
details.reasoning: Verified directly against frontend/app/admin/page.tsx lines 192-203: the audit log list item template interpolates only entry.timestamp, entry.action, and entry.detail; entry.actor_email is never referenced. Confirmed AuditLogEntry in frontend/lib/types.ts (line 123-129) declares actor_email as a distinct nullable field, and backend/app/core/audit.py's list_audit_log() includes actor_email in every returned row (so the data is fetched by the frontend, just not rendered). Confirmed via audit.py's docstring ('detail must be human-readable description text ONLY') and every call site inspected in users.py, runtime_config.py, and security_assessment.py that `detail` describes the action's target/object (e.g. \"Disabled user 'bob@x.com'.\", \"Configured AI provider 'openai'.\") and never the actor -- the actor is passed as a separate actor_user_id/actor_email argument to record_audit for every call site with a real human actor (user.create/update/enable/disable/password_reset, auth.login, ai_provider.configure/activate, ioc_provider.configure). The claimed failure scenario (two admins performing the same action type on different targets produce indistinguishable-by-actor rows) is real and directly reproducible from the code.
