I concur with the original P2 rating -- no basis to elevate to P0/P1 (no exploit, no data loss, no auth bypass) nor to downgrade below P2 (it's not cosmetic; it defeats the actual purpose of the feature).

titles: handleStatusChange has no try/catch; a failed updateCase() silently swallows the error
handleStatusChange/handleAddNote discard the mutation's response body and re-fetch the whole case instead
Shared `error` state causes an unrelated action failure to replace the entire case view

details.title: handleStatusChange has no try/catch; a failed updateCase() silently swallows the error
details.actual_behavior: `await updateCase(caseId, { status })` is not wrapped in try/catch. If updateCase() throws (it throws `new Error("Failed to update case")` on any non-ok response, per lib/api.ts's updateCase), the exception becomes an unhandled promise rejection from the onChange handler. reload() on line 45 is never reached, no `error` state is set, and the <select> (a controlled input bound to `caseDetail.status`) silently reverts to the unchanged value on next render with zero visible feedback.
details.failure_scenario: Analyst leaves a case detail page open past the 30-minute access-token lifetime; the stored refresh token has since been revoked (e.g. they logged out from another tab, or an admin reset their password, both of which bump token_version per lib/api.ts's logout()/authedFetch flow). They pick a new status from the dropdown: authedFetch's 401->refresh retry fails, updateCase() rejects, and the dropdown just snaps back with no error message, no redirect to /login, nothing in the UI indicating why the change didn't take.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the body in try/catch (mirroring handleAddNote), setError() on failure, and re-throw or ignore only after showing feedback.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading of frontend/app/cases/[id]/page.tsx lines 42-46: handleStatusChange awaits updateCase(caseId, { status }) with no try/catch, unlike the structurally parallel handleAddNote (lines 48-61) which wraps its body in try/catch and calls setError() on failure. Cross-checked lib/api.ts: updateCase (line 478-485) does `if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed to update case")`, and authedFetch (lines 172-183) returns the still-failing (401) response when the refresh-token retry itself fails, so res.ok stays false in exactly the described token-expiry-plus-revoked-refresh scenario. There is no global unhandledrejection handler, toast system, or error boundary anywhere in frontend/ (verified via grep) that would surface this rejection to the user. So any updateCase failure -- expired/revoked session, network error, 500, validation error -- throws inside an async onChange handler with no catch, producing only a console-level unhandled promise rejection; reload() is skipped, setError is never called, and the controlled <select> (bound to caseDetail.status, which never changes) shows no visible feedback that the status change failed. This is a genuine inconsistency/oversight relative to the sibling handler and a real, if not severe, UX/error-handling gap. Severity: P2 is appropriate -- it's a real papercut with legitimate operational impact (an analyst could believe a case status change took effect when it silently failed, e.g. during an incident), but it's not a security vulnerability, data-loss bug, or crash, and the fix is a small, well-understood mirror of the existing handleAddNote pattern.

details.title: handleStatusChange/handleAddNote discard the mutation's response body and re-fetch the whole case instead
details.actual_behavior: Line 44 (`await updateCase(caseId, { status })`) and line 53 (`await addCaseNote(caseId, noteText.trim())`) both discard the returned CaseDetail, then unconditionally call `reload()` right after, which issues a second GET /cases/{id} request to fetch essentially the same data that was just returned by the mutation.
details.failure_scenario: Not a correctness bug (functionally still ends up consistent), just an avoidable extra round trip on every status change and every note add -- doubles backend load/latency for these two actions.
details.proposed_fix: `setCaseDetail(await updateCase(...))` / `setCaseDetail(await addCaseNote(...))` directly instead of discarding the response and calling reload().
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading both sides of the call chain. Frontend frontend/app/cases/[id]/page.tsx lines 42-46 and 48-61: handleStatusChange awaits updateCase(caseId, { status }) and discards the result, then calls reload(); handleAddNote awaits addCaseNote(caseId, noteText.trim()), discards the result, then calls reload(). reload() (lines 27-32) does a fresh getCase(caseId) -> GET /api/v1/cases/{id}. Checked lib/api.ts: updateCase (PATCH /cases/{id}) and addCaseNote (POST /cases/{id}/notes) both have return type Promise<CaseDetail> and both `return res.json()` from the mutation response, identical shape to getCase's return. Checked the backend (backend/app/api/routes/cases.py): update_case (PATCH handler) and add_case_note (POST /notes handler) both already do their own `_load_case` + `_serialize_case` internally after committing and return the full serialized case object -- the exact same shape/content GET /cases/{id} would produce. So the mutation response genuinely already contains everything reload() would fetch; the second GET is a fully redundant round trip (and a redundant DB re-query with eager-loaded iocs/notes/reports on the backend too). This is not any of the 8 documented intentional patterns -- it's a plain missed-reuse-of-response inefficiency. Impact is correctly scoped as low: it only affects two low-frequency, user-initiated actions (manually changing a case's status via a dropdown, manually adding an analyst note), not a hot path or bulk operation, and causes no correctness issue since the two requests return consistent data. That matches a P4 (trivial/cosmetic-inefficiency) severity -- no basis to raise it to P3 or higher given the low call frequency and absence of any user-visible or correctness effect. Proposed fix (setCaseDetail(await updateCase(...)) / setCaseDetail(await addCaseNote(...)) instead of discard+reload) is straightforward and correct given the confirmed matching response shape.

details.title: Shared `error` state causes an unrelated action failure to replace the entire case view
details.actual_behavior: The component has a single `error` state used for two very different failure modes: (1) the initial `reload()`/getCase() failure in the mount effect, and (2) `handleAddNote`'s catch block (line 56-57) on a failed addCaseNote() call. Both funnel into the same early-return branch at lines 63-71, which unconditionally replaces the *entire* page (status control, IOC list, notes, note form) with just the bare error text -- there is no dismiss/retry affordance, and because the component stays mounted, nothing will clear `error` or re-run reload() automatically.
details.failure_scenario: Analyst is viewing a case with several IOCs and notes already loaded. They type a note and hit "Add Note" during a brief network blip (or a 500 from the backend, or the same refresh-token-revoked scenario as the sibling finding above). `addCaseNote` throws, `handleAddNote`'s catch sets `error`, and the whole case view -- including all the IOCs and notes that were already successfully loaded -- vanishes and is replaced by a plain error box. The only recovery is a full browser reload, since Next.js client-side navigation won't remount this already-mounted component.
details.proposed_fix: Use two separate state variables (e.g. `loadError` for the mount-time getCase failure that legitimately blocks rendering, and `actionError` for note/status mutation failures that should render as an inline banner above the still-visible caseDetail), analogous to how basket/page.tsx and cases/page.tsx already do it.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct read of C:/Users/User/ioc-intel-platform/frontend/app/cases/[id]/page.tsx. There is exactly one `error` state (line 23) shared between the mount-time `reload()` failure path (line 31, inside the effect at 34-40) and `handleAddNote`'s catch block (lines 56-57) for a failed `addCaseNote()` call. Lines 63-71 do an unconditional early return whenever `error` is truthy: `if (error) { return
...just the error box...
; }` -- this replaces the entire page (BrandHeader, status selector, IOC list, notes list, and the note form itself) with a bare error message, regardless of whether `caseDetail` is already successfully loaded. Cross-checked the comparison claim: basket/page.tsx (lines 109-113) and cases/page.tsx (lines 95-99) both render `{error && (
{error}
)}` as an inline banner ABOVE their still-rendered content -- the item list / case list / forms remain visible and usable. cases/[id]/page.tsx is the outlier: it uses an early-return guard instead of an inline conditional block, which is the actual defect (not just a stylistic inconsistency -- it changes behavior). The 'no recovery without a full reload' claim also checks out: neither the success branch of `reload()` (line 29-31, only sets caseDetail, never clears error) nor the success branch of `handleAddNote` (line 53-55, only clears noteText and re-triggers reload) ever calls `setError(null)`. Once `error` is set by any cause, it is permanently sticky for the life of the mounted component -- there is no dismiss button, retry button, or any code path that resets it, and since the error branch omits the note form entirely, the user has no in-page way to trigger another action that might succeed and incidentally clear it (it wouldn't clear it anyway, per the above). This matches 'the only recovery is a full browser reload' in spirit even if the precise Next.js remount semantics on same-page param navigation are debatable -- the practical dead-end is real. This is a genuine correctness/UX bug, not one of the listed intentional design patterns. Severity: agree with P2 -- it's a real, easily-triggered (any transient network blip or 500 while adding a note) full loss of an already-loaded, non-trivial view (IOCs + notes) for an analyst mid-investigation, with no in-app recovery path, but it causes no data loss/corruption and no security impact, and is recoverable via a full page reload. That lands squarely at moderate/P2, not P0/P1 (no security or data-integrity impact) and not P3/P4 (it's a full, hard-to-recover functional break of the page, not cosmetic).

titles: Unvalidated `next` query param enables a post-login open redirect
Every login failure mode is shown as the identical "Invalid email or password" message

details.title: Unvalidated `next` query param enables a post-login open redirect
details.actual_behavior: `next` is read verbatim from `useSearchParams().get("next")` (defaulting only if literally absent) and passed straight into `router.push(next)` with zero validation that it is a same-origin relative path. Traced into node_modules/next/dist/client/components/app-router.js and router-reducer/reducers/navigate-reducer.js: `push()` builds `new URL(next, location.href)`, and if that URL's origin differs from the current origin (`isExternalURL`), the reducer sets `mpaNavigation = true`, which app-router.js then turns into a real `window.location.assign(canonicalUrl)` -- i.e. Next.js itself performs a full hard navigation to whatever origin `next` resolved to.
details.failure_scenario: An attacker sends a victim `https://<app-host>/login?next=https://evil.example.com` (or the simpler protocol-relative `next=//evil.example.com`, which resolves to the same external origin). The victim, trusting the real domain in the address bar, enters their genuine credentials and submits. The instant `login()` resolves, `router.push(next)` hard-navigates the freshly-authenticated browser to the attacker's site -- useful for a convincing post-login phishing page (e.g. a fake 'please sign in again' or malware-download page) that inherits the credibility of having just come from a real login.
details.proposed_fix: Reject/ignore any `next` value that isn't a same-origin relative path (e.g. require it to start with a single `/` and not `//`, and contain no `:`), falling back to `/` otherwise.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct file read. frontend/app/login/page.tsx line 13 reads `next` verbatim from the query string (`searchParams.get("next") ?? "/"`, defaulting only when absent), and line 26 passes it straight into `router.push(next)` immediately after a successful `login()` call, with no same-origin/relative-path validation anywhere in this file or in `login()` (frontend/lib/api.ts lines 81-92, which only POSTs credentials and writes tokens to localStorage). Traced the claimed Next.js 14.2.15 internals in frontend/node_modules/next/dist/client/components/: app-router.js's useNavigate() builds `new URL(addBasePath(href), location.href)` and flags `isExternalUrl` via a plain origin comparison (isExternalURL, line 95-97); navigate-reducer.js checks that flag and calls handleExternalUrl(), setting `mpaNavigation = true` and `canonicalUrl = url`; app-router.js's Router() then executes `window.location.assign(canonicalUrl)` (lines 396-404) whenever `mpaNavigation` is set and `pendingPush` is true. This exactly matches the reviewer's claimed chain, confirming that `?next=https://evil.example.com` (or `//evil.example.com`) causes a genuine hard navigation to the attacker's origin right after the victim authenticates. This is not one of the eight documented intentional patterns — it's a plain missing-input-validation open redirect. Severity: tokens live in origin-scoped localStorage so they aren't directly exfiltrated by the redirect itself; the real-world impact is a convincing post-login phishing/malware vector rather than direct session theft, which matches a P2 rating (not P0/P1, but not negligible either) — I concur with the original reviewer's P2.

details.title: Every login failure mode is shown as the identical "Invalid email or password" message
details.actual_behavior: `catch { setError("Invalid email or password."); }` takes no error binding at all, so it cannot distinguish a wrong password (401) from a disabled account (403), a rate-limited attempt (429 "Too many login attempts..."), a 5xx, or a pure network failure where `fetch` itself throws because the backend is unreachable. `login()` in lib/api.ts already collapses all of these into one `Error("Login failed")`, and this page collapses that further into a single fixed, credentials-specific string regardless of the real cause.
details.failure_scenario: The backend is briefly unreachable (e.g. mid-restart/mid-deploy) or the account has just tripped the per-email rate limiter after a few attempts. The user submits their correct password; the request fails for a reason having nothing to do with their credentials, yet the UI tells them 'Invalid email or password' -- actively misleading them into repeatedly re-entering a correct password (which, in the 429 case, only prolongs the lockout window) instead of waiting or checking connectivity.
details.proposed_fix: Bind the caught error and branch on it (or on login()'s own thrown message/status) to show distinct messages for network failure, rate-limiting, and disabled-account cases, reserving 'Invalid email or password' for the actual 401 case.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading both sides of the call chain.

frontend/app/login/page.tsx lines 20-32: `catch { setError("Invalid email or password."); }` — the catch clause takes no error binding at all, so it is structurally incapable of distinguishing the cause of the failure. Every failure path sets the exact same string.

frontend/lib/api.ts login() (lines 81-92): `if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Login failed");` — this already discards the HTTP status code and any response body detail, collapsing every non-2xx response into one generic Error. A network failure (fetch itself rejecting because the backend is unreachable) throws a separate, different error that also lands in the same catch.

backend/app/api/routes/auth.py login() (lines 87-129) proves the backend deliberately returns distinct, meaningful statuses that the frontend then throws away:
- 401 "Invalid email or password" — actual bad credentials (the only case the frontend's message is true for)
- 403 "Account disabled" — inactive account
- 429 "Too many login attempts for this account. Try again in under {window} seconds." — a real, tested (test_auth_login_rate_limit.py) per-email rate limiter, explicitly implemented as a non-lockout fixed window specifically so it doesn't lock out a real admin by itself

So the failure scenario is concrete and reachable in this exact codebase, not hypothetical: a user who trips the 429 limiter with a correct password, or whose account is 403-disabled, or who hits the backend mid-restart (network/5xx), is told "Invalid email or password" — which for the 429 case actively encourages exactly the retry behavior that keeps the fixed window rolling. This is not one of the eight documented intentional patterns; it's a straightforward information-loss bug across two layers (api.ts's collapsing throw, then page.tsx's unbound catch discarding even that).

Severity: this is UX/error-handling degradation confined to edge-case failure paths (rate-limit, disabled account, transient outage) — the mainline "correct credentials → logged in" and "wrong password → correctly told so" paths are unaffected, there's no security bypass, data loss, or crash, and a workaround (wait and retry, or contact an admin) always exists. That profile matches a low/minor severity rather than a moderate-or-above functional break, so P3 (as originally claimed) is appropriate; I don't see grounds to raise it to P2 or higher, nor to downgrade it to P4 given the concrete, documented rate-limit-prolongation harm.

titles: AiComparisonPanel ('Analyze with a different AI') is never imported or rendered on the completed-lookup detail page, even though its backing feature is specifically designed for a completed lookup viewed later

details.title: AiComparisonPanel ('Analyze with a different AI') is never imported or rendered on the completed-lookup detail page, even though its backing feature is specifically designed for a completed lookup viewed later
details.actual_behavior: frontend/app/lookup/new/page.tsx imports AiComparisonPanel (line 39) and renders it inside its `isDone && lookupId` block (line 212). frontend/app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx has no import of AiComparisonPanel anywhere and never renders it -- confirmed by grepping the whole app/lookup directory, the component name only appears in new/page.tsx. The analogous `isCompleted && lookupId` block in [id]/page.tsx (lines 223-231) renders VerdictAnalysisPanel/EvidencePanel/PivotPanel/HuntingCenterPanel/InvestigationCopilot but omits AiComparisonPanel entirely.
details.failure_scenario: An analyst finishes a live investigation on /lookup/new?value=... without using 'Analyze with a different AI backend' before navigating away (or the tab is closed/refreshed). Later they open the same investigation via /lookup/{id} (e.g. via the login-redirect `next` param, a saved/shared link, or simply returning to it) -- there is now no UI control anywhere on that page to trigger or view any AI-backend comparison for that lookup, even though the backend fully supports doing so for any COMPLETED lookup by id and the component itself needs nothing but `lookupId`.
details.proposed_fix: Import AiComparisonPanel in frontend/app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx and render `<AiComparisonPanel lookupId={lookupId} />` inside the existing `isCompleted && lookupId` block, matching new/page.tsx's placement.
details.reasoning:
Verified by reading frontend/app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx in full: it imports VerdictAnalysisPanel, EvidencePanel, PivotPanel, HuntingCenterPanel, InvestigationCopilot, InvestigationActions, SecurityAssessmentPanel, etc. (lines 40-46) and renders VerdictAnalysisPanel/EvidencePanel/PivotPanel/HuntingCenterPanel/InvestigationCopilot inside the `isCompleted && lookupId` block (lines 223-231, where `isCompleted = status === "completed"`) — but AiComparisonPanel is never imported or referenced anywhere in this file.

Cross-checked frontend/app/lookup/new/page.tsx: it imports AiComparisonPanel (line 39) and renders `<AiComparisonPanel lookupId={lookupId} />` inside its analogous `isDone && lookupId` block (line 212) — confirming this is a deliberate, working, already-wired feature that the sibling page simply omits.

Confirmed the component's design and backend contract: AiComparisonPanel.tsx's own docstring (lines 3-12) states the feature is meant to let an analyst "re-run JUST the final-assessment AI step" on "an investigation's evidence" that "has been collected" already, comparing backends on durable records fetchable via GET /assessments — and it takes only a `lookupId` prop (no live-stream state). The backend route POST /{lookup_id}/reanalyze (backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py lines 364-408) explicitly rejects any lookup whose `status != LookupStatus.COMPLETED` (line 407-408: "Lookup must be completed before it can be re-analyzed."), i.e. it is designed around exactly the persisted/completed-lookup-by-id scenario that [id]/page.tsx exists to serve, not the live-SSE scenario that new/page.tsx serves.

I also checked whether new/page.tsx offers an alternate path back to an old completed lookup's AiComparisonPanel — it doesn't; its docstring and code confirm it only starts a fresh SSE-streamed investigation from a raw `?value=` query param, never loads an existing lookup by id. So once a user navigates away from a live /lookup/new session (tab closed, refresh, or simply moving on), the only surface that can display that investigation again is /lookup/{id}, which has zero UI path to invoke or view AI-backend comparisons for it, despite the backend fully supporting it and the component needing nothing else. This is a genuine, verified missing-feature gap, not one of the documented intentional patterns.

Severity: P2 is appropriate. It's not a crash, security issue, or data-loss bug — all core investigation data (verdict, evidence, provider results, MITRE mappings, hunting, copilot) remains fully accessible on this page. The gap is confined to one specific secondary feature (cross-backend AI comparison) becoming completely unreachable for any investigation viewed after the live session ends, which is a real but non-critical functional/parity gap. This matches the original reviewer's P2 claim.

titles: isDone is never set on a fatal SSE `error` event, so the UI freezes in a permanent loading state after any live-investigation failure
A whole-pipeline investigation failure leaves the UI showing permanent 'pending/awaiting' skeletons instead of a failed state

details.title: isDone is never set on a fatal SSE `error` event, so the UI freezes in a permanent loading state after any live-investigation failure
details.actual_behavior: `onError` (lines 132-135) only calls `setStreamError(payload.message)`; it never sets `isDone` (or any other 'finished' flag). Per backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py's stream_lookup, the `error` SSE event (line 314) is only ever emitted from the outer exception handler that wraps the ENTIRE pipeline, and after that handler's `finally` block runs, the generator returns with no further `yield` -- i.e. `done` (only emitted at line 291, on the success path immediately after `final_assessment`) is NEVER sent following an `error` event. Because `isDone` therefore stays `false` forever: ThreatScoreGauge (`loading={!isDone}`, line 193) and MitreMatrix/DetectionRulesPanel (`loading={!isDone}`, lines 204/206) show their internal 'Waiting for the final assessment...' spinner permanently, ignoring the fact that a fatal error already happened; the `isDone && lookupId` block (line 210) that renders AiComparisonPanel, VerdictAnalysisPanel, EvidencePanel, PivotPanel, HuntingCenterPanel, InvestigationCopilot, and SecurityAssessmentPanel never renders at all; and the header's 'complete' badge (line 176) never appears.
details.failure_scenario: A live lookup where every provider call succeeds but the final-assessment AI call throws (e.g. Ollama busy/timeout, exactly the scenario the backend's own comments in lookup.py describe as having been confirmed live) -- the backend marks the lookup FAILED and sends an `error` event, then closes the stream normally. The user sees the red streamError banner AND, simultaneously and permanently, spinning 'Waiting for the final assessment...' placeholders in the score gauge/MITRE matrix/detection panel, with no SecurityAssessmentPanel or any of the analysis tools ever appearing -- even though SecurityAssessmentPanel only needs the IOC value/type (already known) and nothing about the failed AI call, per the exact reasoning the sibling page documents for using investigationFinished instead of isCompleted.

details.title: Export JSON/Markdown completely bypasses the dedicated lookup:export permission
details.actual_behavior: handleExportJson (lines 118-125) and handleExportMarkdown (lines 127-134) never call that backend endpoint at all -- they build the file entirely client-side from the `assessment` prop, which is populated purely from GET /api/v1/lookup/{id} (gated only on lookup:read; see frontend/app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx line 103's getLookup() call and the identical pattern in app/lookup/new/page.tsx). Both buttons are rendered unconditionally for every role with no permission check of any kind on the frontend, and there is no server-side check on this path since no request to the export-gated route ever occurs.
details.failure_scenario: A VIEWER role user (lookup:read but NOT lookup:export per ROLE_PERMISSIONS in backend/app/models/user.py lines 71-75) opens any completed lookup's detail page and clicks 'Export JSON' or 'Export Markdown'. The full FinalAssessment (executive summary, MITRE mappings, detection rules, risk score, etc.) is downloaded to disk as a real file with zero permission check -- the exact action lookup:export exists specifically to prevent for this role. The dedicated permission is only enforced for 2 of the 4 export formats.
details.proposed_fix: Either route JSON/Markdown export through a permission-checked backend call (e.g. reuse a lightweight export-permission check before building the blob), or fetch the current user's permission set and conditionally hide/disable the JSON and Markdown buttons for any role lacking lookup:export, matching the PDF/CSV buttons' effective gating.

Confirmed by direct reading of the code, not just the reviewer's description.

frontend/components/dashboard/ExportMenu.tsx lines 118-134: handleExportJson and handleExportMarkdown both early-return only if `assessment` (a prop) is null; otherwise they build a Blob purely client-side (JSON.stringify(assessment) or buildMarkdown(assessment, lookupId)) and call triggerDownload — no fetch, no backend call, no permission check of any kind. Buttons for all four formats (PDF, Markdown, CSV, JSON) are rendered unconditionally at lines 163-174 regardless of role.

Contrast with handleServerExport (lines 136-158), used only for PDF/CSV, which does call POST /api/v1/lookup/{id}/export — the backend route at backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py lines 771-786 is gated on require_permission("lookup:export") with an explicit docstring: "Gated on the dedicated `lookup:export` permission (ADMIN/ANALYST only, per ROLE_PERMISSIONS...) rather than `lookup:read`. VIEWER holds `lookup:read` but not `lookup:export`, and exporting a real [file]... [is] materially different... than viewing JSON in the app."

Confirmed backend/app/models/user.py: Role.VIEWER's permission set (lines 71-72) contains "lookup:read" but not "lookup:export"; ADMIN/ANALYST (lines 50, 64) have both.

Confirmed the data-flow claim: frontend/app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx calls getLookup(lookupId) (line 103), which hits GET /{lookup_id} — gated only on require_permission("lookup:read") per lookup.py line 547 — stores the result into finalAssessment state (line 137), and passes it directly as the `assessment` prop into <ExportMenu lookupId={lookupId} assessment={finalAssessment} /> (line 244). So a VIEWER, who is authorized to read but explicitly NOT authorized to export, can trivially get a downloadable JSON/Markdown file of the full assessment via the client-only export paths, bypassing the specifically-designed lookup:export gate. This is a genuine RBAC bypass, not one of the eight documented intentional patterns (it doesn't match stale-JWT-role, provider-not-configured, AI-narration-only, basket-privacy, toolkit/pentest-suite overlap, nmap-flag-safety, or provider-status patterns).

Severity correction: The original reviewer's confidence is high and the bug is real, but P1 overstates real-world impact. The VIEWER role already has full on-screen access to every field in the assessment via the lookup:read-gated GET endpoint (executive summary, MITRE mappings, detection rules, risk score, etc. are all rendered in the dashboard per FinalAssessmentPanel/RecommendedActionsPanel). The bypass only lets that already-authorized viewer persist the same already-visible data to a local file (or trivially copy/screenshot it) instead of being blocked from producing a file artifact -- it does not expose any additional data, escalate privileges, or leak cross-tenant/cross-user information. It's a policy-compliance/authorization-consistency gap (the intended viewing-vs.-exporting distinction is bypassed for 2 of 4 formats) rather than a confidentiality breach exposing new data. That merits fixing but is more consistent with P2 (real, should be fixed soon, contained/no new data exposure) than P1.

details.title: Server export bypasses the app's shared authedFetch/token-refresh helper
details.actual_behavior: `authHeaders()` (lines 13-16) is a local re-implementation of only the header-building half of lib/api.ts's pattern; `handleServerExport` (lines 136-158) calls `fetch()` directly with it instead of going through lib/api.ts's `authedFetch`, which is the one place in the codebase that catches a 401, calls `refreshAccessToken()`, and retries. A 401 here falls straight into the generic `!res.ok` branch.
details.failure_scenario: An analyst has a lookup page open for longer than the access-token lifetime (30 minutes, per the comment above lib/api.ts's authedFetch) while still holding a valid refresh token -- every other action on the page (loading evidence, asking Copilot questions, etc., all via authedFetch) keeps working transparently. Clicking "Export PDF" or "Export CSV" instead gets a bare 401 and shows "Export failed with status 401.", even though the session is still effectively valid and no other part of the UI would have failed.
details.proposed_fix: Route handleServerExport's fetch through the shared authedFetch (exporting it from lib/api.ts, or adding an exported blob-fetch helper) so it gets the same refresh-and-retry-on-401 behavior as every other API call.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading both files. lib/api.ts defines `async function authedFetch(...)` (line 172, NOT exported) which is the sole place that catches a 401, calls refreshAccessToken(), and retries once (lines 172-183) -- every other exported API helper in that file (getLookup, listLookups, getEvidence, askCopilot, listAssessments, etc.) routes through it. ExportMenu.tsx cannot import authedFetch since it isn't exported, so it locally re-implements only the header-building half as its own `authHeaders()` (lines 13-16, a verbatim duplicate of api.ts's private authHeaders at lines 76-79) and `handleServerExport` (lines 136-158) calls `fetch()` directly with those headers. On a 401 it falls straight into the generic `if (!res.ok)` branch (line 147-150) and shows 'Export failed with status 401.' with no refresh/retry attempt, while every other authenticated action on the same page (loading evidence, Copilot, etc., all via authedFetch) would have transparently refreshed and kept working. This is a genuine cross-file inconsistency, not one of the documented intentional design patterns (none of the 8 listed patterns concern token refresh or this file). Severity: this is a functional/UX auth-adjacent bug, not a security bypass -- it fails closed (shows an error) rather than granting unauthorized access, and a workaround exists (any other action that refreshes the token first, then retry export). But it's highly likely to be hit in normal use, since analysts commonly keep a lookup page open past 30 minutes before exporting a report, so P2 (as originally claimed) is accurate rather than inflated.

details.title: Server export (PDF/CSV) bypasses the app-wide 401 refresh-and-retry pattern
details.actual_behavior: handleServerExport (lines 136-158) uses a raw `fetch()` with its own locally-defined `authHeaders()` (lines 13-16), never calling authedFetch. A 401 response falls through the generic `!res.ok` branch (line 147-150) and shows 'Export failed with status 401' instead of transparently refreshing and retrying like every other call in the app.
details.failure_scenario: A user leaves a completed lookup's detail page open for more than 30 minutes (a plausible SOC-analyst workflow -- reviewing a report, stepping away, coming back) then clicks 'Export PDF'. Every other action on the page (e.g. re-fetching evidence, asking Copilot) would silently refresh the token and succeed, but export alone surfaces a raw 401 failure message and requires a full page reload to recover.
details.proposed_fix: Replace the raw fetch()+authHeaders() call in handleServerExport with authedFetch() (adjusted to return the raw Response for blob handling), so export gets the same transparent refresh-and-retry behavior as the rest of the app.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of both files.

frontend/components/dashboard/ExportMenu.tsx lines 13-16 define a local `authHeaders()` that just reads `access_token` from localStorage, with no refresh logic. `handleServerExport` (lines 136-158) calls `fetch()` directly with `headers: authHeaders()`, then branches on `res.status === 404` (line 143) and generic `!res.ok` (line 147) -- a 401 falls straight into the generic branch and produces "Export failed with status 401." with no retry.

frontend/lib/api.ts defines `authedFetch` (lines 172-183) which every other authenticated call in that file (getLookup, listLookups, getEvidence, listBasket, listCases, admin/*, pentest/*, etc. -- dozens of call sites) goes through. Its logic: do the fetch, and if `res.status === 401`, call `refreshAccessToken()` and retry once. This is exactly the "transparently refresh and retry once on 401" behavior the docstring claims, and `access_token_expire_minutes: int = 30` in backend/app/core/config.py confirms the 30-minute TTL. The export backend route (`POST /{lookup_id}/export` in backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py) is gated by the same `require_permission` JWT dependency as every other authenticated route, so it 401s identically on an expired token -- there's nothing special about this endpoint that would make it exempt.

I verified there is no global fetch monkey-patch or interceptor elsewhere in frontend/ that would retroactively add refresh behavior to ExportMenu's raw fetch call (grep for `authedFetch`/`window.fetch =` across frontend/ only turns up the definition and callers inside lib/api.ts itself). So the described failure scenario is real: after 30+ minutes on an open lookup detail page, clicking Export PDF/CSV will show a raw "Export failed with status 401" instead of silently refreshing like every other action on the page, and the user must reload (which happens to trigger other authedFetch calls that refresh the token) to recover.

This is a genuine inconsistency/bug, not one of the documented intentional patterns (it doesn't match any of the 8 listed exceptions). Severity: I agree with the original P3 rating. It's a real, user-visible reliability/UX bug with a clear plausible trigger, but it's narrowly scoped (only the two server-rendered export formats, only after a specific idle-time threshold), has an easy workaround (reload the page and retry), causes no data loss or security exposure, and does not block the primary investigation workflow. That places it solidly at P3 (minor, edge-case, workaround exists) rather than P2 (core-flow-affecting) or P1/P0.

details.title: 404 from the export endpoint is always mislabeled as "format not yet available"
details.actual_behavior: `backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py`'s `POST /{lookup_id}/export` (lines 771-800) fully implements both `pdf` and `csv` via `_render_pdf`/`_render_csv` -- the only place it can 404 is `_load_lookup_detail` (lines 498-511) raising `HTTPException(404, "Lookup not found")` when `lookup_id` doesn't exist. Since ExportMenu.tsx only ever requests format="pdf" or format="csv" (both implemented), this component's special-cased 404 branch will, in practice, only ever fire for a lookup that has been deleted or never existed -- yet it always shows "Export format not yet available."

Instead of learning the investigation record is gone, they're told the export format itself isn't implemented -- actively misleading and likely to mask a real data-loss/retention bug rather than surface it.

The only 404 in the whole call chain is `_load_lookup_detail` (lines 498-511) raising HTTPException(404, 'Lookup not found') when the lookup_id doesn't exist. I also checked the auth/permission dependency chain (require_permission in backend/app/auth/rbac.py lines 74-86) to rule out a permission-denial path producing a 404 -- it raises 403, not 404, so that's not an alternate source either. So the claimed call chain is accurate: a 404 from this endpoint can only mean the lookup record itself is gone, yet the UI unconditionally tells the analyst the export *format* isn't available, which is factually wrong and actively misleading about the real cause (a missing/deleted investigation record). details.title: Misleading 'Export format not yet available' message shown for both a real 404 and any network failure

titles: Hunting-package generation failure is a silent, unlabeled blank UI (no error, no empty-state message)

details.title: Hunting-package generation failure is a silent, unlabeled blank UI (no error, no empty-state message)
details.actual_behavior: `handleHunt` awaits `huntThisIOC(lookupId, HUNT_FORMATS)` (lib/api.ts) and only treats a non-2xx HTTP response as failure (`if (!res.ok) throw ...`). So `handleHunt` sees this as success: `setHuntPackage(await huntThisIOC(...))` stores an object with `exact_match_queries: []`, `expansion_targets: []`, `broader_queries: []`, and `error` stays null. The render then hits `{huntPackage && (<TabsPrimitive.Root ...>)}` (huntPackage is a truthy, non-null object) which renders an empty `<TabsPrimitive.List>` (no `<Tabs.Trigger>`s, since it maps over an empty array) and zero `<Tabs.Content>` panels, and the expansion block at line 150 is hidden because `expansion_targets.length > 0` is false. The button label also flips from "Hunt This IOC" to "Regenerate", implying a completed, successful run.
details.failure_scenario: AI backend (Ollama/cloud) is unreachable or misconfigured when the analyst clicks "Hunt This IOC" on a completed lookup. The POST /hunt call returns 200 with an all-empty HuntingPackage. The panel silently renders an odd, content-less bordered strip with no triggers/content and no error text, while the button now reads "Regenerate" -- nothing tells the analyst the generation failed; it looks like the feature is broken or that there's simply nothing to hunt for.
details.proposed_fix: In HuntingCenterPanel, after a successful call, check `huntPackage.exact_match_queries.length === 0` (and no expansion targets) and render an explicit "no hunting queries generated" message instead of (or in addition to) the empty Tabs.Root, so this state is visually distinguishable from both the pre-click and successful states.
details.reasoning:
