1. backend/app/ai/hunting_service.py:60-72 — generate_hunting_package wraps the AI call in try/except Exception, logs a warning, and returns a bare `HuntingPackage()` on ANY failure (AI backend down, misconfigured, rate-limited, unparseable JSON, etc.). HuntingPackage's fields (analysis_schemas.py:129-138) all default to empty lists via Field(default_factory=list), so this is `exact_match_queries=[], expansion_targets=[], broader_queries=[]`. Contrast with generate_detection_rule's except block (lines 102-113 same file) which returns a clearly-labeled placeholder ("Detection rule unavailable for X", rule="# Generation failed -- see platform logs.") — confirming the reviewer's claim that this file itself has an established, better pattern that the hunting path doesn't follow.

2. backend/app/api/routes/hunting.py:33-45 — the /hunt route declares `response_model=HuntingPackage` and does `return await generate_hunting_package(...)` directly, so on the failure path it returns this empty package with the default HTTP 200 — no error status is ever surfaced.

3. frontend/lib/api.ts:389-394 — huntThisIOC only throws when `!res.ok` (non-2xx). Since the backend always returns 200, this throw path never fires on AI-failure; huntThisIOC resolves successfully with the empty package. lib/types.ts:307-311 confirms HuntingPackage has no error/status field to detect degraded state from the payload itself.

4. HuntingCenterPanel.tsx:67-77 (handleHunt) — calls `setHuntPackage(await huntThisIOC(...))` inside try, only catching real exceptions (network failure / non-2xx). On the AI-failure case above, no exception occurs, so `error` state stays null, and huntPackage is set to the truthy-but-empty object.

5. Render logic: line 105 `{huntPackage && (<TabsPrimitive.Root ...>` only checks truthiness/non-null, not content — with empty exact_match_queries, this renders a TabsPrimitive.Root with an empty TabsPrimitive.List (no triggers) and no TabsPrimitive.Content children: a content-less bordered strip. Line 150 `{huntPackage && huntPackage.expansion_targets.length > 0 && (...)}` correctly hides the expansion block when empty, but there's no positive "no results" message anywhere. Line 99 flips button text from "Hunt This IOC" to "Regenerate" purely based on huntPackage being non-null, actively signaling to the analyst that generation succeeded.

Every link in the claimed chain is confirmed by direct inspection of the actual code, not just the reviewer's description. This is a genuine silent-failure UX gap, not one of the documented intentional design patterns (it doesn't match any of patterns 1-8 — it's not graceful multi-provider degradation like pattern 2/8, since here there's exactly one AI-backed synthesis step per hunt request and the whole feature silently no-ops with zero signal).

Severity: P2 is reasonable and I'm keeping it. This is UI-only (no data corruption, no security bypass, no crash), so not P0/P1. But the failure mode plausibly occurs in realistic conditions (AI backend down/misconfigured/rate-limited) and has real analyst-facing consequences: during active threat hunting/incident response, a SOC analyst could mistake "AI silently failed" for "no hunting queries/related indicators exist," potentially causing a missed pivot on a real threat. That's more than cosmetic, warranting P2 rather than a lower P3/P4 polish-only rating.

titles: Failed case-list fetch is cached as an empty list, permanently masquerading as 'no cases exist' with no retry path
No in-flight guard on the case-list fetch allows duplicate concurrent listCases() calls

details.title: Failed case-list fetch is cached as an empty list, permanently masquerading as 'no cases exist' with no retry path
details.actual_behavior: `handleOpenCasePicker` calls `listCases()` only `if (!cases)`. On failure the `catch {}` block sets `setCases([])` (line 51), discarding the actual error. Because `[]` is not `null`, the `!cases` guard is false on every subsequent open, so the fetch is never retried, and the UI renders 'No cases yet -- create one first.' (line 88) even though the list was never successfully loaded.
details.failure_scenario: Backend is briefly unreachable (or the request 401s) the first time the analyst clicks 'Add to Case'. `cases` becomes `[]`, the picker shows 'No cases yet -- create one first.' For the rest of the session, every subsequent click on 'Add to Case' re-renders the same misleading empty state and never calls `listCases()` again, even after the backend recovers, until the whole component unmounts/remounts.
details.proposed_fix: Track fetch failure separately (e.g. a `casesError` state) instead of conflating it with an empty array, and/or don't cache the empty result on the catch path so the next open retries.
details.reasoning: Read the actual file (lines 22-54 and render logic 85-100). Confirmed exactly as claimed: cases state starts null; handleOpenCasePicker fetches only `if (!cases)`; on error the catch block discards the error and sets cases to `[]`; since `[]` is truthy, `!cases` is false on all subsequent opens, permanently skipping re-fetch; the render logic at line 88 treats `cases?.length === 0` identically whether it came from a real empty backend response or a swallowed failure, showing 'No cases yet -- create one first.' with no way to distinguish or retry. Checked the only usage site (app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx line 246) and confirmed no key prop resets the component across re-renders within the same lookup view, so the stale-failure state persists for repeated 'Add to Case' clicks until the page/component remounts (e.g., navigating to a different lookup) or a full reload. This does not match any of the 8 documented intentional patterns (provider NOT_CONFIGURED status, JWT role re-derivation, AI narration-only scoring, basket privacy, toolkit/pentest separation, exploit gating, nmap flag safety boundary, per-call provider status) — it is plain silent error-swallowing producing a misleading permanent UI state. Severity: confined to one frontend feature (case-linking), no data loss/security impact, and has a workaround (navigate/reload), so P2 is appropriate and matches the original reviewer — no basis to escalate or downgrade.

details.title: No in-flight guard on the case-list fetch allows duplicate concurrent listCases() calls
details.actual_behavior: `handleOpenCasePicker` only guards on `!cases` (state that starts `null` and stays `null` until the promise resolves). There is no separate 'loading' flag, so rapidly toggling the case picker closed/open again before the first `listCases()` promise settles triggers a second concurrent `listCases()` call.
details.failure_scenario: Analyst double-clicks 'Add to Case' quickly (open, close, open) before the network round trip for the first `listCases()` completes; two identical GET /api/v1/cases requests are in flight simultaneously, and whichever resolves last silently overwrites `cases` set by the other (harmless here since both return the same data, but it's an unbounded-fan-out pattern that becomes a real bug if `listCases()` is ever given side effects or per-call cost).
details.proposed_fix: Add a `casesLoading` ref/state guard so a fetch already in flight is not started again.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the file directly: handleOpenCasePicker (lines 45-54) guards the listCases() fetch only with `if (!cases)`, where `cases` is React state initialized to null and only updated after the fetch promise resolves via setCases(). Because the callback's closure captures `cases` from the render at click time, and the callback's own dependency array is [cases], every click that happens before the first fetch resolves sees cases still equal to null and re-enters the fetch branch, firing another concurrent listCases() call. There is no separate loading/ref flag anywhere in the file to prevent this, so the race is real and easily reproducible with an ordinary fast double-click (open/close/open) before the network round trip completes. This isn't one of the eight documented intentional patterns -- it's a genuine missing in-flight guard. However, the real-world impact is negligible: both concurrent requests hit the same idempotent GET endpoint and return identical data, so the 'last write wins' overwrite is harmless, there's no data corruption, no incorrect UI state, and no security implication -- only a wasted duplicate network call. That is closer to a cosmetic/efficiency nit than a P3 'low but tangible' issue, so I'm downgrading the severity to P4.

titles: Chat history/context not reset when lookupId prop changes, leaking prior investigation's Q&A into new one

details.title: Chat history/context not reset when lookupId prop changes, leaking prior investigation's Q&A into new one
details.actual_behavior: The component's `turns`, `question`, and `error` state are only ever mutated by `ask()`/its callbacks; there is no `useEffect` keyed on `lookupId` that clears them when the prop changes. `ask()` builds the `notes` array sent to the backend from the full accumulated `turns` history (line 53) regardless of which lookup those turns were originally asked about. Both call sites (app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx:229 and app/lookup/new/page.tsx:217) render `<InvestigationCopilot lookupId={lookupId} .../>` with no `key={lookupId}`, and Next.js App Router reuses the same page component instance (and therefore the same mounted InvestigationCopilot instance) when navigating between different `/lookup/[id]` routes, so `lookupId` changes as a prop without an unmount/remount.
details.failure_scenario: Analyst opens lookup A, asks the Copilot 2-3 questions (turns accumulate), then clicks through to a different lookup B (client-side navigation, same route pattern, no full page reload). The panel still displays lookup A's Q&A thread under lookup B's data. If the analyst then asks a new question about B, `notes` (built from A's turns) is sent alongside B's `lookupId` to `askCopilot`, contaminating the AI's context with a different investigation's Q&A, and clicking 'Show Receipts' on an old turn calls `onShowReceipts` with evidence IDs that belong to lookup A while the page is showing lookup B's evidence ledger.
details.proposed_fix: Add `React.useEffect(() => { setTurns([]); setQuestion(""); setError(null); }, [lookupId]);` (or key the component by `lookupId` at the call site).
details.reasoning:
I read InvestigationCopilot.tsx in full and confirmed every code-level claim in the finding is accurate: `turns`/`question`/`error` are only ever set inside `ask()`/its callbacks (lines 39-66), there is no `useEffect` keyed on `lookupId` that clears them, and `ask()` builds the `notes` array sent to `askCopilot` from the *entire* accumulated `turns` history (line 53) regardless of which lookup produced those turns. I also confirmed backend/app/ai/analysis_service.py's `answer_copilot_question` folds `analyst_notes` verbatim into the AI prompt as 'Analyst notes so far' (lines 373-379), so stale notes really would leak into the model's context for a different lookup if this state were carried over. Both call sites (app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx:229 and app/lookup/new/page.tsx:217) indeed render `<InvestigationCopilot lookupId={lookupId} .../>` with no `key={lookupId}` on the component itself -- confirmed by reading both files.

However, the claimed failure scenario -- 'analyst clicks through to a different lookup B via client-side navigation, same route pattern, no full page reload' -- does not have an actual trigger anywhere in this codebase today. I grepped and read every navigation path that touches `/lookup/`: every 'investigate'/'pivot'/'next action' button (PivotPanel, RelationshipGraph, cases page, basket page) routes to `/lookup/new?value=...`, never directly to an existing `/lookup/{id}`. There is no history/search-results list anywhere that links from one completed lookup directly to another. Critically, app/lookup/new/page.tsx already guards against exactly this bug class: its inner component is wrapped as `<LookupNewPageInner key={rawValue} />` specifically 'so pivoting to a new IOC via TopSearchBar... fully remounts... instead of reusing the mounted instance' (explicit comment, lines 264-273), which means `InvestigationCopilot` on that page only ever receives a single stable `lookupId` per mount and the bug can't manifest there. On app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx there is no such key and, per Next.js App Router semantics, navigating between two URLs that resolve to the same page.tsx with only the dynamic segment changing does not remount the component -- but I could not find any code path in this app that actually performs such an A-to-B client-side transition between two live `/lookup/[id]` instances; every route to `/lookup/[id]` is either a hard page load (typed URL/bookmark) or arrives via the structurally different `/lookup/new` route (a genuine unmount).

So this is a real, verifiable state-management defect and a real violation of the component's own documented invariant ('scoped to the current lookup's evidence ledger'), and it's a clear landmine given how trivial it would be to add a feature (e.g. linking a case's IOC list or a future 'recent lookups' view to an existing lookup id) that would immediately trigger the exact contamination described -- especially since the same codebase demonstrably treats this exact bug class as worth guarding against elsewhere. But because no current UI flow in the shipped app actually reaches the described contamination scenario, the P1 'analyst opens lookup A, asks questions, clicks through to lookup B, contamination happens today' framing overstates present real-world impact. I'm downgrading to P2: a genuine, fix-worthy defensive gap/inconsistency with an already-established pattern in the same codebase, not an actively exploitable P1 issue in the current build. The proposed fix (reset state in a `useEffect` keyed on `lookupId`, or key the component) is correct and cheap regardless.

titles: Post-save reset of plaintext fields uses stale pre-save provider prop, reproducing the exact bug the comment says was fixed
Save reverts a plaintext field (Ollama base_url) to its pre-save value instead of the value just saved, due to a stale closure over the `provider` prop
handleSave has no try/catch around onSave, unlike the parallel handleTest, so a rejected save is silently swallowed with no user feedback
"Test Connection" on an already-configured, working AI/IOC provider always reports a false failure unless the credential is retyped
handleTest's comment claims a masked-credential fallback that does not exist in the code, and self-contradicts in the same comment block

details.title: Post-save reset of plaintext fields uses stale pre-save provider prop, reproducing the exact bug the comment says was fixed
details.actual_behavior: handleSave (created during the render before the user's save, closing over that render's `provider` prop) calls `setValues(plaintextInitialValues())` on line 85. `plaintextInitialValues` (lines 61-68) reads from `provider.masked_credentials`, not from the `values` the user actually typed. Because ProviderConfigRow is rendered with a stable `key={p.provider_id}` in app/providers/page.tsx (confirmed: lines 117 and 152 of that file), React reuses the same component instance across the save, and the JS closure for the in-flight `handleSave` invocation still references the OLD `provider` object from before the parent applied the update -- even though the parent's onSave handler does update its own state with the fresh, post-save provider object. So the value written back into `values` is whatever `masked_credentials[field]` was BEFORE this save, not what was just typed/saved.
details.failure_scenario: First time configuring Ollama: expand the row, type a base_url (e.g. http://localhost:11434) into the previously-empty field, click Save. Because the pre-save `provider.masked_credentials.base_url` was empty/undefined, `plaintextInitialValues()` returns `{}` for that field, so `values.base_url` is reset to '' right after save -- the field goes visibly blank even though the backend did persist the value correctly. If the user then clicks 'Test Connection' without noticing and retyping, `onTest` is called with an empty base_url. For an edit (changing an already-set base_url from A to B), the field instead silently reverts to displaying the OLD value A after Save (not the new B), until the page is fully reloaded/remounted.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading frontend/components/dashboard/ProviderConfigRow.tsx and frontend/app/providers/page.tsx. handleSave and plaintextInitialValues (lines 61-89) are ordinary functions recreated per render that close over that render's `provider` prop; there is no ref or effect resyncing `values` from `provider`. page.tsx uses a stable key={p.provider_id} (lines 117, 152), so ProviderConfigRow's local `values` state survives the save instead of being reset by a remount. The parent's onSave (page.tsx lines 122-130) updates its own provider state with the fresh, post-save provider only after the child's in-flight handleSave call already captured the pre-save `provider` in its closure — so line 85's setValues(plaintextInitialValues()) rebuilds `values` from the stale, pre-save masked_credentials, not from what was just typed/saved. This reproduces exactly the two scenarios claimed: (1) first-time Ollama base_url entry gets wiped back to blank right after a successful save (since pre-save masked_credentials.base_url was empty), and (2) editing base_url from A to B causes the field to silently revert to displaying A after a successful save of B, persisting until a true remount. plaintextFields is only ever passed for Ollama's base_url (page.tsx:120), so the bug's real-world scope is narrow (one field, one provider) but genuine and user-facing (a subsequent Test Connection click can send blank/stale data despite correct backend persistence). This matches a bounded-impact, non-security, non-data-loss functional defect — consistent with the originally claimed P2, no basis to escalate or downgrade.

details.title: Save reverts a plaintext field (Ollama base_url) to its pre-save value instead of the value just saved, due to a stale closure over the `provider` prop
details.actual_behavior: handleSave (lines 77-89) calls `setValues(plaintextInitialValues())` right after `await onSave(...)` resolves. `plaintextInitialValues` (lines 61-68) reads `provider.masked_credentials` via closure over this render's `provider` prop -- which is still the PRE-save value, because the parent's state update (frontend/app/providers/page.tsx's setAiProviders in the onSave callback) has not yet propagated into a new render of this already-executing closure. React does not re-run an in-flight event handler when props change mid-execution, and nothing else in this component re-derives `values` from `provider` after mount.
details.failure_scenario: Ollama has no base_url configured yet. Operator types 'http://192.168.1.50:11434' and clicks Save. The save succeeds server-side (masked_credentials.base_url is now that URL), but `setValues(plaintextInitialValues())` recomputes from the OLD provider prop (masked_credentials.base_url was previously undefined), so the input reverts to blank/'Not set'. If the operator then clicks 'Test Connection' expecting to verify what they just saved, `values.base_url` is empty, the test call sends an empty base_url, and it fails with a connection/validation error -- exactly the 'test click sends it blank again' bug this component's comment claims was fixed, just reproduced for the very next render after Save rather than after a remount.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading both files. handleSave (lines 77-89) and plaintextInitialValues (61-68) are ordinary closures created fresh each render, closing over that render's `provider` prop. handleSave is invoked on click, suspends at `await onSave(...)`, and resumes with the SAME closure regardless of any re-render that happens in between -- this is deterministic JS closure semantics, not a timing race. The parent (frontend/app/providers/page.tsx lines 122-130) does update `aiProviders` state after save, which does eventually give the child a fresh `provider` prop on its next render, but that only affects a NEW handleSave closure for the next click, not the already-suspended one from this click. Since `setValues(plaintextInitialValues())` passes a plain recomputed object (not a `prev =>` updater) and no useEffect re-derives `values` from `provider` after mount (useState's lazy initializer only runs once, on mount), the just-saved plaintext value (e.g. Ollama base_url) gets overwritten back to blank/stale immediately after save resolves. This reproduces exactly the pre-fix bug the component's own comment (lines 81-84) says was addressed: an immediate 'Test Connection' click after Save sends an empty base_url. Scope is narrow (only AI-provider rows using plaintextFields, currently just Ollama's base_url; IOC rows never set plaintextFields) and easily worked around (retype or reload), so P3 as claimed is appropriate -- not higher, not lower.

details.title: handleSave has no try/catch around onSave, unlike the parallel handleTest, so a rejected save is silently swallowed with no user feedback
details.actual_behavior: handleSave only wraps the await in try/finally (line 79, 86-88) -- there is no catch. If onSave rejects, the exception propagates out of the async onClick handler as an unhandled promise rejection; the only visible effect is `saving` reverting to false (from the finally), with no error message shown anywhere in this component.
details.failure_scenario: If ProviderConfigRow is reused by a future caller whose onSave implementation does not itself catch backend errors (the current two call sites in app/providers/page.tsx happen to wrap their bodies in try/catch and never rethrow, which is why this isn't visible today), a network failure or 500 during Save would leave the user with a button that simply stops saying 'Saving...' and reverts to 'Save', with zero indication anything went wrong.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of ProviderConfigRow.tsx lines 77-89: handleSave wraps only try/finally around `await onSave(...)`, with no catch block, while the parallel handleTest (lines 91-107) has a catch that populates testResult, which is rendered in JSX (lines 187-192). There is no equivalent save-error state or rendering path anywhere in the component. onSave's type (line 24) is `Promise<void>` with no guarantee against rejection, so this is a real, verifiable inconsistency between the two handlers in the same file.

I also verified the cross-file claim: both current call sites in app/providers/page.tsx (AI provider onSave ~line 122, IOC provider onSave ~line 155) wrap their bodies in try/catch and call setError on failure without rethrowing, so in the current codebase no unhandled rejection actually reaches handleSave today. This matches the reviewer's own caveat and means the bug is latent/defensive rather than actively broken right now.

This doesn't match any of the 8 documented intentional patterns. It's a legitimate, minor error-handling gap: a reusable component (explicitly documented in its own header comment as a general-purpose row "for both AI providers and IOC providers") that isn't self-contained against its own prop contract, unlike its sibling handler. Given zero live impact today (both real call sites already prevent rejection) but a real risk for future callers or regressions, P3 (low) is the correct severity -- not higher, since nothing currently breaks, but not dismissible either since the inconsistency and latent risk are concrete and easy to point to in the code.

details.title: "Test Connection" on an already-configured, working AI/IOC provider always reports a false failure unless the credential is retyped
details.actual_behavior: ProviderConfigRow's `values` state (line 71, `useState<Record<string,string>>(plaintextInitialValues)`) starts empty for every real secret field -- only plaintextFields (Ollama's base_url) get pre-filled; masked_credentials are shown only as an input placeholder hint, never as the real value (per this same file's design and runtime_config.py:96-132's own docstring about the identical trap on the Save path). handleTest (lines 91-107) sends `values` as-is to onTest, which calls testAIBackend()/testIOCProvider() -> backend/app/ai/connection_test.py's `_check_*` handlers (e.g. _check_openai, connection_test.py:81-83; _check_anthropic, line 274-276; all of groq/kimi/deepseek/xai/mistral/openrouter). Every one of those unconditionally returns `AITestResult(ok=False, message="No API key provided.")` when the passed-in api_key is empty -- with no distinction between "never configured" and "already configured, just not retyped this session."
details.failure_scenario: An admin has a fully working, previously-tested Anthropic key saved. Days later they open Manage Providers, expand the Anthropic row, and click "Test Connection" without retyping the key (a completely ordinary interaction -- the masked placeholder looks like a value is already there). The UI reports "Failed: No API key provided." for a backend that is in fact correctly configured and currently in active use, which is indistinguishable in the UI from an actually-broken/revoked key, and can lead an administrator to needlessly reconfigure or distrust a working AI backend right before or during live use.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the full chain: ProviderConfigRow.tsx's `values` state (lines 61-71) is seeded only from plaintextFields (e.g. Ollama base_url); real secret fields start empty and the masked credential is used only as a placeholder hint, never copied into state. handleTest (lines 91-107) sends `values` as-is with no fallback, through testAIBackend/testIOCProvider (lib/api.ts) to ai_config.py's /test route, into connection_test.py's _check_* handlers, every one of which returns ok=False/"No API key provided." on an empty api_key, using only the candidate value (explicitly never reading stored settings, per its own docstring). This asymmetry is confirmed as a real gap by runtime_config.py's _merge_credentials (lines 96-132), whose own docstring documents that the exact same 'blank values on an already-configured provider' trap was found and fixed for the Save path (falls back to stored encrypted credential when incoming fields are blank) — but no equivalent fallback exists for the Test path. The false-negative result is then persisted via record-test (runtime.py), so the misleading 'last tested: failed' status survives page reloads, not just the single click. This doesn't match any of the 8 documented intentional-design patterns. Severity: real and reproducible via ordinary use, misleads admins about a working provider's health and can prompt needless reconfiguration, but causes no security bypass, data loss, or actual service outage (the provider keeps functioning in production regardless of the test result) — P2 as originally claimed is accurate, not over- or under-stated.

details.title: handleTest's comment claims a masked-credential fallback that does not exist in the code, and self-contradicts in the same comment block
details.actual_behavior: The comment says the test 'falls back to the already-saved (masked) credential's field names so re-testing a saved key doesn't require re-typing it,' but the code on line 100 only ever sends `values` (what's currently typed) -- there is no fallback to any stored/masked value. The comment's own final clause ('we can only usefully re-test values just typed in this form') directly contradicts the earlier claim that re-typing isn't required.
details.failure_scenario: A maintainer reading only the comment could believe clicking 'Test Connection' on a previously-saved, never-retyped secret field will re-validate the stored key; in fact it sends an empty string for that field, since `values` is never pre-filled for true secrets.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading of ProviderConfigRow.tsx. handleTest (lines 95-100) sends `values` with no fallback logic of its own. The only "fallback" in this component is plaintextInitialValues() (lines 61-68), which pre-populates `values` exclusively for fields listed in `plaintextFields` (non-secret config like Ollama's base_url) -- true secret fields (e.g. api_key) are deliberately left blank per the props-level comment at lines 30-34 ("instead of leaving them blank like a true credential"). So the handleTest comment's claim that re-testing "a saved key" doesn't require re-typing is inaccurate for true secrets, and its own final clause ("we can only usefully re-test values just typed in this form") directly contradicts that earlier claim. This is a real, verifiable comment-accuracy defect, not one of the documented intentional design patterns. It has no functional/behavioral impact (the actual code behavior is correct and consistent with the rest of the file's documentation) -- it's purely a misleading comment that could confuse a future maintainer, which matches the claimed P4 (lowest) severity. No adjustment needed.

titles: ResetPasswordDialog also lacks self-awareness; self-reset silently breaks the very next auto-refresh
ToggleActiveDialog has no self-disable guard, unlike EditUserDialog's self-role-change guard

details.title: ResetPasswordDialog also lacks self-awareness; self-reset silently breaks the very next auto-refresh
details.actual_behavior: Like ToggleActiveDialog, ResetPasswordDialog (lines 425-501) and its invocation (lines 250-256) never check whether `user.id === currentUser.id`. Resetting your own password invalidates every access/refresh token already issued to you (per backend/app/core/users.py's reset_password, which calls the same token-version-bump mechanism used by logout). Immediately after a successful reset, the dialog calls `onReset()` (line 464), which is `refresh` from the parent (line 254), and `refresh()` calls `listUsers()` using the now-invalidated access token. `authedFetch` (frontend/lib/api.ts lines 172-183) will get a 401, attempt a token refresh with the also-invalidated refresh token, fail, and call `logout()` (clearing localStorage only, no navigation). `listUsers` then throws 'Failed to fetch users', which `refresh`'s `.catch` turns into the generic error banner at lines 94-98 ('Failed to load users' or similar) -- there is no redirect to /login anywhere in this component or its caller (frontend/app/admin/page.tsx only checks `isLoggedIn()` once on mount, line 46).
details.failure_scenario: An admin uses 'Reset Password' on their own account row. The dialog reports success and closes, but the panel's immediate auto-refresh silently fails with a generic 'Failed to load users' banner instead of any indication that the admin just logged themselves out; they must manually notice this and re-login.
details.reasoning: Verified the full call chain across all six files involved. (1) UsersManagementPanel.tsx confirms ResetPasswordDialog (lines 425-501) and its invocation (lines 250-256) have no isSelf/currentUser.id check, unlike the sibling EditUserDialog which does gate role-editing on isSelf. (2) backend/app/core/users.py reset_password() bumps user.token_version, invalidating outstanding tokens. (3) backend/app/auth/rbac.py get_current_user() rejects an access token whose embedded token_version is stale (line 69). (4) Critically, backend/app/api/routes/auth.py refresh() ALSO checks token_version on the refresh token (line 145) and rejects it too -- so unlike a normal expired-access-token case, the automatic refresh-and-retry in frontend/lib/api.ts's authedFetch() cannot succeed, because both tokens were issued before the reset and share the same now-stale token_version. (5) authedFetch's refreshAccessToken() failure triggers logout() (clears localStorage only, no navigation) and authedFetch returns the original failed response. (6) listUsers() throws 'Failed to fetch users', caught by the panel's refresh() and rendered as a generic red banner. (7) admin/page.tsx only calls isLoggedIn() once on mount (line 46), so nothing redirects to /login afterward -- the page is stuck showing a stale table and a generic error with no indication the admin just logged themselves out. Every link in this chain is real and verified directly in the source, not just asserted by the original reviewer. One caveat: ResetPasswordDialog's own DialogDescription (lines 446-449) does generically warn 'This immediately signs the user out of every existing session' before submission, so it isn't wholly undisclosed -- but it doesn't call out the self-target case, and the actual post-submit failure mode (confusing generic fetch error instead of a clean logout/redirect) is exactly as claimed. Impact is narrow (only triggers if an admin resets their own password via this admin table rather than a self-service flow), non-security, no data loss, and trivially recoverable by manually logging back in, so P3 (minor UX issue) is an accurate severity call -- I see no basis to raise or lower it.

details.title: ToggleActiveDialog has no self-disable guard, unlike EditUserDialog's self-role-change guard
details.actual_behavior: EditUserDialog is given an explicit `isSelf={editingUser.id === currentUser.id}` prop (line 245) and uses it to disable the role select and show an explanatory message so an admin cannot demote/change their own role from this UI (lines 397, 407-409). ToggleActiveDialog (lines 503-557) receives no such prop at all -- its invocation at lines 257-263 passes only `user`, `onOpenChange`, `onToggled` -- and the dialog body never checks `user.id === currentUser.id`. The 'Disable' button in the table (lines 213-219) is rendered identically for the current admin's own row (only a passive '(you)' label is shown next to the email at line 190, with no effect on the Disable button). Backend `set_user_active` (backend/app/core/users.py lines 235-259) only raises `LastAdminError` when disabling would leave zero active admins; it does not special-case self-disable when other admins still exist.
details.failure_scenario: An admin viewing the Users tab while at least one other admin account exists clicks 'Disable' on their own row, then confirms in ToggleActiveDialog. The account is disabled immediately server-side; the admin's own session becomes invalid on its next request, with no client-side warning or friction beyond the generic dialog text, in contrast to the deliberate self-role-change protection elsewhere in the same file.
details.reasoning:
Verified directly against both the frontend component and the full backend call chain.

Frontend (UsersManagementPanel.tsx):
- EditUserDialog is explicitly given `isSelf={editingUser.id === currentUser.id}` (line 245), uses it to `disabled={isSelf}` the role `<select>` (line 397) and render an explanatory message "You can't change your own role -- ask another administrator." (lines 407-409).
- ToggleActiveDialog (lines 503-557) receives only `user`, `onOpenChange`, `onToggled` at its call site (lines 257-263) — no `isSelf` or `currentUser` prop at all, and its body never references `currentUser.id`. The Disable/Enable button in the table (lines 213-219) is rendered with identical logic (`u.is_active ? "destructive" : "default"`, label toggled the same way) regardless of whether `u.id === currentUser.id`; the only nod to self-detection anywhere near this control is the passive "(you)" text label at line 190, which has zero effect on button behavior or the dialog that follows.

Backend confirms there is no second-layer guard either:
- `backend/app/core/users.py`'s `update_user()` (lines 211-215) explicitly raises `SelfRoleChangeError` when `user.id == actor_user_id` for a role change, on top of the existing last-admin race-safe lock — a deliberate, purpose-built protection.
- `set_user_active()` (lines 235-259) only checks `_remaining_active_admins(...) == 0` (last-admin protection); there is no `if user_id == actor_user_id` check anywhere in this function.
- `backend/app/api/routes/admin.py`'s `set_user_active` route (lines 79-88) passes straight through to the service and only catches `LastAdminError`/`UserNotFoundError` — no self-target check, and no `SelfDisableError`-equivalent exception exists in the codebase (confirmed by inspecting the full `UserManagementError` subclass list in `core/users.py`, which defines only `LastAdminError`, `SelfRoleChangeError`, `DuplicateEmailError`, `UserNotFoundError`).

This is a genuine, verified asymmetry, not one of the documented intentional patterns (JWT role never trusted, provider NOT_CONFIGURED status, AI-narration-only scoring, Basket vs. Lookup/Case visibility, Security-Assessment-vs-Pentest overlap, Pentest exploit gating, Nmap flag safety boundary, provider per-call status) — none of which relate to this admin self-action guard. The failure path is real: an admin with at least one other active admin peer can click Disable on their own row and confirm, and `set_user_active` will disable their own account with no self-specific warning (the dialog text is generic — "They will immediately lose access..." — and doesn't even switch to "You" for the self case) and no extra confirmation friction, in clear contrast to the deliberate `isSelf` guard built for the analogous role-change action in the very same file/service.

Severity: I'm keeping this at P2 rather than escalating or downgrading further. Mitigating factors that keep it from being P1: the action requires the admin to deliberately target their own already-"(you)"-labeled row and pass through an explicit two-step confirm dialog that does state the immediate-access-loss consequence; it's fully recoverable by any other existing admin (no permanent lockout, no data loss, no privilege escalation or cross-account exposure — this is a self-inflicted footgun, not an exploitable vulnerability). But it's a real, reachable functional gap with genuine operational impact (accidental admin self-lockout requiring another admin's intervention), and the codebase's own established pattern (guarding the structurally identical self-role-change case both in UI and service layer) shows this was clearly meant to be covered — making it more than a cosmetic nitpick. P2 (moderate, real, worth fixing but not urgent/critical) fits.

titles: Single shared `loading` ModeKey is clobbered by whichever concurrent fetch finishes first

details.title: Single shared `loading` ModeKey is clobbered by whichever concurrent fetch finishes first
details.actual_behavior: `loading` (line 62) is a single `ModeKey | null`, not a per-mode set. `handleClick` (lines 66-102) only short-circuits when the SAME mode is re-clicked and already cached (`if (results[mode]) return`, line 69); it never checks whether a DIFFERENT mode's fetch is currently in flight, and nothing disables the other 5 buttons while one is loading (each button's `disabled` prop, line 117, is scoped to `loading === key` for that one key only). If the user clicks mode A then mode B before A's promise resolves, both `handleClick` closures run concurrently, each with its own `try/finally`. Whichever one resolves first executes `setLoading(null)` (line 98) unconditionally, wiping out the loading indicator/disabled-state for the mode that is still in flight.
details.failure_scenario: User clicks "WHY?" (uncached) - loading="why", fetch starts. Before it returns (a real AI-generation call, commonly 1-10s), user clicks "What is this?" (also uncached) - loading="what", a second fetch starts. If the "why" call resolves first, its `finally` sets loading=null even though the "what" call is still pending; the "What is this?" button now renders as idle (not "Generating...", not disabled) while its request is still outstanding, so the user can click it again and fire a second concurrent `explainWhatIsThis` call for the same mode (since `results.what` isn't populated yet to hit the cache short-circuit), wasting duplicate expensive AI calls and leaving the loading UI inconsistent with actual in-flight state.
details.proposed_fix: Track in-flight modes as a Set/Record keyed by ModeKey instead of a single value, and in the `finally` clear only the entry for the mode that just completed (e.g. `setLoading(prev => { const next = new Set(prev); next.delete(mode); return next; })`), or block starting a new fetch entirely while any fetch is in flight.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the full file. `loading` (line 62) is a single ModeKey|null shared across all six modes. handleClick's only cache guard (line 69) is `if (results[mode]) return`, with no guard against a different mode already being in flight. setLoading(mode) at line 70 and the unconditional setLoading(null) in the finally block at line 98 both operate on the single shared value with no mode-scoping (e.g. no `if (loading !== mode) return` inside finally). The disabled/label logic (lines 117, 120) is scoped per-button to `loading === key`, so it only ever reflects the single most-recently-clicked in-flight mode, not the true in-flight set. Trace: click "why" (loading="why"), then before it resolves click "what" (button not disabled since loading!=="what") sets loading="what" and starts a second fetch; "why"'s Generating/disabled state is now gone even though fetch A is still pending. If fetch A resolves first, its finally sets loading=null, which also clears "what"'s loading/disabled indicator while fetch B is still outstanding and results.what is still unset - the user can click "what" again and pass the `if (results[mode]) return` cache check, firing a duplicate concurrent explainWhatIsThis call. No AbortController, debounce, or per-mode tracking exists anywhere in the file to prevent this. This does not match any of the eight documented intentional design patterns. Real-world trigger (clicking a second analysis button before the first's AI call returns) is plausible and not contrived. Impact is UI inconsistency plus wasted duplicate AI-generation calls, but not data corruption/crash/security - consistent with the claimed P2 severity, not over- or under-stated.

titles: OLLAMA_BASE_URL is never set, and its config.py default (host.docker.internal) doesn't resolve in a real Kubernetes cluster
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL is hardcoded to "http://localhost:8000" instead of replicating docker-compose's empty-by-default auto-detect behavior

details.title: OLLAMA_BASE_URL is never set, and its config.py default (host.docker.internal) doesn't resolve in a real Kubernetes cluster
details.actual_behavior: configmap.yaml sets no OLLAMA_BASE_URL, and none of backend-deployment.yaml/celery-worker-deployment.yaml/celery-beat-deployment.yaml define a hostAliases entry (the Kubernetes equivalent of docker-compose's extra_hosts) for host.docker.internal. Every pod therefore falls back to config.py's literal string "http://host.docker.internal:11434", which is a Docker-Desktop/Docker-Compose-specific DNS alias with no meaning on a generic Kubernetes cluster (EKS/GKE/AKS/kubeadm/etc).
details.failure_scenario: A fresh `kubectl apply -k k8s/base` on any real cluster (not Docker Desktop's built-in single-node k8s) leaves the platform's default AI backend permanently unreachable out of the box -- every AI-narration call fails DNS resolution for host.docker.internal, with no documented override path (unlike docker-compose's HOST_GATEWAY_TARGET machinery) and no comment in configmap.yaml even flagging that this needs to be set.
details.proposed_fix: Either default OLLAMA_BASE_URL in the ConfigMap to a real, cluster-reachable address (or point AI_BACKEND at a non-Ollama backend by default for k8s), and document that operators running their own Ollama need to override it to a reachable host/Service.
details.reasoning: Verified directly against the source. backend/app/core/config.py:146,150 hardcodes ai_backend default = "ollama" and ollama_base_url default = "http://host.docker.internal:11434" with no environment-detection override. k8s/base/configmap.yaml (read in full) sets POSTGRES/REDIS/NEO4J/OPENSEARCH/Bedrock/app/frontend vars but never sets OLLAMA_BASE_URL or AI_BACKEND. A grep across all of k8s/base/*.yaml confirms zero occurrences of 'hostAliases' or 'host.docker.internal' anywhere in the k8s manifests, and backend-deployment.yaml wires the pod's env via `envFrom: configMapRef` pointing at this exact ConfigMap, so the pod falls straight through to config.py's literal default. By contrast, docker-compose.yml explicitly sets OLLAMA_BASE_URL AND adds `extra_hosts: host.docker.internal:${HOST_GATEWAY_TARGET:-host-gateway}` on backend/celery-worker/celery-beat (lines ~191, 218-219, 260-264, 286-288) with extensive comments about Docker Desktop/WSL2/native-Linux host-gateway differences -- i.e., docker-compose deliberately built the exact plumbing that makes the host.docker.internal default resolve, and the k8s manifests dropped that plumbing entirely with no substitute. I checked k8s/README.md's 'Notes / things to adjust before using this for real' section, which explicitly calls out other environment-specific gaps (image refs, ingress host, TLS, storage class) but says nothing about AI_BACKEND/OLLAMA_BASE_URL -- confirming the reviewer's claim that there's no comment or documented override path anywhere. .env.example also ships AI_BACKEND=ollama / OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434 by default, and the k8s README's own Secret-creation instructions (`--from-env-file=.env`) would just carry that same Docker-Desktop-specific literal into the Secret unchanged -- it doesn't fix anything. Net effect: a fresh `kubectl apply -k k8s/base` on any non-Docker-Desktop cluster leaves the default AI backend pointed at an unresolvable hostname, exactly as claimed. This does not match any of the 8 listed intentional-design exclusions. On severity: backend/app/ai/service.py shows a deliberate 'graceful-degradation philosophy' with try/except around the AI call and a distinct failed-outcome fallback, so this does not crash the platform or block core IOC lookup/scoring (computed deterministically per intentional-pattern #3); only AI narration/verdict generation silently fails by default. That graceful degradation, plus the fact k8s/base is already explicitly flagged by its own README as needing several other before-real-use adjustments, keeps this from rising to P0/P1 pure-availability-failure territory. But it does silently break the platform's advertised default/headline AI-narration feature on every fresh non-Docker-Desktop k8s deploy with zero documentation anywhere pointing at the cause or fix. P2 (as originally assessed) is the right call: moderate, feature-breaking-by-default, easily fixable once found, but currently undocumented.

details.title: NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL is hardcoded to "http://localhost:8000" instead of replicating docker-compose's empty-by-default auto-detect behavior
details.actual_behavior: configmap.yaml hardcodes NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL to the non-empty string "http://localhost:8000", which per line 66 of api.ts (`if (process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL) return process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL;`) always wins over the auto-detect path for every single browser-side fetch call, for every deployment of this manifest set. NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_PORT (the fallback docker-compose also wires through) is not set anywhere either.
details.failure_scenario: A user reaches the frontend via any URL other than exactly the machine port-forwarding localhost:8000 (e.g. via a LoadBalancer IP, NodePort, or the Ingress host from configmap.yaml's own comment 'https://ioc-intel.example.com') -- every browser-side API call still targets http://localhost:8000, which resolves to the visiting user's own machine, not the cluster. All authenticated fetches fail (connection refused / nothing listening), breaking the entire app for any real remote client, unless an operator remembers the manual edit called out in this file's own comment.
details.proposed_fix: Leave NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL empty by default (matching docker-compose) and add NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_PORT so the built-in auto-detect logic in api.ts works out of the box across access patterns.
details.reasoning:
Verified directly against the source. configmap.yaml lines 48-53 hardcode NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL to "http://localhost:8000", and api.ts line 66 confirms any non-empty NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL always wins over the browser-side auto-detect fallback (lines 67-69). docker-compose.yml (lines 316-321) deliberately leaves this var empty specifically to let the auto-detect logic run, and grep confirms NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_PORT (the auto-detect's port fallback) is never set anywhere under k8s/. The configmap's own comment ("When you have the Ingress host set up, change this...") independently corroborates that the current default is known to require manual editing per environment, and k8s/README.md's explicit "things to adjust before using this for real" checklist (images, ingress host, TLS, storage) never mentions this value, making it an easy trap. This is a genuine deviation from the documented auto-detect design intent, not one of the listed intentional patterns.

One correction to the original reviewer's reasoning: their proposed fix (leave it empty, rely on auto-detect) would not actually work correctly for this repo's specific k8s topology either — ingress.yaml routes a single host's /api path (no port suffix) to the backend Service, whereas the auto-detect fallback in api.ts constructs `${window.location.hostname}:${port}` (defaulting to :8000), which the Ingress never exposes externally. The right fix is to explicitly set NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL to the real ingress host, exactly as the configmap's own comment already says. But this only affects the quality of the *proposed fix*, not whether the underlying defect (silently-broken default for any non-localhost:8000 access pattern, undocumented in the deployment checklist) is real — it is.

Severity: P2 is appropriate. Real, total breakage of every authenticated browser fetch for any real k8s access pattern (LoadBalancer/NodePort/Ingress), but scoped to one reference manifest/one env var in a template explicitly documented as needing pre-production customization, with an in-file comment already hinting at the fix. Not P0/P1 (no security impact, single contained value, not on the primary docker-compose runtime path used by this project), not P3/P4 (causes complete functional failure once triggered, not cosmetic).

titles: No proxy-buffering annotation for the SSE lookup stream the ingress comment itself calls out

details.title: No proxy-buffering annotation for the SSE lookup stream the ingress comment itself calls out
details.actual_behavior: Only nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout and proxy-send-timeout are raised to 300; there is no `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"` annotation. ingress-nginx buffers proxied response bodies by default (proxy_buffering on), which delays flushing of chunked/streamed responses to the client until buffer thresholds are hit or the upstream connection closes.
details.failure_scenario: A user runs an investigation through the Ingress; instead of seeing per-provider results stream in live as the backend emits them (the entire point of building an SSE-style endpoint), the browser receives nothing until nginx's buffering releases the response, typically producing one delayed batch dump near the end of the investigation instead of incremental updates.
details.proposed_fix: Add `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"` (and consider `configuration-snippet: proxy_cache off;`) alongside the existing timeout annotations.
details.reasoning: Confirmed against the actual file. k8s/base/ingress.yaml lines 11-16 set only nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout and proxy-send-timeout to 300, directly preceded by a comment naming the SSE lookup stream as the reason. There is no nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering annotation anywhere in the file, and a repo-wide search turns up no proxy_buffering/X-Accel-Buffering setting anywhere else in k8s/, docker*, or nginx* paths either -- so nothing else in the stack compensates for the default. I verified the referenced endpoint is a genuine incremental stream, not just named as if it were one: backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py's stream_lookup returns StreamingResponse(event_stream(), media_type="text/event-stream"), and backend/app/main.py has an explicit comment describing '/lookup/stream's SSE generator' as something whose body generator 'actually runs' after headers are sent -- i.e. a real lazy async generator, not a pre-buffered body. frontend/lib/api.ts's streamLookup() fetches this endpoint and reads it via a manual ReadableStream reader specifically because "EventSource can't send an Authorization header," confirming the frontend is built to consume results incrementally as they arrive. ingress-nginx (built on stock nginx) defaults proxy_buffering to on, which buffers upstream response bytes and only flushes to the client once internal buffers fill or the upstream connection closes -- exactly the batched-dump failure mode the finding describes, and a widely-documented real gotcha for SSE/chunked responses behind ingress-nginx. This isn't one of the 8 documented intentional patterns (none relate to ingress/streaming config). It's also not merely a reference/demo file: k8s/README.md explicitly documents this manifest set as meant for real deployment ("Notes / things to adjust before using this for real") and lists other ingress.yaml adjustments (host, ingressClassName, TLS) but never mentions proxy-buffering -- so a user following the README's own checklist would still ship this gap. I'm raising severity from the claimed P3 to P2: this doesn't crash anything or lose data, but it fully defeats the specific, deliberately-built incremental-streaming UX (the entire reason this endpoint and its manual-reader frontend consumption exist) for every production Kubernetes deployment that uses these manifests as provided, which is more than a minor/cosmetic efficiency nit.

titles: Ingress only routes /api to the backend; root-level backend endpoints the frontend calls directly (/health/detailed, /network-info) fall through to the frontend and 404

details.title: Ingress only routes /api to the backend; root-level backend endpoints the frontend calls directly (/health/detailed, /network-info) fall through to the frontend and 404
details.actual_behavior: ingress.yaml only defines two path rules: `/api` (Prefix) -> backend:8000, and `/` (Prefix) -> frontend:3000. Since "/health/detailed" and "/network-info" don't match the "/api" prefix, ingress-nginx's longest-prefix match routes them to the catch-all "/" rule, i.e. to the frontend service, not the backend.
details.failure_scenario: Once an operator follows configmap.yaml's own instructions and points NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL at the externally reachable Ingress host (e.g. https://ioc-intel.example.com), the browser's calls to https://ioc-intel.example.com/health/detailed and /network-info are routed to the Next.js frontend server instead of the backend, which has no route for those paths -- the header's SYSTEM STATUS indicator and the network-info panel break (404/unexpected response) for anyone accessing the app through the Ingress.
details.proposed_fix: Add explicit Ingress path rules for /health, /health/detailed, and /network-info pointing at the backend service (or have the frontend call these under /api/v1 instead, with a matching backend route change).
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading all four files directly. backend/app/main.py mounts every real feature router under settings.api_v1_prefix ("/api/v1") via app.include_router(..., prefix=...) (lines 233-247), but declares @app.get("/health"), @app.get("/health/detailed"), and @app.get("/network-info") directly on the app object with no prefix (lines 410, 430, 470). frontend/lib/api.ts's getSystemHealth() (explicitly commented as feeding the header's system-status indicator) and getNetworkInfo() fetch `${getApiUrl()}/health/detailed` and `${getApiUrl()}/network-info` respectively (lines 654-671) -- unlike every other call in the file, which uses `/api/v1/...`. k8s/base/ingress.yaml defines exactly two path rules: `/api` (Prefix) -> backend:8000 and `/` (Prefix) -> frontend:3000 (lines 31-49); a request path like `/health/detailed` does not match the `/api` prefix and falls through to the catch-all `/` rule, landing on the frontend container, which has no route for it (confirmed no rewrites exist in frontend/next.config.js either). k8s/base/configmap.yaml explicitly instructs operators to point NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL at the externally reachable Ingress host once configured -- exactly the condition needed to trigger the bug. This is a real, deterministic cross-file routing gap, not one of the eight documented intentional patterns. Severity: P2 is appropriate -- it's a guaranteed, 100%-reproducible break of two non-critical UI features (system-status indicator, network-info panel) for anyone using the documented Ingress + configmap external-access setup, with an easy fix, but it does not affect security or core lookup/investigation functionality (all of which is correctly routed under /api/v1), so it doesn't rise to P0/P1, and it's not a rare edge case or purely cosmetic issue either, so P3/P4 would understate it.

titles: NEO4J_USER is exposed as a free-form Secret value, but Neo4j Community Edition requires the NEO4J_AUTH username to be literally 'neo4j'
Pod command overrides the neo4j image's ENTRYPOINT, bypassing tini (the image's zombie-reaping/signal-forwarding init process)

details.title: NEO4J_USER is exposed as a free-form Secret value, but Neo4j Community Edition requires the NEO4J_AUTH username to be literally 'neo4j'
details.actual_behavior: This StatefulSet builds `NEO4J_AUTH="$NEO4J_USER/$NEO4J_PASSWORD"` from a new `NEO4J_USER` secret key that docker-compose.yml never exposes at all -- docker-compose hardcodes the username in-line (`NEO4J_AUTH: neo4j/${NEO4J_PASSWORD:-changeme-neo4j}`, docker-compose.yml line 100), only templating the password. secret.example.yaml (lines 31-33) presents `NEO4J_USER: ""` as a blank fillable credential with no comment stating it must be exactly the string 'neo4j' -- unlike POSTGRES_USER immediately above it in the same file, which genuinely is a free choice. The official neo4j:5-community docker-entrypoint.sh validates that the NEO4J_AUTH username component equals 'neo4j' and exits with a fatal error otherwise (Community Edition does not support a custom initial admin username).
details.failure_scenario: An operator follows k8s/README.md's instruction to 'Make sure your .env also includes ... NEO4J_USER ...' and, reasonably assuming it behaves like POSTGRES_USER (a real, customizable credential), sets it to something other than 'neo4j' (or leaves it blank, producing NEO4J_AUTH="/<password>"). The neo4j container's entrypoint rejects this at startup and the pod crash-loops indefinitely, and there is nothing in this file, secret.example.yaml, or k8s/README.md that states the required fixed value.
details.proposed_fix: Either hardcode the username 'neo4j' directly in the command (dropping the NEO4J_USER secret key entirely, matching docker-compose's actual behavior) or, if keeping it configurable, add an explicit comment in secret.example.yaml stating NEO4J_USER must be the literal string 'neo4j' for Neo4j Community Edition.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading all relevant files. docker-compose.yml:100 hardcodes NEO4J_AUTH's username as the literal 'neo4j' (only the password is templated via ${NEO4J_PASSWORD:-changeme-neo4j}); NEO4J_USER does not exist anywhere in docker-compose.yml or .env.example. The k8s translation (neo4j-statefulset.yaml:26-40) invents a brand-new free-form NEO4J_USER secret key and builds NEO4J_AUTH="$NEO4J_USER/$NEO4J_PASSWORD" from it. secret.example.yaml presents NEO4J_USER: "" (line 32) immediately below the genuinely-free POSTGRES_USER (line 24) with identical blank-field styling, and the only nearby comment (line 31) shows docker-compose's literal inline value without stating the username must be exactly 'neo4j'. k8s/README.md (lines 61-63) instructs operators to add NEO4J_USER to .env alongside real free-choice credentials with no caveat. This matches the official neo4j:5-community image's real, well-documented behavior: Community Edition's docker-entrypoint.sh requires NEO4J_AUTH to be exactly 'neo4j/<password>' (or 'none') and exits fatally on any other username, causing a crash-loop. This is a genuine cross-file documentation/config gap, not one of the eight listed intentional patterns. Severity: real and would fully block a fresh k8s deployment's Neo4j pod (and hence the platform) until diagnosed, but the official image typically emits an explicit fatal error in pod logs, no data loss occurs (fails before data-dir init), and the fix is a one-line config change -- consistent with the original P2 rating (significant deployment blocker, recoverable, no security/data-integrity impact), so I'm keeping it at P2 rather than escalating or downgrading.

details.title: Pod command overrides the neo4j image's ENTRYPOINT, bypassing tini (the image's zombie-reaping/signal-forwarding init process)
details.actual_behavior: The neo4j:5-community image's own ENTRYPOINT is `tini -g -- /startup/docker-entrypoint.sh` with CMD `neo4j`. Kubernetes' `command:` field fully replaces the image ENTRYPOINT (and, since no `args:` is set, the image's CMD is discarded too), so this Pod runs `sh -c 'export NEO4J_AUTH=... && exec /startup/docker-entrypoint.sh neo4j'` with no tini supervising it at all.
details.failure_scenario: During Pod shutdown (rolling update, node drain, `kubectl delete pod`) or plugin-install subprocess spawning (apoc download at first boot), the absence of tini means SIGTERM handling and zombie-process reaping rely entirely on whatever the entrypoint script/JVM does on its own rather than on the supervisor the vendor image was designed to run under, which is a real (if likely low-frequency-impact) deviation from the vendor-supported startup path for a stateful database.
details.proposed_fix: Prepend `tini -g --` to the exec'd command (e.g. `exec tini -g -- /startup/docker-entrypoint.sh neo4j`) so the same init/signal-forwarding behavior as the stock image is preserved.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct inspection of k8s/base/neo4j-statefulset.yaml lines 26-29. The pod's `command:` field is a full `sh -c 'export NEO4J_AUTH=... && exec /startup/docker-entrypoint.sh neo4j'`, and there is no `args:` field. In Kubernetes, `command` replaces the image's Docker ENTRYPOINT entirely, and since no `args` is given, the image's CMD is also discarded rather than passed through. The neo4j:5-community image's real ENTRYPOINT is `tini -g -- /startup/docker-entrypoint.sh` with CMD `neo4j`, so this Pod spec does bypass tini exactly as claimed -- this part of the finding is technically accurate, not a misreading.

However, the practical impact is much smaller than the P3 rating suggests. Because the shell script itself uses `exec` (replacing `sh` rather than forking) and neo4j's own internal entrypoint chain also uses `exec`, the eventual PID 1 in the container is the actual neo4j/JVM process itself -- there's no intermediate non-exec'd shell to swallow signals, so tini's 'signal forwarding' role is largely moot here (SIGTERM reaches the JVM directly, which has its own shutdown-hook-based graceful shutdown). Tini's other role, zombie reaping, only matters if child processes are forked and abandoned; plugin installation (apoc download) runs synchronously in the foreground during entrypoint execution, so there's no obvious path to zombie accumulation in normal use. And even an abrupt SIGKILL on grace-period timeout is not catastrophic for Neo4j, which has WAL-based crash recovery. So this is a real deviation from the vendor's tested startup path and a reasonable, cheap fix to make (prepend `tini -g --`), but the concrete failure scenario is speculative/narrow rather than demonstrated -- more of a hardening nit than a P3 issue, so I'm downgrading to P4.

titles: No vm.max_map_count init step for OpenSearch, unlike the Docker Desktop environment this was translated from

details.title: No vm.max_map_count init step for OpenSearch, unlike the Docker Desktop environment this was translated from
details.actual_behavior: OpenSearch (like Elasticsearch) performs a bootstrap check requiring the host kernel's `vm.max_map_count` to be at least 262144, or it fails to start ('max virtual memory areas vm.max_map_count [65530] is too low'). This manifest has no privileged initContainer (e.g. `sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144`) to guarantee that on the node running the Pod, unlike the docker-compose environment which was implicitly validated on Docker Desktop's bundled Linux VM (which typically ships with a sufficient default).
details.failure_scenario: Deploying this StatefulSet onto a real Kubernetes node whose default `vm.max_map_count` is the common Linux default (65530) causes the opensearch container to fail its bootstrap checks and crash-loop indefinitely, with no indication in this manifest that a node-level sysctl needs to be set first.
details.proposed_fix: Add a privileged initContainer (or a node-level DaemonSet/sysctl) that runs `sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144` before the opensearch container starts, as is standard practice in most OpenSearch/Elasticsearch Kubernetes manifests.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading k8s/base/opensearch-statefulset.yaml in full: the pod spec has no initContainers block (goes directly from spec: to containers: at lines 21-24), and a repo-wide search across k8s/ found no sysctl/max_map_count/initContainer/privileged/DaemonSet anywhere that could set vm.max_map_count on the node. The manifest mirrors docker-compose's discovery.type=single-node and does not set network.host to loopback, so like the docker-compose service (and every OpenSearch/Elasticsearch Docker single-node quickstart) it binds 0.0.0.0 and triggers OpenSearch's production-mode bootstrap checks, of which the max-map-count check is always enforced regardless of single-node discovery. On a real k8s node with the common default (65530), this container will fail its bootstrap check and crash-loop, exactly as claimed. k8s/README.md's own 'things to adjust before using this for real' section lists several other known gaps (image tags, TLS, ingress class, storage class) but never mentions this one, confirming it's a genuine oversight rather than a documented/deferred item. This matches standard, universally-documented OpenSearch/Elasticsearch-on-Kubernetes practice (every mainstream Helm chart ships a privileged sysctl initContainer for this exact reason), so the proposed fix is correct and standard. Severity: P3 slightly understates it — this is a hard install-blocker for a core stateful service on most vanilla clusters (not just a hardening nice-to-have like the TLS/ingress/image-tag items the README does flag), so P2 is more accurate; not P0/P1 because the failure is loud and self-diagnosing (the container's own crash log names the exact remediation) and the fix is a single well-known one-liner.

titles: Redis Deployment has no PVC/volume, reintroducing a data-loss bug docker-compose already fixed

details.title: Redis Deployment has no PVC/volume, reintroducing a data-loss bug docker-compose already fixed
details.actual_behavior: The file's header comment (lines 1-4) claims this mirrors docker-compose's redis service, which it says has 'no persistent volume ... so it's a plain Deployment here (no PVC) matching that ephemeral-storage behavior.' That premise is false for the current docker-compose.yml: the actual docker-compose redis service (docker-compose.yml lines 65-92) has both a custom `command: ["redis-server", "--save", "900", "1", ...]` and `volumes: - redis_data:/data`, added specifically because (per docker-compose.yml's own inline comment) it was 'confirmed live that Redis previously had no volume at all -- every recreation ... silently reset it to empty' -- i.e. this was a real, previously-identified and fixed bug. The k8s Deployment has neither a `command:` override nor any `volumes:`/`volumeMounts:`/PVC at all, so it never got the same fix and reproduces the original bug in the k8s deployment path.
details.failure_scenario: Any Pod recreation of the redis Deployment in k8s (rolling restart, node eviction/drain, image update, OOM-kill, `kubectl rollout restart`) discards the container's ephemeral filesystem entirely, silently wiping the Celery broker/result backend and the entire provider-response cache and rate-limiter counters -- exactly the behavior change the docker-compose comment says was 'confirmed live' as a real, avoidable problem and was fixed there.
details.proposed_fix: Add a `volumes`/`volumeMounts` (or convert to a StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate, matching the other three datastores) mounting a PVC at /data, and add the same `command: ["redis-server", "--save", "900", "1", "--save", "300", "10", "--save", "60", "10000"]` used in docker-compose.yml; update the stale header comment to reflect that docker-compose now does persist redis data.
details.reasoning: Verified directly. redis-deployment.yaml lines 1-4 justify the absence of any PVC by claiming docker-compose's redis service has no persistent volume. Reading the actual docker-compose.yml (lines 65-92) shows this premise is false: the redis service there has both a custom `command: ["redis-server", "--save", "900", "1", "--save", "300", "10", "--save", "60", "10000"]` and `volumes: - redis_data:/data`, added because (per that file's own comment) 'confirmed live that Redis previously had no volume at all -- every recreation ... silently reset it to empty.' The k8s redis-deployment.yaml (full file read, 64 lines) has no `command:` override, no `volumes:`, no `volumeMounts:`, and is a plain Deployment (not a StatefulSet) -- it never received the equivalent fix. I also checked the other three k8s datastores: postgres-statefulset.yaml, neo4j-statefulset.yaml, and opensearch-statefulset.yaml are all StatefulSets with volumeClaimTemplates (grep confirmed `kind: StatefulSet` and `volumeClaimTemplates` in postgres-statefulset.yaml), so redis is a genuine outlier among sibling resources, and the proposed fix (align with the other three, add PVC + save schedule) matches the codebase's own established pattern. This is not one of the listed intentional design patterns -- it's a real stale-comment-driven divergence between the two deployment paths (compose vs. k8s) for the same underlying bug. On severity: docker-compose.yml's own comment about this exact issue states the impact is 'never data-loss in the disaster-recovery sense' since redis only holds a Celery broker/result-backend for one lightweight periodic task, provider-response cache, and rate-limiter counters -- but is still 'a real, avoidable behavior change' on any pod recreation (rolling restart, node drain, OOM-kill, image update). That self-assessed impact (real but non-catastrophic operational regression, not silent data corruption of a system of record) matches P2 well; it is neither P0/P1-critical nor a cosmetic P3/P4 nitpick, so the original P2 rating is correctly calibrated and not over- or under-stated.
