details.title: Script checks for dpkg-deb but not rsync, and fails immediately when run exactly as documented
details.actual_behavior: Lines 22-25 explicitly probe for `dpkg-deb` and exit with a friendly, actionable error message if it's missing. But `rsync` -- used at lines 64 and 70 to stage the entire backend/ and frontend/ trees, i.e. the actual application payload -- is never checked for. I ran the script's own documented invocation verbatim (`docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src -w /src debian:12 bash linux/build-deb.sh`, per the header comment at line 18) against a real debian:12 container and confirmed rsync is not present in that base image; the script aborts at line 64 with a bare `linux/build-deb.sh: line 64: rsync: command not found` (exit 127) instead of the guided message the script gives for the analogous dpkg-deb case. Installing rsync first lets the same script complete successfully (verified: produces a valid horizon-grid_0.3.9_amd64.deb).
details.failure_scenario: Anyone who copies the exact command from the script's own header comment (a fresh debian:12 container, no extra setup) to build the package hits an immediate, unexplained 'command not found' failure instead of a clear prerequisite message, because the script only guards the one prerequisite (dpkg-deb) it happens to check and silently assumes rsync is already present.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reproduction, not just static reading. linux/build-deb.sh lines 22-25 probe for dpkg-deb and exit with a friendly, actionable message if missing, but no equivalent check exists for rsync, which is invoked at lines 64 and 70 to stage backend/ and frontend/ into the package. I ran the script's own documented invocation verbatim, `docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src -w /src debian:12 bash linux/build-deb.sh` (this exact command also appears in linux/README.md line 47, so it's the officially documented build path, not a one-off), and confirmed empirically:
- `docker run --rm debian:12 bash -c "command -v rsync"` -> NOTFOUND (rsync is not present in the stock debian:12 image)
- `command -v dpkg-deb` -> FOUND (so the one guard the script has is for a tool that's already present, while the tool that's actually missing goes unchecked)
- Actually running `linux/build-deb.sh` inside a fresh debian:12 container produces exactly: `linux/build-deb.sh: line 64: rsync: command not found`, and the script aborts there (set -euo pipefail), well before producing a .deb.

This is a genuine inconsistency in the script's own error-handling design -- it checks one prerequisite but not the other equally-required one used moments later in the same script -- and it directly contradicts the script's own documented zero-setup invocation. It does not match any of the listed intentional-design exceptions.

However, P1 overstates real-world impact: this is a release/build-tooling script, not runtime application code -- it has no security, data-loss, or production-availability consequence, only affects whoever is building the .deb package (not end users of the shipped app), and the fix is a single well-known command (`apt-get install -y rsync`) away, with a very recognizable "command not found" error that any Debian-packaging-literate engineer will immediately understand, even without a custom guided message. That places it as a real but moderate quality/error-handling gap rather than a high-severity blocker, so I'm correcting the severity down to P2.

details.title: No trap to clean up the mktemp -d staging directory on a failed/aborted build
details.actual_behavior: BUILD_ROOT is created via mktemp -d at line 30 and only removed at line 120, at the very end of a fully successful run. Under set -euo pipefail (line 20), any failing command earlier in the script (confirmed live: the rsync-not-found failure above) causes the script to exit immediately without reaching line 120, so BUILD_ROOT is never cleaned up. There is no trap ... EXIT to guarantee removal on the error path.
details.failure_scenario: On a real (non-containerized) Debian/Ubuntu build host -- one of the two invocation modes the script's own header comment explicitly supports ('MUST run on a real Debian/Ubuntu system (or container)') -- every failed run (missing rsync, a missing source file, a permissions problem, etc.) leaves a /tmp/tmp.XXXXXXXXXX directory containing a partial copy of the backend/frontend source tree behind permanently, accumulating disk usage over repeated failed CI/build attempts.
details.reasoning:
Read linux/build-deb.sh directly and confirmed the finding's claims line-for-line:
- Line 20: `set -euo pipefail`
- Line 30: `BUILD_ROOT="$(mktemp -d)"`
- Line 120 (last line): `rm -rf "$BUILD_ROOT"` — the only cleanup of BUILD_ROOT in the entire script
- grep for "trap" across the file returns no matches — there is no `trap ... EXIT` (or any trap) anywhere.

Given `set -e`, any failing command between line 30 and line 120 (e.g. a `cp`/`rsync` on a missing source file, a permissions error, `sed`/`dpkg-deb` failure, etc.) causes immediate script exit, skipping the line-120 cleanup and leaking the `mktemp -d` staging directory (which by that point may contain a partial rsync'd copy of backend/frontend) under /tmp.

This isn't any of the documented intentional patterns (JWT role re-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED status, AI-narration-only scoring, Basket vs. shared visibility, Security-Toolkit vs Pentest-Suite overlap, Nmap flag safety boundary, provider status semantics) — it's an unrelated shell-script resource-cleanup gap in a completely different subsystem (Debian packaging build script). So none of the listed exemptions apply, and the finding is a genuine, verifiable bug: a straightforward missing `trap 'rm -rf "$BUILD_ROOT"' EXIT` (or similar) right after line 30 would fix it.

Severity check: this only manifests as leaked space in /tmp on a persistent build host (or a CI runner reused across invocations) when the script fails partway through — it does not corrupt the shipped .deb, does not affect runtime/production behavior, and is not a security issue. The scale is bounded (a partial copy of backend/frontend minus already-excluded node_modules/venvs, cleaned by a reboot or tmpwatch/systemd-tmpfiles in most distros). This matches a P4 (minor/cosmetic, no functional or security impact, easy fix) rather than anything higher — I agree with the original reviewer's severity and see no basis to escalate it (e.g. to P3/P2) since there's no evidence of unbounded growth, sensitive-data exposure, or build-correctness impact, nor grounds to downgrade it since it is a real, concretely reproducible leak on one of the script's own documented supported invocation modes (bare Debian/Ubuntu host, not just the --rm container example).

details.title: Frontend rsync has no .env exclusion, unlike the backend rsync a few lines above
details.actual_behavior: The backend rsync (lines 64-69) explicitly excludes .venv/.venv_test/venv/.env, with a comment (lines 51-63) that specifically reasons about not shipping host-only artifacts and secrets. The frontend rsync (lines 70-72) only excludes node_modules, .next, and *.tsbuildinfo -- it has no equivalent exclusion for any dotenv-style file. Next.js projects conventionally keep real secrets (API keys, NEXTAUTH_SECRET, DB URLs) in frontend/.env, .env.local, or .env.production. Currently no such file exists in this checkout's frontend/ directory (confirmed by search), so this is a latent gap rather than an active leak today, but the exclusion logic applied to backend/ is simply absent for frontend/ despite the same rationale applying.
details.failure_scenario: If a developer later adds a frontend/.env or frontend/.env.local (a very standard Next.js pattern) containing a real secret and then builds the .deb with this script, that secret file would be copied verbatim into the shipped package at /opt/horizon-grid/app/frontend/.env(.local), with no exclusion catching it the way the backend's .env is caught.
details.reasoning:
Read linux/build-deb.sh directly (lines 44-94). Confirmed verbatim: the backend rsync (lines 64-69) has an explicit --exclude '.env' (plus .venv/.venv_test/venv), backed by a comment block (51-63) reasoning about host-only secrets/artifacts. The frontend rsync (lines 70-72) immediately below excludes only node_modules, .next, and *.tsbuildinfo -- no dotenv exclusion whatsoever. Cross-checked supporting claims: repo-root .gitignore does ignore .env/.env.* (explaining why backend needed an explicit rsync exclude, since gitignore doesn't filter rsync over a live working tree); frontend/ currently has no .env file (confirmed via directory listing), so this is indeed a dormant/latent gap rather than an active leak; frontend/Dockerfile does blanket COPY . . and docker-compose.yml currently passes frontend config via compose environment vars rather than a dotenv file, consistent with no current trigger. None of the 8 documented intentional-design-pattern exceptions apply to this finding (it's not about JWT roles, provider status, AI narration, BasketItem visibility, Security/Pentest suite overlap, or Nmap flags).

This is a real, unaddressed inconsistency: if a developer later adds a standard Next.js frontend/.env or .env.local containing real secrets and runs this script (which the script's own header comment says should be run directly against a repo checkout), that secret file would be copied verbatim into the shipped .deb with no exclusion catching it, unlike the parallel backend case. Severity P3 is appropriate: real and exploitable in principle, high impact if triggered, but currently zero likelihood (no such file exists today) and requires a specific future action to activate -- matching the original reviewer's P3/medium-confidence rating rather than warranting escalation or dismissal.

details.title: hg_open_firewall_ports (Linux's equivalent of Windows's New-AppFirewallRule) is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase
details.actual_behavior: linux/scripts/common.sh:295-322 defines hg_open_firewall_ports (and its counterpart hg_remove_firewall_ports at line 324), explicitly documented as mirroring 'Common.ps1's New-AppFirewallRule -- opens inbound TCP for the frontend/backend ports so the platform is reachable from other devices on the LAN, same intent as the Windows Private-profile-only rule.' details.failure_scenario: On a Linux host with an active default-deny ufw or firewalld (common on hardened Ubuntu/Debian/RHEL server installs), running 'sudo horizon-grid configure' completes successfully, the wizard prints a LAN URL using DetectedLanIp, and the operator tries that URL from another device on the network -- but the inbound port was never opened by the installer, so the connection times out. This directly contradicts the wizard's own Finish-page claim, with no message anywhere indicating the LAN URL might not actually be reachable (unlike Windows, which really does open the corresponding Windows Firewall rule).
details.proposed_fix: Call hg_open_firewall_ports (sourcing common.sh, or reimplementing its logic in setup_wizard.py) from run_install() right after the ports are finalized/containers are started, and hg_remove_firewall_ports from the uninstall path (prerm/postrm), mirroring Windows's New-AppFirewallRule/Remove-AppFirewallRule call sites exactly.
details.reasoning:
Verified directly against the source. linux/scripts/common.sh:295-322 defines hg_open_firewall_ports (and :324-335 hg_remove_firewall_ports), explicitly commented as mirroring Common.ps1's New-AppFirewallRule. A repo-wide grep for these two function names finds only their own definitions — no call site anywhere (not in linux/wizard/setup_wizard.py, linux/bin/horizon-grid, linux/scripts/service-start.sh, or linux/debian/postinst|postrm|prerm). setup_wizard.py's run_install() (read in full, lines 830-1004) does write the env file, sync it, run docker compose up, enable systemd units/timers, create the admin account, and validate the AI backend — but never sources common.sh, never subprocesses into it, and never opens a firewall port. Its caller run() (lines 1044-1058) then unconditionally prints 'From another device on this network: http://<DetectedLanIp>:<port>' whenever a LAN IP was detected, with no caveat.

Cross-checked the Windows side to confirm the asymmetry is real and not just a description of intended design: windows/scripts/Common.ps1:376 defines New-AppFirewallRule, and windows/wizard/Setup-Wizard.ps1:1573-1580 genuinely calls it during install ('Configuring Windows Firewall (Private networks only)...'), with try/catch that WARNs on failure but still attempts it every time. So Windows really does back its Finish-page LAN claim with an actual firewall rule attempt, while Linux's equivalent function is unreachable dead code. Also checked linux/README.md — no mention of 'firewall' anywhere, so there's no documented caveat softening the misleading Finish message either.

This doesn't match any of the listed intentional-design exceptions (JWT roles, provider NOT_CONFIGURED, AI-narration-only scoring, Basket/Case visibility, Security-Assessment-vs-Pentest-Suite overlap, exploit gating, Nmap flag restrictions, per-call ProviderStatus) — it's a straightforward install-time asymmetry between the two platforms' wizards, exactly as the original reviewer described, confirmed by reading the actual call sites rather than trusting the description.
