details.title: ufw active-check hardcodes the English-locale status string
details.actual_behavior: `ufw status 2>/dev/null | grep -qi "^Status: active"` matches only the English-locale output of `ufw status`. ufw's user-facing strings are translated when a non-English `LANG`/`LC_ALL` is active on the host.
details.failure_scenario: On a Linux host configured with a non-English locale, `ufw status` prints a translated status line (e.g. a French/German/Spanish equivalent of 'Status: active'); the grep never matches even though ufw is actively enforcing rules, so hg_open_firewall_ports silently falls through to 'no active firewall manager detected -- nothing to configure', leaving the platform's ports blocked by ufw with no rule ever added and no error surfaced beyond an informational log line.
details.proposed_fix: Force a stable, locale-independent check, e.g. `LC_ALL=C ufw status` (ufw supports this) before grepping, or parse `ufw status verbose`'s machine-consistent exit behavior instead of matching translated text.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading common.sh lines 295-322: hg_open_firewall_ports's ufw branch is `command -v ufw >/dev/null 2>&1 && ufw status 2>/dev/null | grep -qi "^Status: active"`. ufw is a Python tool whose status-line strings are wrapped in gettext and translated via shipped .mo catalogs for many locales (fr/de/es/it/pt/ru, etc.), so on a host configured with a non-English LANG/LC_ALL, `ufw status` prints a translated status line and the English-only grep never matches. Because that grep is ANDed into the same if-condition, the branch is skipped even though ufw is genuinely active; execution falls through past the (also-false) firewalld elif to the else branch, and the script logs/echoes "No active firewall manager detected -- nothing to configure" -- a factually incorrect diagnostic -- and never adds the allow rule for the app's ports. This matches the reviewer's described mechanism exactly and is a real, if narrow, correctness bug not covered by any of the documented intentional-design exceptions. Severity is appropriately low: it fails safe (no unintended port is ever opened, nothing insecure is exposed), only affects non-English-locale Linux hosts with ufw active, and only defeats a best-effort LAN-reachability convenience feature that already has an explicit non-fatal fallback path by design -- worst case the user manually runs `ufw allow <port>`. P4 (trivial, locale-dependent, non-security, easily worked around) matches the actual impact; I would not raise it higher since the code's own stated design already tolerates "no firewall rule added" as an acceptable outcome, and this bug only makes that outcome trigger under an extra condition (translated locale) rather than introducing any new risk.

titles: hg_read_env_var's sed pattern does not actually strip trailing whitespace from the parsed value

details.title: hg_read_env_var's sed pattern does not actually strip trailing whitespace from the parsed value
details.actual_behavior: The extraction pattern is `s/^\s*${key}\s*=\s*\(.*\)\s*$/\1/p`. Because `.*` is greedy and POSIX/GNU regex leftmost-longest matching lets the capture group consume the rest of the line (including any trailing spaces), the trailing `\s*$` matches zero characters and contributes nothing -- any trailing whitespace on the value's line is returned as part of the value instead of being trimmed. I reproduced this directly: `printf 'HOST_PORT_BACKEND=8080  \n'` piped through the exact pattern from this function returns `8080  ` (two trailing spaces preserved), not `8080`.
details.failure_scenario: An admin manually edits /etc/horizon-grid/.env (a plain text file they are told is 'the real environment file') and leaves a trailing space after a value, e.g. `POSTGRES_USER=ioc `. backup-database.sh and restore-database.sh call `hg_read_env_var POSTGRES_USER` and pass the result straight into `pg_dump -U "$PG_USER" "$PG_DB"` / `psql`; the trailing-space-corrupted username no longer matches the real Postgres role, so the backup/restore silently fails (logged as an ERROR, but not surfaced anywhere the operator is likely to see it if run from cron/watchdog). The same corruption applies to HOST_PORT_BACKEND/HOST_PORT_FRONTEND used by hg_test_backend_health/hg_test_frontend_health, which build `base_url="http://${host}:${port}"` -- a trailing-whitespace port breaks the constructed URL and the watchdog reports the service unhealthy even when it is fine.
details.proposed_fix: Use a pattern that actually trims, e.g. capture non-greedily or post-process: `sed -n "s/^[[:space:]]*${key}[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*//p" file | sed -e 's/[[:space:]]*$//' -e 's/\r$//'`, or trim in bash afterward with `value="${value%%[[:space:]]}"`-style loops / `read -r` based parsing.
details.reasoning:
Verified by reading C:/Users/User/ioc-intel-platform/linux/scripts/common.sh lines 337-345 and reproducing the exact sed invocation:

`sed -n "s/^\s*${key}\s*=\s*\(.*\)\s*$/\1/p" "$HORIZON_GRID_ENV_FILE" | tail -n1`

Reproduction: `printf 'HOST_PORT_BACKEND=8080  \n' | sed -n 's/^\s*HOST_PORT_BACKEND\s*=\s*\(.*\)\s*$/\1/p'` returns `8080  ` (trailing spaces intact, confirmed via `cat -A`). This is exactly the greedy-`.*`-vs-zero-width-anchor issue the finding describes: `.*` inside the capture group greedily consumes to end of line, so the trailing `\s*$` outside the capture always matches zero characters and never trims anything, while the leading `^\s*${key}\s*=\s*` (outside the capture group) does correctly strip leading whitespace. This asymmetry is real, not a description error by the reviewer.

Confirmed the call chain exactly as claimed:
- `hg_test_backend_health`/`hg_test_frontend_health` (common.sh lines 251, 276) call `hg_read_env_var HOST_PORT_BACKEND`/`HOST_PORT_FRONTEND` and build `base_url` directly from the unstripped result.
- `backup-database.sh` line 45 and `restore-database.sh` line 64 both do `PG_USER="$(hg_read_env_var POSTGRES_USER)"; PG_USER="${PG_USER:-ioc}"` (the `:-` fallback only triggers on empty string, not on a value with trailing whitespace) and pass `$PG_USER` straight into `pg_dump -U "$PG_USER"` / `psql -U "$PG_USER"`.
- Confirmed backup-database.sh is invoked unattended and quietly: `linux/systemd/horizon-grid-backup.service` runs `horizon-grid backup --quiet` daily via a timer, and in `--quiet` mode `say()` is a no-op, so a failure only reaches `hg_log` (the setup log) via `hg_log "...ERROR"` at line 58 — never surfaced to an operator watching a terminal. This matches the finding's "silently fails ... not surfaced anywhere the operator is likely to see it if run from cron/watchdog" claim precisely.

This is not one of the documented intentional patterns; it's a genuine off-by-design regex bug with a concrete, verified reproduction and a real (if manually-triggered) failure path through two independently-confirmed call sites. Severity: the original P2 is appropriate — real impact (silent backup failures, false-unhealthy watchdog reports) but gated behind a non-default trigger (an admin manually introducing trailing whitespace when hand-editing the plain-text .env file), and the consequence is a stalled/failed backup or a false health alert rather than direct data loss or a security compromise, so it doesn't rise to P0/P1.

titles: Status script uses `docker compose ps` without `-a`, hiding crashed/exited containers
Container-listing subshell's failure is never checked, silently swallowing a real error

details.title: Status script uses `docker compose ps` without `-a`, hiding crashed/exited containers
details.actual_behavior: Line 24 runs `docker compose ... ps` with no `-a`/`--all` flag. Docker Compose's `ps` without `-a` only lists containers that are currently running (or restarting); any container that has exited/crashed (e.g. `restart: "no"`, or a crash loop that has already given up and settled into `Exited`) is silently omitted from the table entirely -- not shown as unhealthy, just absent.
details.failure_scenario: Reproduced live: a compose project with one service that runs `exit 1` (restart: "no") and one that stays up -- `docker compose ps` (no flags) printed only the healthy 'runner' row and completely omitted the 'exiter' row that was sitting in `Exited (1)`; `docker compose ps -a` showed both. In production this means: if the postgres/backend/redis container in HORIZON GRID's compose stack has crashed and is not configured to auto-restart (or has exhausted its restart policy and is sitting Exited), `horizon-grid status` shows nothing at all for it under 'Containers:' -- exactly the scenario (something crashed) that this diagnostic script exists to surface.
details.proposed_fix: Add `-a`/`--all` to the `ps` invocation (or switch to `hg_invoke_docker_compose ps -a` for consistency with the other scripts' env/host-gateway handling).
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct inspection and by running `docker compose ps --help` on this host: without -a/--all, docker compose ps omits stopped/exited containers entirely rather than listing them as down. linux/scripts/service-status.sh line 24 invokes `docker compose ... ps` with no -a, and its own docstring (lines 2-5) states this script exists to show whether the platform is 'installed, running, and healthy' -- i.e. it is the tool meant to surface exactly this failure mode. Cross-checked docker-compose.yml: all services use `restart: unless-stopped`, which narrows (but does not eliminate) the original reviewer's crash-loop scenario, since Docker retries indefinitely under that policy rather than permanently settling into Exited. However, the same restart policy explicitly honors an operator's manual `docker compose stop <service>` (per an in-repo comment explaining this design choice), which is a realistic maintenance scenario -- if an operator stops one container and later checks status, that container's row silently vanishes from 'Containers:' rather than showing as stopped. Also checked the script's Health checks section: it only probes backend/frontend HTTP, giving zero redundant signal for postgres/redis/neo4j/opensearch/celery_worker/celery_beat, so for those six services the ps table is the only signal this script provides and the blind spot is total. Also confirmed the Windows mirror (Service-Status.ps1) has the identical gap. This is not one of the documented intentional design patterns. The fix (add -a, or use hg_invoke_docker_compose ps -a) is trivial and low-risk. Real-world impact is moderate rather than critical -- no data loss/security exposure, most crash scenarios self-heal and would still appear as Restarting/Up -- so P2 (as originally claimed) is the right level, not P0/P1.

details.title: Container-listing subshell's failure is never checked, silently swallowing a real error
details.actual_behavior: The `( cd ... || exit 1; docker compose ... ps )` block's exit status is never checked -- unlike every other docker-compose invocation in this batch (start/stop/restart all wrap `hg_invoke_docker_compose` in an `if`), here the subshell just runs unconditionally and the script falls straight through to the 'Health checks:' section afterward with no message at all if it failed.
details.failure_scenario: If the app repo directory has been moved/removed while `/etc/horizon-grid/.env` still exists (e.g. a partially-completed reinstall), `cd "$HORIZON_GRID_APP_REPO_DIR"` fails inside the subshell, the subshell exits 1, and the script continues to the next section with the 'Containers:' block simply empty -- no 'directory not found' or any other diagnostic, in a script whose entire purpose is diagnostics.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the subshell in an `if ! ( ... ); then echo "Could not list containers (is $HORIZON_GRID_APP_REPO_DIR present?)"; fi` the same way start/stop/restart check `hg_invoke_docker_compose`.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading service-status.sh lines 20-25: the subshell `( cd "$HORIZON_GRID_APP_REPO_DIR" || exit 1; docker compose ... ps )` is invoked with no if/exit-status check, unlike hg_invoke_docker_compose's callers elsewhere in this batch (service-start.sh, service-stop.sh, service-restart.sh, open-platform.sh all wrap the compose call in `if ! hg_invoke_docker_compose ...`). If HORIZON_GRID_APP_REPO_DIR is missing (e.g. a partially completed reinstall that left .env in place but removed the app repo), `cd` fails, `exit 1` fires inside the subshell with no message printed, and control falls straight through to the blank line and 'Health checks:' section -- the 'Containers:' block is left empty with zero diagnostic text, in a script whose sole purpose is diagnostics. This is a genuine gap, not one of the documented intentional patterns (it doesn't involve auth/role trust, provider status semantics, AI narration, basket visibility, toolkit/pentest overlap, or nmap flags). Note diagnostics.sh has the analogous unchecked subshell but redirects compose output to a file, so a failure there is at least captured in the bundle; service-status.sh prints directly to stdout with nothing captured, so a cd failure produces true silence. Severity: real-world impact is low -- this is a read-only status/diagnostic command, no data loss or security exposure, and the operator still gets other signal via the subsequent 'Health checks' section (Backend API / Web interface would likely show NOT RESPONDING) and the Docker Engine / systemd sections below, plus the conspicuously empty 'Containers:' block itself is a (weak) hint. The original P4 (trivial/cosmetic) rating is appropriate; I would not raise it.

titles: Script's own exit code never reflects accumulated [FAIL] results

details.title: Script's own exit code never reflects accumulated [FAIL] results
details.actual_behavior: The script tracks pass/fail purely via textual `[PASS]`/`[FAIL]` markers written to $RESULTS_FILE (via the pass()/fail() helpers), but never accumulates a FAIL_COUNT and never turns that into the script's own process exit status. The final statement executed is `cp "$RESULTS_FILE" "/tmp/final-results-${DISTRO_LABEL}.txt"` (line 249), whose own exit code (almost always 0, since the source file always exists and is just being copied) becomes the script's exit status. Every step from Step 5 onward (health check, admin login, IOC investigation, provider/dashboard endpoints, backup, stop/start persistence, apt remove/reinstall/purge behavior) only ever calls pass()/fail()/info() -- none of those raise the script's own exit status on failure.
details.failure_scenario: A real regression breaks, e.g., investigation persistence across stop/start (Step 10) or apt purge leaving stale volumes behind (Step 13) -- multiple `[FAIL]` lines get written to the results file and printed to console -- but any CI/automation wrapper that runs `bash e2e-test.sh <deb> <distro>` and checks `$?` (the conventional way to gate a pipeline) will see exit code 0 and treat the run as a full pass, silently shipping the regression. Only a human (or a second process) manually re-grepping the log for `[FAIL]` would ever notice.
details.proposed_fix: Track FAIL_COUNT (e.g. increment it inside fail()) and end the script with `[ "$FAIL_COUNT" -eq 0 ]` (or `exit 1` if nonzero), the same pattern already used correctly in the sibling script linux/scripts/test_host_gateway_detection.sh.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of C:\Users\User\ioc-intel-platform\linux\test\e2e-test.sh. The script uses `set -uo pipefail` (no `-e`), and pass()/fail()/info() (lines 22-24) are simple echo+tee helpers that never touch any counter or exit status. Grepping the whole file confirms there is no FAIL_COUNT variable and no `exit` statement anywhere after line 102 (the only two `exit 1` calls, lines 67 and 101, are early-exit guards for docker-compose-plugin/wizard failures, not related to the Step 5-13 pass/fail tracking). The script's tail end (lines 242-249) only prints PASS/FAIL counts via `grep -c` and greps failing lines for visibility; the final statement executed is `cp "$RESULTS_FILE" "/tmp/final-results-${DISTRO_LABEL}.txt"`, whose own exit status (source file always exists, so cp essentially always succeeds) becomes the script's exit code. So a run with real [FAIL] lines from Step 5 onward (health check, login, investigation, provider/dashboard endpoints, backup, stop/start persistence, apt remove/reinstall/purge checks) still exits 0. I also confirmed the sibling script linux/scripts/test_host_gateway_detection.sh implements the correct pattern (PASS_COUNT/FAIL_COUNT incremented in pass()/fail(), final line `[ "$FAIL_COUNT" -eq 0 ]` sets the exit status), proving this is an inconsistency/regression relative to an established in-repo pattern, not a stylistic choice. This doesn't match any of the 8 listed intentional-design-pattern exclusions.

Severity correction: downgrading from P1 to P2. This script's own header states it is 'test infrastructure, not part of the product' (not shipped in the .deb), and I found no CI workflow (checked .github/workflows/*.yml) or wrapper script anywhere in the repo that currently invokes e2e-test.sh and gates on its exit code -- the claimed 'CI/automation wrapper... checks $?' failure scenario is plausible/foreseeable but not something I could confirm is actually wired up today. Additionally, a human running this interactively still sees the printed 'PASS count:'/'FAIL count:' summary and the literal [FAIL] lines on the console before the script exits, so the failure isn't fully silent for an attentive operator -- only exit-code-only automation would be fooled. The bug is real and the fix is trivial and clearly warranted (matching the sibling script's pattern), but given no confirmed current automated consumer depends on this exit code and it's confined to non-shipped QA tooling, P2 (moderate) is a more accurate severity than P1 (high).

titles: Script's own exit code never reflects accumulated [FAIL] results

details.title: Script's own exit code never reflects accumulated [FAIL] results
details.actual_behavior: Same defect as in e2e-test.sh: no FAIL_COUNT is tracked, and the script's final statement is `grep '^\[FAIL\]' "$RESULTS_FILE" || echo "(no failures)"`. If there ARE `[FAIL]` lines, grep finds a match and exits 0 (the `||` branch is skipped) -- so the script exits 0 precisely in the failure case. If there are NO `[FAIL]` lines, grep exits 1 but the `|| echo "(no failures)"` branch runs and exits 0. Either way the script's own exit status is always 0, so it carries zero pass/fail signal.
details.failure_scenario: A real regression in the default-project-name ("app") remove/purge path -- e.g. apt purge leaving Docker volumes behind, or /opt/horizon-grid/app not being fully removed -- produces `[FAIL]` lines in the log, but `bash isolated-purge-test.sh <deb>; echo $?` still prints 0. Any CI step gating on the exit code treats a genuinely broken purge path as a pass.
details.proposed_fix: Track a FAIL_COUNT (increment inside fail()) and end the script with `[ "$FAIL_COUNT" -eq 0 ]`, matching linux/scripts/test_host_gateway_detection.sh's pattern.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading the actual file (C:/Users/User/ioc-intel-platform/linux/test/isolated-purge-test.sh, lines 60-63) and by empirical test. The script uses `set -uo pipefail` (no `-e`), never accumulates a fail counter, and its final statement is `grep '^\[FAIL\]' "$RESULTS_FILE" || echo "(no failures)"`. I reproduced both branches with a minimal repro: when the results file contains a `[FAIL]` line, grep finds a match, prints it, and exits 0 (so the `||` branch is skipped) -> script exits 0. When there are no `[FAIL]` lines, grep exits 1 but the `|| echo "(no failures)"` branch runs and echo exits 0 -> script also exits 0. So the script's own exit status is unconditionally 0 regardless of whether any assertion (pass()/fail() calls on lines 21, 23, 31, 33, 37, 46, 47, 50, 55-58) failed. This exactly matches the claim, and is a real defect in the error-handling/reporting logic: any caller that gates on `$?` alone (without also parsing the printed FAIL count or output) cannot detect a failed purge/remove test run. I also confirmed the codebase has an established better pattern (linux/scripts/test_host_gateway_detection.sh: FAIL_COUNT incremented in fail(), final line `[ "$FAIL_COUNT" -eq 0 ]`), supporting the reviewer's proposed fix as reasonable and consistent with existing conventions.

Severity correction: the original P1 is overstated. This script's own header comment says it is 'Not shipped in the .deb -- test infrastructure only,' and a repo-wide search found no GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/*.yml) or any other script that invokes isolated-purge-test.sh and checks its exit code — it is currently only run manually/ad hoc, and when run manually the FAIL lines and FAIL count are printed directly to stdout, so a human operator would still see them even though $? is wrong. The bug is real and should be fixed (it is a footgun for any future CI wiring, and is inconsistent with the codebase's own established pattern), but its current real-world blast radius is limited to a non-shipped test script with no discovered automated consumer of its exit code today, so P2 (moderate, should-fix, not urgent/high-impact) is a more accurate severity than P1.

titles: http_json() success path crashes the whole wizard on a non-JSON 200 body

details.title: http_json() success path crashes the whole wizard on a non-JSON 200 body
details.actual_behavior: In http_json(), the success branch does `return resp.status, (json.loads(raw) if raw else {})` with no try/except around json.loads. The HTTPError branch a few lines below (470-473) explicitly wraps its own json.loads in `try/except (ValueError, TypeError)` and falls back to a `{"detail": ...}` dict, but the 2xx success path has no equivalent guard.
details.failure_scenario: Any endpoint the wizard calls (/api/v1/auth/login, /api/v1/auth/register, /api/v1/ai/test, /api/v1/providers/{id}/test, /health/detailed) returns HTTP 200/201 with a body that isn't valid JSON -- e.g. a reverse proxy or misconfigured middleware returns a 200 HTML page, or a backend bug/truncated response body. json.loads(raw) raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError subclass), which propagates unhandled out of http_json through every call site (none of which wrap the call in try/except), crashing the entire wizard with a raw traceback instead of the graceful fail()/log() error handling used everywhere else in this file.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the success-path json.loads the same way the HTTPError branch does: on ValueError/TypeError, return (resp.status, {"detail": raw.decode("utf-8", "replace")}) instead of letting the exception escape.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading setup_wizard.py lines 458-476. http_json()'s success path (line 467) does `return resp.status, (json.loads(raw) if raw else {})` inside a bare `try` that only has `except urllib.error.HTTPError` and `except (urllib.error.URLError, OSError)` handlers -- neither catches json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError subclass). The HTTPError branch immediately below (470-473) explicitly wraps its own json.loads in `try/except (ValueError, TypeError)` with a `{"detail": ...}` fallback, proving the author was aware of this exact failure mode and guarded for it in one branch but not the symmetric one -- strong evidence of an oversight rather than intentional design. I grepped every call site (get_or_create_session, test_ai_connection, test_provider_connection, the /health/detailed polling loop, admin register/login in run_install) and none of them wrap the http_json() call in try/except; I also checked Wizard.run() and main() and confirmed there is no top-level try/except Exception anywhere in the file. So an unhandled JSONDecodeError from a 2xx-with-non-JSON-body response would propagate all the way out of main() as a raw traceback, breaking the fail()/log() error-handling convention used consistently elsewhere in this file. The failure trigger is plausible, not contrived: BACKEND_HOST is overridable via the HORIZON_GRID_BACKEND_HOST env var (not hardcoded to loopback), and the file's own comments (line 400) explicitly anticipate 'reverse-proxy or other non-default setup' deployments -- exactly the topology that can turn a healthy 200 into an HTML/proxy body on redirect or misconfiguration. The /health/detailed polling loop and the --non-interactive/--answers-file unattended install path (explicitly documented as being for 'the automated test suite / unattended installs') make this more than theoretical since there's no human present to notice and retry. This doesn't match any of the 8 documented intentional-pattern exclusions. Severity: P2 is appropriate -- it's a real, plausible crash-on-edge-input bug in installer/reconfigure error handling (not P0/P1 since it's confined to the setup wizard rather than runtime app behavior, causes no data loss or security exposure, and is generally retryable), but it's more than a cosmetic P3/P4 nit given the documented reverse-proxy deployment path and the unattended-install use case where a raw traceback replaces a clear failure message.

titles: _remove_stale_volume() discards docker volume rm's exit code, silently defeating its own purpose on failure
_remove_stale_volume()'s docker label filter hardcodes the Compose project name as "app", breaking silently under a customized APP_REPO_DIR

details.title: _remove_stale_volume() discards docker volume rm's exit code, silently defeating its own purpose on failure
details.actual_behavior: `subprocess.run(["docker", "volume", "rm", volume_id], capture_output=True)` on line 1042 never checks `.returncode` and never logs/prints on failure -- contrast with `_backup_before_upgrade()` earlier in the same file (lines 822-828), which explicitly checks `result.returncode` and logs a WARN plus prints a message on failure. This function's own docstring at the call site explains it exists specifically so 'the new password can initialize cleanly.'
details.failure_scenario: A previous failed install attempt left a Postgres volume plus still-running containers referencing it (common: `docker compose up` was interrupted or errored after creating the volume but before writing .env). `docker volume rm` then fails with "volume is in use" (or a permissions error). The fresh install proceeds anyway with the stale volume still mounted, initialized under the OLD Postgres password, while the newly generated .env carries a brand-new POSTGRES_PASSWORD; Postgres never reinitializes its already-populated data directory, the backend can't authenticate to it, and the wizard eventually fails with the generic, misleading 'Backend did not become healthy in time' message -- with zero trace anywhere pointing back at the real root cause (the un-removed volume).
details.proposed_fix: Capture text output and check the return code; on non-zero, log a WARN with stderr and print an actionable message telling the operator to stop any containers using the volume and remove it manually before re-running.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading setup_wizard.py lines 1030-1042 directly. _remove_stale_volume() runs `docker volume ls -q` to find a leftover postgres_data volume from a prior failed install attempt (only called on fresh installs, line 856-857: `if not self.is_upgrade: self._remove_stale_volume()`), and if found, calls `subprocess.run(["docker", "volume", "rm", volume_id], capture_output=True)` on line 1042 without ever inspecting `result.returncode` or the captured stdout/stderr, and without any logging or printing on failure. This is a clear, direct contrast with `_backup_before_upgrade()` at lines 803-828 in the very same file, which explicitly checks `result.returncode`, prints a WARNING with the exit code on failure, and logs a WARN -- that function's own docstring even states the design principle being violated here: "reflect what actually happened, don't just print success."

I also traced the call chain: there is no other cleanup of leftover containers anywhere in this file (verified via grep for "docker"/"container" across the whole file), so a container left behind by an interrupted/failed prior `docker compose up --build` attempt can still hold a reference to the postgres_data volume, making `docker volume rm` fail with a "volume is in use" error. Because the return code is discarded, execution proceeds straight to `docker compose up -d --build` (lines 870-877, no --remove-orphans, no prior `compose down`), which will reuse the pre-existing volume (Postgres only applies POSTGRES_PASSWORD on first init of an empty data directory) while the freshly written .env carries a brand-new password. The backend then can't authenticate to Postgres, the /health/detailed poll times out, and the wizard fails with the generic "Backend did not become healthy in time. Run 'horizon-grid status' for detail." (line 894) -- with no log line or printed message anywhere pointing back at the actual root cause (the volume-removal failure). This is a genuine error-handling gap that defeats the function's own stated purpose, and none of the 8 documented intentional-design exceptions apply.

Severity: the precondition (a prior failed install leaving a container still attached to the volume) is narrow rather than routine, and it only affects fresh installs, but when it fires it can fully block a working install with a misleading error and zero diagnostic trail. That matches the moderate-but-real-impact profile of P2 as originally claimed -- I don't see grounds to escalate to P1 (no data loss/security impact, and recoverable via manual `docker container rm` + `docker volume rm` once diagnosed) or downgrade to P3 (impact is a complete, hard-to-diagnose install failure, not merely cosmetic).

details.title: _remove_stale_volume()'s docker label filter hardcodes the Compose project name as "app", breaking silently under a customized APP_REPO_DIR
details.actual_behavior: The docker volume filter uses the literal string `label=com.docker.compose.project=app` (line 1033). Docker Compose derives the project name from the basename of the compose project directory (no `name:` key is set in docker-compose.yml/docker-compose.prod.yml, confirmed by inspection) -- so this filter only matches when APP_REPO_DIR's basename is literally "app", which is true only for the default `/opt/horizon-grid/app`.
details.failure_scenario: HORIZON_GRID_APP_REPO_DIR is a documented, supported override (used by, e.g., the Docker-sibling-container test harness mentioned in this file's own module docstring for BACKEND_HOST). If it's set to any path whose final component isn't "app" (e.g. `/srv/horizon-stack`), docker compose's real project name differs from "app", the label filter matches zero volumes, `_remove_stale_volume()` becomes a silent no-op, and the exact stale-volume/wrong-password failure mode this function exists to prevent (see the P2 finding above) can occur with no cleanup attempted at all -- and no warning that the check was skipped.
details.proposed_fix: Derive the expected project label from `os.path.basename(os.path.normpath(APP_REPO_DIR))` instead of the literal "app", or pass an explicit `-p`/COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME consistently everywhere docker compose is invoked and filter on that same value.
details.reasoning: Verified by reading setup_wizard.py directly: APP_REPO_DIR (line 61) is env-overridable via HORIZON_GRID_APP_REPO_DIR; docker compose is invoked with cwd=APP_REPO_DIR and no -p/project-name flag (lines ~866-874); _remove_stale_volume() (1030-1036) hardcodes label=com.docker.compose.project=app. Confirmed docker-compose.yml/docker-compose.prod.yml have no top-level `name:` key, so Compose's project name defaults to the basename of the invocation directory (or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME env var, which run_install() passes through unmodified via os.environ.copy()). Cross-file evidence in the same repo proves this isn't theoretical: common.sh's bash equivalent has the identical hardcoded 'app' filter; backup-database.sh's own comment acknowledges the Windows/bash version's hardcoded name only matches Compose's default 'app' project and breaks for anyone customizing COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME or for "the automated multi-distro test harness, which deliberately uses a non-default project name per distro"; and e2e-test.sh literally does `export COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME="hgtest_${DISTRO_LABEL}"` before invoking setup_wizard.py --non-interactive, which will produce actual Docker volumes/containers labeled with that project name while _remove_stale_volume's filter still looks for 'app'. This is a genuine, reproducible bug in a supported code path (not one of the documented intentional patterns). Severity: default single-host installs are unaffected (basename 'app', no override), so blast radius is limited to non-default APP_REPO_DIR or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME configurations; the failure mode is a silent no-op reverting to the pre-mitigation crash-loop symptom, recoverable manually, with no data loss or security impact — consistent with the reviewer's P3 rating.

titles: "Remove Everything" uninstall path unconditionally DelTrees ProgramData even if the docker compose down -v Exec call fails, so a failed volume removal still results in permanent config/credential loss with the containers/volumes left orphaned
No timeout on any blocking docker compose Exec call during uninstall -- a hung Docker Desktop freezes the entire uninstaller with no visible feedback

details.title: "Remove Everything" uninstall path unconditionally DelTrees ProgramData even if the docker compose down -v Exec call fails, so a failed volume removal still results in permanent config/credential loss with the containers/volumes left orphaned
details.actual_behavior: The Exec call at lines 349-354 populates ResultCode but the code never inspects it (nor Exec's own Boolean return value) before proceeding unconditionally to `if DirExists(DataDir) then DelTree(DataDir, True, True, True);` at lines 356-357.
details.failure_scenario: Docker Desktop is not running (or is mid-update/unresponsive) when the admin uninstalls with Remove Everything. `docker compose ... down -v` fails immediately with a non-zero exit code and removes nothing. The code does not notice and proceeds to permanently delete C:\ProgramData\IOC Intelligence Platform (config\.env with credentials, logs, backups) anyway. Result: the Postgres/Neo4j/OpenSearch volumes and containers are left running/orphaned on disk indefinitely (nothing left to manage or reference them, since ProgramData and the app binaries are now both gone), while the admin was told this action removes everything.
details.proposed_fix: Check ResultCode (and Exec's Boolean return) after the down -v call; if it's non-zero, warn the admin (MsgBox) before proceeding with DelTree, or retry, rather than silently deleting ProgramData regardless of outcome.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading windows/installer.iss directly (InitializeUninstall, lines 275-370).

The RemoveEverything branch (329-357) is exactly as described:
- Lines 349-354: `Exec('powershell.exe', ... 'docker compose ... --env-file ... down -v"', AppDir+'\app', SW_HIDE, ewWaitUntilTerminated, ResultCode);` — ResultCode is populated (ewWaitUntilTerminated means it waits for the process and fills in the real exit code), and Exec's own Boolean return is discarded as a bare statement.
- Lines 356-357: `if DirExists(DataDir) then DelTree(DataDir, True, True, True);` runs immediately after, with zero reference to ResultCode or Exec's return value anywhere in between.

The surrounding comments (269-274, 331-348) make the intent explicit: `down -v` is "the actual data-destroying step," and the whole confirm-with-typed-DELETE ceremony exists because this is supposed to be a verified, irreversible teardown. Yet nothing verifies it. I confirmed the codebase does have a precedent for checking ResultCode correctly (RunPrereqCheck, lines 154-168: `Result := (ResultCode = 0);`), so the omission here is inconsistent with the codebase's own pattern, not a stylistic choice.

I also checked for any earlier gate that would prevent this scenario (e.g., a Docker-running precheck before uninstall) — there is none. RunPrereqCheck only runs during install's NextButtonClick (line 185-198), not during uninstall. UninstallSilent() only affects whether the destructive path is offered at all, not whether Docker is verified to be reachable once chosen. So there is nothing stopping an admin from choosing "Remove Everything," having `docker compose down -v` fail (Docker Desktop not running/mid-update/unresponsive — Exec still returns cleanly with a non-zero ResultCode in that case, it doesn't hang), and the installer proceeding to permanently wipe ProgramData (config\.env with credentials, logs, backups) with no MsgBox, no retry, and no indication to the admin that the "permanently deletes all cases, investigations, watchlists, notes, the database, and all saved credentials" promise they just typed DELETE to confirm was not actually fulfilled for the Docker-side data. The Postgres/Neo4j/OpenSearch volumes remain on disk indefinitely in that failure case, orphaned, with the app binaries and ProgramData now both gone.

This isn't one of the listed intentional design patterns — it's a straightforward missing error-check on a self-described "verified teardown" step, contradicting the codebase's own comments about what this branch is for.

Severity: I agree with the original P2. It requires a specific precondition (Docker Desktop not running/responsive at the moment of uninstall) rather than firing on every uninstall, and the local impact — leftover local Docker volumes/containers + a false "everything removed" impression — is real but bounded to the admin's own machine with a manual `docker volume prune`/reinstall recovery path available; it doesn't rise to a crash, remote exposure, or routine-path data loss that would justify P0/P1, but it is a genuine violation of an explicitly promised, security-sensitive irreversible operation and warrants a real fix (check ResultCode/Exec's return, MsgBox-warn or abort on failure) rather than being dismissed.

details.title: No timeout on any blocking docker compose Exec call during uninstall -- a hung Docker Desktop freezes the entire uninstaller with no visible feedback
details.actual_behavior: All Exec calls in InitializeUninstall (lines 349-354, 364-369, 378-381, 390-395) use ewWaitUntilTerminated with SW_HIDE and no timeout. Pascal Script's Exec has no timeout parameter, and none of these calls are wrapped in a manual polling/timeout loop.
details.failure_scenario: Docker Desktop is stuck (e.g. still starting up, or its named pipe is unresponsive) when the admin uninstalls. `docker compose ... down` (or `down -v`) hangs indefinitely. Because the window is hidden (SW_HIDE) and there's no timeout, the uninstaller appears completely frozen with zero visual indication of why -- indistinguishable from a crash -- and the admin has no way to proceed short of killing the process in Task Manager.
details.proposed_fix: Use ewNoWait plus a manual wait loop with a bounded timeout (polling the process handle / using WaitForSingleObject via a helper), and surface a message if the timeout is hit, rather than an unbounded synchronous wait.
details.reasoning:
Read C:/Users/User/ioc-intel-platform/windows/installer.iss lines 150-416 directly. The finding is accurate to the code: InitializeUninstall (lines 275-415) contains four Exec calls -- the "down -v" data-destroying path (349-354), the keep-data "down" path (364-369), the firewall-rule removal (378-381), and the scheduled-task removal (390-395) -- and every single one uses `ewWaitUntilTerminated` with `SW_HIDE` and no timeout argument. Inno Setup's Pascal Script Exec() signature (Filename, Params, WorkingDir, ShowCmd, Wait, ResultCode) genuinely has no built-in timeout parameter, and none of these four calls is wrapped in any polling/timeout loop -- confirmed by reading the whole function body, there is no such loop anywhere in the file.

Critically, InitializeUninstall runs before Inno Setup's uninstall progress UI exists at all (this is standard Inno Setup event-function ordering, and the file's own comments confirm this: the PromptTypeDeleteToConfirm custom form exists specifically because "there is no wizard page flow during an uninstall"). Combined with SW_HIDE on the docker-compose child process, if `docker compose ... down [-v]` hangs (a real, known Docker Desktop failure mode -- named pipe/daemon unresponsive after sleep/resume, WSL2 backend issues, etc.), the entire Setup process's UI thread blocks indefinitely with literally zero visual feedback, indistinguishable from a crash, and the only recovery is killing it in Task Manager. I also checked Common.ps1 (Invoke-DockerCompose, used by the rest of the app's PowerShell scripts) and found the same lack-of-timeout pattern project-wide, confirming this isn't a one-off but a real, consistent architectural gap -- not something covered by any of the eight documented "intentional design pattern" exemptions (none of which relate to installer process lifecycle).

This doesn't match any known intentional pattern in the exemption list. Severity: this is a real but bounded-impact issue -- it requires a precondition (Docker Desktop already hung) outside the installer's control, causes no data corruption or security exposure (in the RemoveEverything branch, DelTree only runs after the Exec call returns, so a hang there blocks deletion rather than causing partial/corrupt deletion), and has a manual recovery path via Task Manager. That matches a P3 (real reliability/UX defect, not data-loss/security-critical) rather than P0-P2 or a trivial P4, so I'm keeping the original reviewer's severity of P3.

titles: icacls lockdown failure in Initialize-DataDirectories is silently swallowed
icacls /grant:r in Initialize-DataDirectories does not strip pre-existing explicit ACEs for other trustees

details.title: icacls lockdown failure in Initialize-DataDirectories is silently swallowed
details.actual_behavior: `$null = & icacls.exe ... 2>&1` discards all icacls output and never inspects $LASTEXITCODE or the captured text; if icacls fails for any reason the function still returns normally with no warning and no log entry.
details.failure_scenario: icacls.exe fails on this call (e.g. an unexpected filesystem/ACL provider quirk, or icacls rejecting the SID syntax on some Windows build) -- Initialize-DataDirectories returns as if the directory were locked down, the wizard proceeds to write the real .env (API keys, JWT secret) into that still-default-ACL directory, and nothing in setup.log records that the lockdown didn't actually happen.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading Common.ps1 directly. Line 106 is exactly as described:

`$null = & icacls.exe $script:DataDir /inheritance:r /grant:r "*S-1-5-32-544:(OI)(CI)F" "*S-1-5-18:(OI)(CI)F" 2>&1`

This discards icacls's merged stdout/stderr into $null and the function never inspects $LASTEXITCODE afterward, nor is there any try/catch. Initialize-DataDirectories's own docstring (lines 92-94) states its purpose is explicitly security-critical: "locks it down to Administrators + SYSTEM only -- the .env file it will contain has real API keys and a JWT signing secret in it." If icacls.exe fails (non-zero exit, e.g. blocked by AV/EDR heuristics that flag recursive DACL resets, or any other ACL-provider quirk), the function returns exactly as if the lockdown succeeded.

I traced the only two call sites:
- Setup-Wizard.ps1:1553 calls `Initialize-DataDirectories` with no error check at all, then immediately proceeds to `Write-PlatformEnvFile` (writing the real .env with secrets) on the next line.
- Backup-Database.ps1:39 also calls it unconditionally.

This is inconsistent with the rest of this same codebase's own established pattern: every other fallible operation in Setup-Wizard.ps1/Common.ps1 (backup step, firewall rule creation, LAN IP detection, docker compose exit code) explicitly checks $LASTEXITCODE or catches exceptions and calls Write-SetupLog with a WARN level on failure. Initialize-DataDirectories's icacls call is the one place that pattern is dropped entirely — no log entry, no console warning, nothing. (The same swallow-and-ignore pattern also exists at Common.ps1:289 and Write-EnvFile.ps1:149, so this is a systemic gap, not unique to line 106, but the reported instance is real and accurately described.)

This doesn't match any of the listed intentional design patterns (JWT role re-derivation, NOT_CONFIGURED status, AI narration-only scoring, Basket visibility, toolkit/suite duplication, Metasploit gating, Nmap flag safety, provider status semantics) — none of those apply here.

Severity: the failure mode requires icacls.exe to actually fail despite running under a genuinely elevated token (Assert-Elevated is called first), which is not the common case, so this isn't a guaranteed/easily-triggered P0/P1 exposure. But the consequence when it does fail is real and security-relevant: the .env containing live API keys and the JWT signing secret gets written into a ProgramData directory left at default (broader, non-admin-readable-restricted) ACLs, with zero record in setup.log that the lockdown didn't happen — an operator would have no way to know their secrets are locally exposed. That combination of "silent, undetectable security-control failure" with "real secrets at stake" but "requires a comparatively rare triggering condition and local-only exposure" lines up with the original reviewer's P2, so I'm not adjusting it.

details.title: icacls /grant:r in Initialize-DataDirectories does not strip pre-existing explicit ACEs for other trustees
details.actual_behavior: `/inheritance:r` only removes INHERITED ACEs, and `/grant:r "*S-1-5-32-544:(OI)(CI)F" "*S-1-5-18:(OI)(CI)F"` only resets the grant for those two named SIDs -- it does not remove any other pre-existing EXPLICIT ACE for a different trustee that might already be present on an already-existing DataDir (e.g. left over from an earlier install/troubleshooting step or an older installer version).
details.failure_scenario: A machine where DataDir already exists with a stray explicit ACE for a broader group (e.g. added manually for troubleshooting, or by a prior installer version) then runs this installer again on upgrade/reconfigure -- Initialize-DataDirectories re-runs on the pre-existing directory, the stray ACE survives untouched alongside the new Administrators/SYSTEM grant, and the real .env (API keys, JWT secret) remains readable by that other trustee even after 'lockdown.'
details.reasoning: Confirmed against the actual code and against icacls semantics. Initialize-DataDirectories (Common.ps1:91-107) only creates dirs that don't exist (line 95-98 Test-Path guard), but the icacls call on line 106 always runs afterward regardless of whether the directory was pre-existing. That command is `icacls DataDir /inheritance:r /grant:r "*S-1-5-32-544:(OI)(CI)F" "*S-1-5-18:(OI)(CI)F"`. Per documented icacls behavior: `/inheritance:r` removes only INHERITED ACEs (converted/propagated from the parent), leaving any pre-existing EXPLICIT ACE on the object untouched; `/grant:r` replaces the explicit grant only for the two named SIDs (Administrators, SYSTEM) -- it does not remove or touch explicit ACEs belonging to any other trustee. So if DataDir already has a stray explicit ACE for some other trustee (e.g. added by hand during troubleshooting, or by an earlier installer revision), re-running this function on that pre-existing directory will not strip it -- the docstring's claim that the folder is locked down "to Administrators + SYSTEM only" is not actually guaranteed in that case. I verified the call chain: Setup-Wizard.ps1 calls Initialize-DataDirectories unconditionally at line 1553 regardless of $State.IsUpgrade, so this does run again on reconfigure/upgrade over an already-existing ProgramData tree, confirming the "runs again on upgrade" half of the failure scenario is real and not hypothetical. The remaining precondition (a stray explicit ACE already present from some prior action) is plausible but not something I can confirm actually happens in this codebase's history -- it depends on an external/manual event. The technical mechanism is definitely a real gap between documented and actual guarantees, but exploitation requires a specific prior misconfiguration to already exist on the box, so this is a narrow defense-in-depth gap rather than a broadly exploitable flaw. That matches a P3 severity (as originally assessed) -- real and worth a fix (e.g. `icacls /reset` before the grant, or explicitly enumerating/removing other explicit ACEs first), but not a high-impact/likely-to-trigger issue in the common fresh-install path, which is unaffected.

titles: setup.log is excluded from the second-pass secret-redaction sweep because its filename doesn't match the *.txt filter
Missing catch for a missing docker.exe silently drops all container status/log collection with no record in the bundle
Connection-string credential redaction leaks the remainder of any password containing a literal '@'

details.title: setup.log is excluded from the second-pass secret-redaction sweep because its filename doesn't match the *.txt filter
details.actual_behavior: Line 47 copies the setup log into the bundle as `setup.log` (`Copy-Item $script:SetupLogPath (Join-Path $bundleDir "setup.log")`). Line 120's shape-based secret-scrubbing pass is `Get-ChildItem $bundleDir -Filter "*.txt" | ForEach-Object {...}` -- a plain filename-extension filter that does not match `setup.log`. Every other collected file (env-redacted.txt, container-status.txt, logs-$svc.txt, prerequisites.txt, system-info.txt) is a `.txt` file and gets swept; setup.log alone is silently skipped.
details.failure_scenario: If any future (or already-present but currently benign) Write-SetupLog call ever interpolates something secret-shaped -- e.g. a raw exception message from a failed HTTP call to the backend during account setup that happens to include a URL with an embedded credential, or a future debug-log enhancement -- that value would ship in the diagnostics bundle completely unredacted, while every other file in the same bundle would have caught it.
details.proposed_fix: Change the Get-ChildItem filter to something that also matches setup.log (e.g. `-Include *.txt,*.log`, or rename the copied file to setup.log.txt, or drop the -Filter and just include all files in $bundleDir).
details.reasoning: Verified directly against windows/scripts/Diagnostics.ps1. Line 47 copies the setup log into the bundle as literally "setup.log" (Copy-Item $script:SetupLogPath (Join-Path $bundleDir "setup.log")). Line 120's second-pass shape-based secret sweep is Get-ChildItem $bundleDir -Filter "*.txt" | ForEach-Object {...} -- a plain extension filter that does not match "setup.log". Every other file dropped into $bundleDir (env-redacted.txt, container-status.txt, logs-$svc.txt, prerequisites.txt, system-info.txt) ends in .txt and is swept; setup.log alone is skipped. The comment block at lines 82-91 states this second pass is defense-in-depth precisely because application logs can echo secrets with no label nearby, and is "deliberately shape-based... to catch secrets appearing with no nearby label at all" -- with no stated carve-out for setup.log. The comment at line 45 justifying the omission ("already human-readable, never contains secret values") is an unverified assertion, in contrast to the second-pass comment which documents that an identical "this file is safe" assumption was tested and found false elsewhere (a synthetic DATABASE_URL and a bare sk-ant- key both slipped past the original label-only patterns). I traced Write-SetupLog call sites across Common.ps1, Backup-Database.ps1, Restore-Database.ps1, and wizard/Setup-Wizard.ps1; several interpolate raw exception objects/messages into log lines (e.g. around an AI-backend connectivity test whose request carries the user's real AI provider credentials), which is exactly the pattern the code's own comments say has already caused leaks elsewhere. This does not match any of the eight documented intentional design patterns. Severity: real but latent (no demonstrated actively-leaking secret in setup.log under today's normal code paths, per my trace), which is consistent with a P2 defense-in-depth coverage gap with a trivial one-line fix, matching the original reviewer's severity.

details.title: Missing catch for a missing docker.exe silently drops all container status/log collection with no record in the bundle
details.actual_behavior: The `& docker.exe compose ... ps` and the `logs --tail 200 $svc` loop are wrapped only in try/finally (finally just does Pop-Location), with no catch. I verified PowerShell's exact semantics with a live repro: if the invoked executable can't be resolved at all (CommandNotFoundException, e.g. docker.exe not on PATH), the statement-terminating error aborts the REST of the try block outright -- the failing `ps` line's Out-File never even runs (no file gets created for it), and the entire subsequent `foreach` loop over the 8 services' logs is skipped too -- but execution then continues normally after the try/finally to the rest of the script, with the only trace of the failure being a console error message that is never captured into any file in the bundle.
details.failure_scenario: docker.exe is not resolvable on PATH (Docker Desktop uninstalled/reinstalling, or a corrupted PATH) when an admin runs Diagnostics.ps1 to figure out what's wrong. The resulting zip silently contains no container-status.txt and no logs-*.txt for any of the 8 services, with nothing in the bundle explaining why -- support receives a bundle that looks like the container-collection step was never attempted rather than one that failed.
details.proposed_fix: Add a catch around the docker.exe invocations (or check `Get-Command docker.exe` first, as Check-Prerequisites.ps1 does) and write an explanatory line into container-status.txt when docker.exe can't be found or invoked.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by live repro against the actual PowerShell semantics. I wrote a script mirroring the exact structure of Diagnostics.ps1 lines 52-65 (try { & doesnotexist.exe ps 2>&1 | Out-File ...; foreach ($svc in @(...)) { & doesnotexist.exe logs ... } } finally { Pop-Location-equivalent }) and ran it with powershell.exe. Result: when the invoked exe is unresolvable, PowerShell throws a CommandNotFoundException that (a) aborts the rest of the try block immediately -- the foreach loop over services is never entered, so container-status.txt is never created and none of the logs-$svc.txt files are created; (b) is NOT captured by the `2>&1` redirect (it's a runtime command-lookup exception, not stderr from a started process); (c) runs the finally block; (d) then, since there is no catch anywhere and no elevated $ErrorActionPreference, execution continues normally to the rest of the script after the try/finally, with the only trace being a console-only error message. This exactly matches the finding's technical claims, verified rather than assumed.

I also checked Check-Prerequisites.ps1 (lines 77-98), which the same Diagnostics.ps1 run separately captures into prerequisites.txt in the same bundle (lines 67-72). It explicitly does `Get-Command docker.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` and reports "docker.exe not found on PATH -- install Docker Desktop from ..." as one of its JSON checks, and wraps the docker.exe invocations in try/catch. So the bundle is not actually devoid of an explanation for this exact failure mode -- prerequisites.txt (a sibling file in the very same zip) will surface the root cause. This meaningfully undercuts the finding's claim that "nothing in the bundle explaining why" -- a support engineer reading the full bundle (the reasonable path) will find it.

I also confirmed the failure only triggers when docker.exe is completely unresolvable on PATH -- a narrower condition than "Docker Desktop installed but daemon/containers not running" (by far the more common real-world support case), which is handled correctly today: docker.exe still exists and runs, so its stderr output ("cannot connect to the Docker daemon...") is a normal native-command stderr stream that IS captured fine via the existing `2>&1 | Out-File`.

Net: this is a real, narrow robustness gap in error handling (missing catch + no explanatory line specifically inside container-status.txt for the docker.exe-not-on-PATH case), worth fixing as the reviewer proposed (Get-Command check + catch), but the "administrator gets zero explanation" framing is overstated because prerequisites.txt in the same bundle already covers this exact scenario, and the narrow trigger condition (binary literally missing from PATH, not just daemon down) limits real-world frequency. I'm downgrading from the claimed P2 to P3.

details.title: Connection-string credential redaction leaks the remainder of any password containing a literal '@'
details.actual_behavior: The regex `(?i)([a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*://)[^/@\s:]*:[^/@\s]+@` stops at the FIRST '@' after the colon, because `[^/@\s]+` excludes '@'. I verified live: `mongodb+srv://admin:p@ssword@cluster0.mongodb.net/db` becomes `mongodb+srv://***REDACTED***@ssword@cluster0.mongodb.net/db` -- the redaction only consumes 'admin:p', leaving '@ssword@cluster0.mongodb.net/db' -- i.e. most of the real password ('ssword') -- exposed verbatim in the 'redacted' bundle.
details.failure_scenario: Any connection string logged somewhere in the collected container logs whose password happens to contain a literal '@' character (a legal character in many password policies) is only partially redacted, leaking most of the real secret into a bundle explicitly meant to be safe to share. Real-world exposure is narrowed by the fact that this installer's own generated passwords (New-RandomSecret, Base64 with +/= stripped) can never contain '@', so this only fires for secrets originating from some other source that ends up logged.
details.proposed_fix: Match through the LAST '@' before the next '/' instead of the first, e.g. change the value-group to a greedy `.+` restricted to not crossing a '/' or whitespace: `[^/\s:]*:[^/\s]+@(?=[^@]*\/)`-style lookahead, or simpler: redact everything between the scheme and the last '@' before the path separator.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading windows/scripts/Diagnostics.ps1 line 106 and live-testing the exact regex in PowerShell (the actual runtime). Input 'mongodb+srv://admin:p@ssword@cluster0.mongodb.net/db' redacts to 'mongodb+srv://***REDACTED***@ssword@cluster0.mongodb.net/db', exactly as claimed: the value-group [^/@\s]+ excludes '@', so the pattern stops at the FIRST '@' after the colon and treats it as the credential terminator, leaving the remainder of any password containing a literal '@' (plus the real @host) unredacted in the 'safe to share' diagnostic bundle. I also verified the reviewer's scoping caveat: New-RandomSecret (Common.ps1 lines 118-126) generates secrets via Base64 with '+/=' stripped, and '@' is not in the Base64 alphabet at all, so the installer's own generated PostgresPassword/Neo4jPassword/JwtSecretKey can never trigger this -- the bug only fires for externally-sourced credentials (e.g. a user-pointed external DB with a hand-chosen password containing '@') that end up logged unlabeled. This is not one of the documented intentional design patterns; it's a genuine regex-correctness defect in a defense-in-depth redaction pass whose stated purpose (per the adjacent comment) is full credential redaction. Severity P3 is appropriate: real secret exposure, but gated behind multiple compounding preconditions (external non-generated credential, literal '@' in password, unlabeled log appearance, and the bundle subsequently being shared) and it's a secondary safety net, not the primary control (the .env file itself is never copied).

titles: Postgres readiness check only confirms the container is 'running', not that it is accepting connections, before issuing psql commands

details.title: Postgres readiness check only confirms the container is 'running', not that it is accepting connections, before issuing psql commands
details.actual_behavior: When the postgres container was not already running, the script starts it (line 63) and polls up to 40s for `docker ps` to report the container name as running (lines 68-72), then immediately proceeds to run psql commands (lines 104, 108, 109, 112) with no pg_isready or connection-retry check.
details.failure_scenario: On a cold start (e.g. right after a host reboot, or immediately following Remove-StaleDatabaseVolumeIfFreshInstall-style volume work) `docker ps` reports the container 'running' well before the postgres process inside has finished its own startup/WAL recovery. The first `psql -U ioc -d postgres -c ...` (line 104) can hit 'the database system is starting up' and fail -- an error that, per the related finding on lines 101-113, is silently discarded, letting the restore proceed on the false assumption that termination/drop/create actually happened.
details.proposed_fix: Poll with `docker exec $containerName pg_isready -U $pgUser` (or retry the first psql call with backoff) instead of relying solely on `docker ps` container state.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading windows/scripts/Restore-Database.ps1 lines 59-77 and 100-113 directly, plus docker-compose.yml. The cold-start branch only polls `docker ps --filter name=$containerName --format {{.Names}}` (lines 68-72), which reports the container as soon as its process is running -- it does not check container health. Crucially, docker-compose.yml (lines 59-63) already defines `healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ..."]` for the postgres service, and the backend/celery_worker services already use `depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy` (lines 222-227, 265-269) specifically because the authors know 'running' != 'accepting connections' for this exact image. Restore-Database.ps1's ad hoc `docker ps` loop ignores that existing, correct signal and checks the wrong thing, so it can proceed to line 104's `psql` call while Postgres is still in its own startup/recovery phase. That first psql call's stderr/exit code is discarded (2>$null | Out-Null, no exit-code check) at lines 104/108/109, so a transient 'the database system is starting up' failure is silently swallowed, matching the reviewer's claimed chain. I also found the actual risk window is arguably broader than the finding states: if Postgres was *already* 'running' per docker ps (e.g. just started seconds earlier by the boot-time Service-Start.ps1 task) the whole lines 59-77 branch is skipped entirely and there is zero readiness wait before line 104 -- an even more direct hit of the same root cause. Real-world impact is self-limiting in the common case: if DROP/CREATE silently no-op due to the race, the subsequent bulk restore (line 112) replays a clean (no --clean/--if-exists) dump onto a still-existing, non-empty database, which throws real primary-key/relation-exists errors that DO get caught by the $restoreExitCode -ne 0 check (lines 115-123) and reported as a failure -- so the dominant failure mode is 'restore visibly fails, admin must retry' rather than always-silent corruption. But on a disaster-recovery script (exactly the kind of script invoked after a crash/reboot, i.e. precisely when Postgres cold-start latency is most likely), a race that can produce a failed or inconsistent restore is a genuine, non-hypothetical defect, well-precedented as a classic Docker/Postgres pitfall that this same codebase has already solved correctly elsewhere (the compose healthcheck) but simply didn't reuse here. This does not match any of the 8 documented intentional-design exceptions. Severity: keeping the original P2 -- real impact on a DR-critical path, triggered by a plausible (arguably under-scoped-in-the-finding, i.e. broader) real scenario, with a straightforward fix (poll `docker exec $containerName pg_isready -U $pgUser`, or check container health status) available using infrastructure already present in the repo.

titles: Frontend health check ignores configured HOST_PORT_FRONTEND, always probes :3000

details.title: Frontend health check ignores configured HOST_PORT_FRONTEND, always probes :3000
details.actual_behavior: Service-Status.ps1 line 31 calls `Test-FrontendHealth` with no arguments. Common.ps1's Test-FrontendHealth signature is `param([string]$BaseUrl = "http://localhost:3000")` -- there is no analogous Get-ConfiguredFrontendPort helper (grep of windows/scripts confirms only Get-ConfiguredBackendPort exists), so the frontend check always probes port 3000 no matter what HOST_PORT_FRONTEND was actually set to.
details.failure_scenario: Wizard/installer detects port 3000 is already in use on the host and remaps HOST_PORT_FRONTEND to e.g. 3001 (via Common.ps1's Find-FreePort, exactly the scenario the code comments describe as real and already handled for the backend). The frontend container is genuinely healthy on :3001. Running 'Service Status' from the Start Menu shows 'Web interface: NOT RESPONDING' in red even though the platform is fully up, misleading the operator into thinking something is broken and potentially causing an unnecessary restart/troubleshooting cycle.
details.proposed_fix: Add a Get-ConfiguredFrontendPort helper analogous to Get-ConfiguredBackendPort (read HOST_PORT_FRONTEND from $script:EnvFilePath) and pass it into Test-FrontendHealth's BaseUrl at the Service-Status.ps1 call site.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code reading. Test-FrontendHealth (Common.ps1 L328-329) defaults to the hardcoded "http://localhost:3000" and has no port-parameterizing helper analogous to Get-ConfiguredBackendPort (which exists specifically because this exact bug class was already found and fixed for the backend, per its own docstring at L293-301). Service-Status.ps1 L31 calls Test-FrontendHealth with no arguments, so it never reads HOST_PORT_FRONTEND. Confirmed the scenario is reachable, not hypothetical: Write-EnvFile.ps1 writes HOST_PORT_FRONTEND from Settings.PortFrontend (default 3000), and Setup-Wizard.ps1's Ports page (L1367-1390) actively detects a port-3000 conflict via Test-PortFree and offers a Find-FreePort remap for PortFrontend specifically. So a real installer flow (3000 already in use on the host) leads to a permanently-wrong frontend health check. Checked Watchdog.ps1: it only calls Test-BackendHealth, never Test-FrontendHealth, so this bug cannot trigger an unwanted automatic restart -- its impact is confined to a misleading manual "Service Status" diagnostic (and the same hardcoded pattern separately affects Open-Platform.ps1, but that's a different file). Given no automated destructive action results and the failure requires a port remap plus a manual status check, P2 (degraded/misleading operator-facing diagnostic, no outage/data-loss/auto-action) is the accurate severity, matching the original reviewer's rating.

titles: Watchdog has no maintenance-mode awareness and can fire a conflicting docker compose restart mid-restore
20-second recheck window after a recovery restart is inconsistent with (likely shorter than) how long this codebase elsewhere waits for the identical health-recovery condition

details.title: Watchdog has no maintenance-mode awareness and can fire a conflicting docker compose restart mid-restore
details.actual_behavior: Once registered during initial setup, the Watchdog scheduled task runs unconditionally every 5 minutes indefinitely (Common.ps1's Register-BootAndWatchdogTasks). Watchdog.ps1 treats any Test-BackendHealth failure as an incident and unconditionally issues `docker compose restart` (line 55), with no check anywhere for a maintenance/lock flag that a long-running operation like a database restore could set.
details.failure_scenario: An operator runs the 'Restore Database' Start Menu shortcut on a database large enough that the restore (Restore-Database.ps1 lines 100-126: stop backend/celery, drop+recreate the DB, replay the dump, then restart backend/celery) takes longer than a few minutes. The already-registered Watchdog task fires mid-restore, Test-BackendHealth correctly reports unhealthy (backend is deliberately stopped), and Watchdog issues its own `docker compose restart`, bringing backend/celery back up and reconnecting them to Postgres WHILE Restore-Database.ps1's own DROP DATABASE/CREATE DATABASE/psql-replay sequence is still running against that same database -- precisely the 'concurrent write races the restore' scenario Restore-Database.ps1's docstring states its stop-then-restore ordering exists to prevent. The same gap applies to Setup-Wizard.ps1's upgrade path (`docker compose up --build`, which its own comment says 'can take several minutes'), during which the already-active Watchdog task can likewise fire a competing docker compose action.
details.proposed_fix: Have long-running maintenance scripts (Restore-Database.ps1, and the setup wizard's upgrade path) write a maintenance-mode marker file that Watchdog.ps1 checks and skips remediation for, or temporarily Unregister/Disable the Watchdog scheduled task for the duration and re-register it at the end (mirroring how Register-BootAndWatchdogTasks is already re-run at the end of setup).
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading. Common.ps1's Register-BootAndWatchdogTasks (lines 435-448) registers 'Watchdog' as a SYSTEM-run scheduled task firing every 5 minutes for 10 years, unconditionally, right after the wizard's own docker compose up succeeds (Setup-Wizard.ps1 lines 1608-1615), and it persists across all future runs. Watchdog.ps1 (lines 47-58) has no maintenance/lock-file check anywhere in the file: it calls Test-BackendHealth, and on any failure unconditionally runs Invoke-DockerCompose "restart" (with no service list, i.e. it restarts every compose service including postgres) after only writing a log line -- there is genuinely no gating logic to remove.

Restore-Database.ps1 confirms the exact race: it stops backend/celery_worker/celery_beat (line 101), terminates Postgres connections, does DROP DATABASE/CREATE DATABASE (lines 108-109), then streams the dump through `docker exec -i ... psql` (line 112) with no time bound -- for a large dump this can easily exceed 5 minutes. During that whole window Test-BackendHealth genuinely fails (backend is deliberately stopped), which is exactly the trigger condition the already-running Watchdog task acts on. If it fires mid-restore, `docker compose restart` brings backend/celery back up (reconnecting to a DB that may be mid-drop/mid-replay) and, because no service list is passed, also restarts the postgres container itself, which would kill the in-flight psql restore process outright -- a genuinely destructive collision, not a benign no-op. I grepped the whole windows/ tree for any maintenance/lock/mutex mechanism (Common.ps1, Setup-Wizard.ps1, Open-Platform.ps1, installer.iss) and found nothing that gates Watchdog or coordinates it with Restore-Database.ps1 or the wizard's own upgrade path (`docker compose up -d --build`, Setup-Wizard.ps1 line 1583) -- confirming the reviewer's "no maintenance-mode awareness anywhere" claim rather than just restating it.

This is a real, unguarded race condition with a plausible, non-contrived trigger (an operator running the documented "Restore Database" shortcut on a large case-data DB, or reconfiguring/upgrading an already-deployed install where the watchdog task is already active from a prior setup run). I'm lowering the severity from the claimed P1 to P2: it requires a fairly specific precondition (restore or rebuild genuinely exceeding ~5 minutes) and, in the restore case, the script's own error handling (checks $LASTEXITCODE, logs to setup.log, and restarts backend/celery on failure) means the operator gets a clear failure signal and can re-run the restore rather than being left with silent, undetected data loss. It's a genuine, fixable operational hazard worth the proposed maintenance-marker-file or Disable/Enable-ScheduledTask fix, but not quite P1 production-down-with-no-recovery-path severity.

details.title: 20-second recheck window after a recovery restart is inconsistent with (likely shorter than) how long this codebase elsewhere waits for the identical health-recovery condition
details.actual_behavior: After issuing `docker compose restart` (line 55), Watchdog waits a single flat 20 seconds (line 60) before re-checking health and logging success or 'Manual attention needed' (lines 61-65). Restore-Database.ps1's equivalent wait for 'backend becomes healthy again after being restarted' is up to 90 seconds (30 x 3s, lines 130-133 of that script), and Setup-Wizard.ps1 allows up to 3 minutes (60 x 3s) after its own `up --build`.
details.failure_scenario: If backend startup routinely takes more than 20 seconds after a restart (DB migrations, waiting on Postgres/Redis/OpenSearch to also finish restarting), Watchdog logs 'Recovery restart did NOT resolve the issue -- Manual attention needed' (line 64) even in cases where the platform would have reported healthy given the ~90s this codebase allows elsewhere for the same condition -- producing a false alarm in the one log an unattended, remote site's operator relies on to know whether an incident actually occurred.
details.proposed_fix: Poll with retries over a longer window (e.g. up to 90s, matching Restore-Database.ps1's wait) instead of a single sleep-then-check.
details.reasoning:
Verified directly against the code. Watchdog.ps1 lines 54-65: after `Invoke-DockerCompose "restart"` (which itself just issues `docker compose restart` and returns as soon as Docker reports the containers restarted — it does not wait for the application inside to become ready), the script does a single `Start-Sleep -Seconds 20` (line 60) followed by exactly one `Test-BackendHealth` check, logging "Manual attention needed" on failure with no retry.

Cross-checked the two comparison points cited by the reviewer, both confirmed accurate:
- Restore-Database.ps1 lines 130-133: `for ($i = 0; $i -lt 30; $i++) { if (Test-BackendHealth) {...}; Start-Sleep -Seconds 3 }` — up to 90s of polling for the identical "backend healthy again after a restart" condition.
- Setup-Wizard.ps1 lines 1595-1597: `for ($i = 0; $i -lt 60; $i++) { if (Test-BackendHealth ...) {...}; Start-Sleep -Seconds 3 }` — up to 180s.

So the same codebase gives the same condition (backend becoming healthy again after a compose restart/up, which involves the same migrations/Postgres/Redis dependency chain each time) 90s and 180s elsewhere, but only a single check after a flat 20s in Watchdog. This is a real, demonstrable inconsistency, not one of the documented intentional patterns (it doesn't match any of the 8 listed exemptions).

Real-world consequence: Watchdog only logs on the unhealthy path (the happy path is silent by design per the header comment), so a restart that would have reported healthy within, say, 30-60s produces a permanent "Recovery restart did NOT resolve the issue -- Manual attention needed" as the last line in the one log an unattended remote-site operator relies on, with no later line correcting it once the backend does become healthy on a subsequent cron run (since that run would just exit 0 silently). This is a genuine false-alarm/log-trustworthiness bug, matching the reviewer's failure scenario exactly.

Severity: this does not cause a missed real incident (the underlying restart already happened) or any data loss/security exposure — it only produces a misleading log entry that could trigger unnecessary manual dispatch/investigation for a self-resolving condition. That impact profile is consistent with the original P3 rating (minor/quality issue in error-handling/observability), so I'm not adjusting it.
