Also confirmed list_ai_providers (runtime_config.py 218-223) returns every kind=AI row unfiltered, with no equivalent to list_ioc_providers' explicit join against get_all_providers() (runtime.py 103-130) -- so a phantom AI row created this way is returned indefinitely by GET /runtime/ai-providers and would appear in the Manage Providers panel, while set_active_ai_backend (runtime_config.py 332-333) still validates against AI_BACKENDS so the phantom entry can never actually be activated. Every specific claim in the finding checks out against the real code, and none of the 8 documented intentional-design patterns apply here. Severity: this requires provider:manage (an already-privileged/admin capability), causes no data corruption, no security-boundary bypass, and no functional breakage of real providers -- the impact is DB clutter plus a confusing but inert extra entry in an admin-only UI panel that can never be selected. That matches a minor input-validation hygiene issue with no meaningful blast radius, so the original P3 rating is correct; it doesn't rise to P2/P1 since nothing exploitable or functionally broken results, and it's not P4-trivial since it does leave permanent unwanted DB state and a real (if cosmetic) UI artifact.

titles: audit_log's limit query parameter has no upper or lower bound

details.title: audit_log's limit query parameter has no upper or lower bound
details.actual_behavior: `async def audit_log(limit: int = 200, ...)` passes `limit` straight through to `svc.list_audit_log(limit)` (app/core/audit.py line 39-45), which does `select(ConfigAuditLog)...limit(limit)` with no clamping anywhere in the call chain.
details.failure_scenario: A caller with audit:read (admin-only role in this app, but still just one compromised/careless admin session away from abuse) requests GET /runtime/audit-log?limit=50000000, forcing the query to attempt to return the entire audit table in one response (unbounded memory/response-size growth as the table grows). A request with limit=-1 is passed to PostgreSQL's LIMIT clause, which PostgreSQL rejects for negative values, surfacing as an unhandled exception (generic 500) instead of a clean 400 like every other validated input in this router.
details.proposed_fix: Declare `limit: int = Query(200, ge=1, le=<sane max e.g. 1000>)` (or validate/clamp manually) instead of a bare `int` default.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of both files. backend/app/api/routes/runtime.py lines 188-190:

```python
@router.get("/audit-log")
async def audit_log(limit: int = 200, user: CurrentUser = Depends(require_permission("audit:read"))):
    return await svc.list_audit_log(limit)
```

`limit` is declared as a bare `int` with a default of 200 -- no `Query(..., ge=1, le=...)`, no manual clamping, no validation of any kind. It is passed straight through to `app/core/audit.py`:

```python
async def list_audit_log(limit: int = 200) -> list[dict]:
    async with new_session() as db:
        rows = (
            await db.execute(
                select(ConfigAuditLog).order_by(ConfigAuditLog.timestamp.desc()).limit(limit)
            )
        ).scalars().all()
```

which uses the raw value directly in SQLAlchemy's `.limit(limit)`, which maps to a SQL `LIMIT` clause with zero clamping anywhere in the chain. This exactly matches the finding's described call chain and confirmed line numbers.

Impact check:
- `limit=50000000` (or any huge value): the query would attempt to return the entire audit table in one response once the table grows large enough -- unbounded memory/response-size growth, a real resource-exhaustion vector.
- `limit=-1` (or any negative int): FastAPI's bare `int` type only does type coercion, not range validation, so `-1` passes through unchanged to SQL `LIMIT -1`, which PostgreSQL rejects (`ERROR: LIMIT must not be negative`), producing an unhandled exception the app has no explicit handler for -- i.e. a generic 500 instead of a clean validation 400. I checked the rest of runtime.py: there are zero `Query(...)` usages anywhere in the file (all other endpoints take path params or Pydantic-validated JSON bodies), so this genuinely is the one unguarded/unvalidated input surface in the router -- not an inconsistency invented by the reviewer.

I checked this against all 8 documented intentional-design exceptions (role re-derivation, NOT_CONFIGURED graceful degradation, AI-narration-only risk scores, BasketItem visibility asymmetry, security-toolkit/pentest-suite overlap, nmap flag safety boundary, per-call provider status) -- none apply; this is a plain missing-bounds-validation gap on a paging parameter, not a deliberate pattern.

Severity: the endpoint is gated behind `require_permission("audit:read")`, which per the finding is admin-only, so this is not exploitable by an arbitrary unauthenticated/low-privilege caller. The worst-case outcomes are (a) a resource-exhaustion/slow-response condition triggerable by an admin session (careless or compromised) rather than data exfiltration or privilege escalation, and (b) a cosmetic robustness issue (500 instead of 400) on negative input. That lines up with a low-severity input-validation hygiene issue rather than anything higher -- P3 (as originally claimed) is well-calibrated; I see no basis to raise it to P2/P1/P0 (no auth bypass, no cross-tenant data exposure, requires an already-privileged actor) nor to lower it to P4 (it is a concrete, easily-triggered, unhandled-exception-causing gap on a live endpoint, not purely theoretical/cosmetic).

titles: get_redis() never closes the stale client when it recreates one for a new event loop
get_redis() never closes the previous client when recreating it for a new event loop

details.title: get_redis() never closes the stale client when it recreates one for a new event loop
details.actual_behavior: get_redis() (lines 34-39) reassigns `_pool = aioredis.from_url(...)` whenever `_pool_loop is not current_loop`, but never calls `.close()`/`.aclose()` (or schedules cleanup) on the previous `_pool` first -- the old client and its connections are simply dropped, relying on GC (which, once the loop that owned them is closed, can't cleanly tear down the async sockets at all).
details.failure_scenario: Any process that recreates event loops repeatedly while this module stays imported (documented as happening across pytest-asyncio test files, per this file's own docstring and app/tests/unit/test_cache_redis_client_lifecycle.py) leaks one abandoned Redis connection/pool object per loop change instead of closing it, which can surface as 'unclosed connector'/ResourceWarning noise and wasted server-side Redis connections during a long test run or any other loop-recreation scenario.
details.proposed_fix: Before reassigning `_pool`, capture the old client and call `await old_pool.close()` (or fire-and-forget via `asyncio.ensure_future` if called from sync context) when it is non-None and its loop is no longer current.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading backend/app/core/cache.py lines 15-39 directly. `_pool`/`_pool_loop` are module-globals; `get_redis()` does `if _pool is None or _pool_loop is not current_loop: _pool = aioredis.from_url(...)`. When the loop-changed branch fires, the previous `_pool` (a redis.asyncio.Redis client wrapping a ConnectionPool) is simply overwritten -- there is no `.close()`/`.aclose()` call anywhere in this file, and a repo-wide grep confirms no other call site (main.py only calls `get_redis().ping()` for health checks) ever closes the old client either. So the core factual claim is accurate.

I verified this isn't just theoretical by inspecting the installed redis==5.0.8 package (backend/.venv_test/Lib/site-packages/redis/asyncio/{client,connection}.py): for the default (non-single-connection) client this module creates, `Redis.connection` stays None between commands, so `Redis.__del__`'s own warning never fires; but the individual `Connection` objects sitting in `ConnectionPool._available_connections`/`_in_use_connections` each have `__del__` that warns `ResourceWarning: unclosed Connection ...` and calls `self._writer.close()` -- and if the owning loop is already closed (exactly the scenario this branch handles), that close raises `RuntimeError: Event loop is closed`, printed as "Exception ignored in..." noise, without going through the transport's graceful shutdown path.

I also found a concrete, non-test production trigger the original reviewer didn't cite: app/workers/tasks.py's `run_osint_crawl` Celery task runs hourly via Celery Beat (celery_app.py's `beat_schedule`) and calls `asyncio.run(_run_osint_crawl_async())` -- by the task's own docstring, "each task run gets its own asyncio event loop via asyncio.run()". `_run_osint_crawl_async` calls `set_cached_result` -> `get_redis()`, so every hourly beat tick creates a new loop and hits the stale-pool branch, abandoning the prior hour's Redis client every single time for the life of the worker process (no `worker_max_tasks_per_child` or similar is configured in celery_app.py to periodically recycle the process).

That said, the real-world blast radius is capped: CPython's raw `socket` object has its own finalizer that closes the underlying fd (and thus properly terminates the TCP connection Redis-side) once refcount/cyclic-GC reclaims it, independent of the dead event loop -- so this degrades to periodic log/stderr noise and delayed-but-not-permanently-leaked connections rather than an unbounded fd/connection leak that would reliably cause an outage. That matches (and does not exceed) the original P3, low-confidence rating -- I'm not adjusting it, since the mechanism is real but self-limiting.

None of the 8 documented intentional-design exclusions apply to this file/pattern.

details.title: get_redis() never closes the previous client when recreating it for a new event loop
details.actual_behavior: When `_pool_loop is not current_loop`, get_redis() (lines 36-38) simply overwrites the module-level `_pool` global with a brand-new `aioredis.from_url(...)` client. The previous `aioredis.Redis` instance (and whatever sockets/connection-pool resources it holds) is dropped with no call to `.close()`/`.aclose()`/`.disconnect()`.
details.failure_scenario: Any process that legitimately recreates its running event loop mid-lifetime (the exact scenario this function was written to handle, per its own docstring: pytest-asyncio giving each test module a fresh loop) leaks one abandoned Redis client object per loop transition -- e.g. running many test modules that each touch rate-limiting in one pytest session accumulates one unclosed client per module. In normal production (uvicorn keeps a single loop for the process lifetime) this path is rarely hit, so real-world impact is low, but the gap is real: there is no code path that ever releases the old client, and by the time the mismatch is detected the old loop is already closed, so a clean async close is no longer even possible after the fact -- it would need to happen before/at the moment the loop is torn down, which this function has no hook into.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of backend/app/core/cache.py lines 15-39. get_redis() maintains module-level globals _pool/_pool_loop. When a loop change is detected (_pool is not None and _pool_loop is not current_loop), it does `_pool = aioredis.from_url(...)` — a plain reassignment — with no call to close/aclose/disconnect on the previous _pool value anywhere in this function or the rest of the file (checked cache_key, get_cached_result, set_cached_result, RateLimiter — none reap old clients). The old aioredis.Redis instance and its connection-pool sockets are simply dropped. Since get_redis() is synchronous, there's also no way to await a graceful async close even if someone wanted to patch it in place, and per the docstring's own account, by the time this path fires the old loop is typically already gone (pytest-asyncio per-module loops), so it's not even possible to schedule a clean close against the old loop after the fact. This is not covered by any of the 8 documented intentional patterns — it's a genuine, distinct resource-management gap. titles: get_credential()'s per-field independent env fallback can silently combine a DB-stored value for one field of a multi-field credential with a legacy .env value for the other, producing a pair that was never validated together

details.title: get_credential()'s per-field independent env fallback can silently combine a DB-stored value for one field of a multi-field credential with a legacy .env value for the other, producing a pair that was never validated together
details.actual_behavior: get_credential (lines 38-47) falls back to `fallback` independently PER FIELD (`override['credentials'].get(field) or fallback`), and base.py's effective_configured (backend/app/providers/base.py lines 162-164) allows fetch() to run whenever EITHER the DB override OR the static env-derived self.configured is fully-configured on its own -- it does not require the fields actually used to come from a single fully-configured source. When the DB row for a multi-field provider is partially populated (one field set, the other never saved) while the static .env-derived value is separately complete, effective_configured becomes True via the env side, but backend/app/providers/stubs/censys.py's fetch() (lines 40-41) still pulls each field independently, so it can end up sending the DB-stored personal_access_token together with the .env-sourced organization_id (or vice versa) -- a combination that was never entered or tested together.
details.failure_scenario: A Censys row was seeded/saved in the DB with only personal_access_token set (organization_id never entered via the UI). Separately, .env still has a complete, different (personal_access_token, organization_id) pair from before this feature existed, so self.configured=True for Censys. effective_configured is True (via the env OR), so fetch() runs get_credential('censys','personal_access_token', env_token) -> returns the DB token (present, so no fallback), and get_credential('censys','organization_id', env_org) -> returns env_org (DB has none). The outbound Censys API call now uses a token from one account paired with an organization_id that may belong to a different account, producing authorization failures or, in principle, cross-account data exposure if the token happens to also be valid for that stale org id.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading the full chain across runtime_context.py, runtime_config.py, providers/base.py, providers/stubs/censys.py, api/routes/runtime.py, and ProviderConfigRow.tsx.

runtime_context.py:38-47 get_credential() does `override['credentials'].get(field) or fallback` -- a per-field, independent fallback with no notion of "this field's sibling came from a different source." runtime_config.py's get_ioc_provider_snapshot() (lines 383-401) builds the override credentials dict straight from whatever partial JSON is stored in the DB row, and _is_fully_configured() (lines 135-155) correctly requires ALL of IOC_PROVIDER_CREDENTIAL_FIELDS['censys'] = ['personal_access_token','organization_id'] to be truthy before reporting the DB-side "configured" as True -- so a DB row with only personal_access_token set correctly yields configured=False on the DB side, exactly as its own docstring intends.

However base.py's BaseProvider.run() computes `effective_configured = (override.get("configured") or self.configured) if override else self.configured` -- an OR against the env-derived self.configured (set once at process start in CensysProvider.__init__ from settings.censys_personal_access_token/organization_id, independent of the DB, per stubs/censys.py). If .env still holds a complete legacy pair, self.configured=True, so effective_configured is True even though the DB-side pairing check said False. fetch() in stubs/censys.py then calls get_credential() separately for each field: personal_access_token resolves to the DB value (present, so `or fallback` short-circuits), organization_id resolves to the env fallback (absent in DB). The outbound Authorization/X-Organization-ID pair was never validated together -- exactly as claimed.

I also verified this is reachable via ordinary use, not a contrived edge case: configure_ioc_provider (api/routes/runtime.py) accepts an arbitrary partial `credentials: dict[str,str]` with zero server-side validation that IOC_PROVIDER_CREDENTIAL_FIELDS's required set is fully present, and ProviderConfigRow.tsx's Save button has no client-side requirement to fill in both input boxes before submitting -- an operator editing only the token field and clicking Save produces precisely this partial DB row while a pre-existing complete .env pair sits underneath it as the fallback. This directly undermines the pairing invariant _is_fully_configured's own docstring says it exists to enforce ("any field truthy would wrongly report configured with only one of the two set") -- the base.py OR against self.configured reintroduces exactly the hole that check was meant to close, for the one provider (Censys) with a multi-field pairing requirement among registered IOC providers.

Severity: keeping the original P3. It's a genuine data-integrity/logic bug, not cosmetic, but the blast radius is narrow (only Censys among IOC providers has this multi-field requirement) and requires a specific precondition (a stale-but-complete legacy .env pair coexisting with a newer, only-partially-saved DB credential). The realistic failure mode is a Censys API authorization error (401/403) surfacing as ProviderStatus.ERROR to the analyst -- confusing but not silently catastrophic. The original finding's "cross-account data exposure" framing is speculative (requires the stale token to also happen to be valid for the mismatched org). P3 (low/narrow-trigger functional and credential-hygiene bug) is the right call, not P0-P2.

titles: list_users() pagination has no deterministic tiebreaker, so tied sort-column values can duplicate or skip rows across pages
list_users() search filter doesn't escape SQL LIKE wildcard characters

details.title: list_users() pagination has no deterministic tiebreaker, so tied sort-column values can duplicate or skip rows across pages
details.actual_behavior: The ORDER BY clause is built purely from the single caller-selected `sort_by` column (`column.asc()`/`column.desc()`), with no secondary tiebreaker such as `User.id`. Rows with identical values in the sort column have no guaranteed stable relative order between the separate `count_stmt`/`list_stmt` queries and between successive page fetches.
details.failure_scenario: An admin sorts the user list by `role` (a column with only a handful of distinct values, e.g. most users are 'analyst') in a deployment with more than one page of analysts. Paging from page 1 to page 2 with page_size=25 can show the same analyst row on both pages, or skip one entirely, because Postgres provides no ordering guarantee among rows that tie on the sort key across separate query executions.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading backend/app/core/users.py lines 99-120 directly. sort_columns maps sort_by to exactly one column (email/full_name/role/created_at/last_login_at); `order = column.asc() if sort_dir == "asc" else column.desc()` (line 107) and `list_stmt = select(User).order_by(order).offset(...).limit(...)` (line 120) use only that single column -- there is no secondary key such as User.id appended to break ties. This is a textbook OFFSET/LIMIT pagination hazard: SQL (and Postgres specifically) makes no guarantee about the relative order of rows that tie on the ORDER BY key across separate query executions, so if the physical/plan-level ordering of tied rows shifts between the page-1 and page-2 SELECTs (e.g. due to concurrent inserts/updates/deletes, autovacuum, or a different query plan being chosen), a row can appear on two pages or be skipped entirely.

I verified the claimed failure scenario is plausible, not hypothetical, by checking the User model (app/models/user.py) and TimestampMixin (app/models/base.py): Role is a 3-value enum (ADMIN/ANALYST/VIEWER) so sorting by role produces long runs of tied rows once there is more than a handful of users -- exactly the scenario the reviewer describes. Even the *default* sort (sort_by='created_at') is not immune: TimestampMixin uses `server_default=func.now()`, which in Postgres returns the transaction start time, so any users created in the same transaction (e.g. a seed/bootstrap script inserting several accounts at once) share an identical created_at value.

This does not match any of the 8 documented intentional patterns (JWT role re-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED status, AI narration-only scoring, basket privacy asymmetry, pentest-suite naming overlap, no-destructive-pentest-by-design, nmap flag safety boundary, or per-call provider status) -- it's an unrelated, genuine gap in the pagination query construction.

Severity: this affects only the admin user-management console's list view, is read-only (no data mutation/corruption), requires a fairly specific combination of conditions (a low-cardinality or otherwise tied sort column, more than one page of tied rows, and an actual reordering event between the two page fetches) to manifest visibly, and is trivially worked around by an admin re-sorting or refreshing. That matches a minor/moderate correctness bug rather than anything security-relevant or data-destructive, so I concur with the original reviewer's P3 rating -- not P0/P1/P2, and not lower than P3 either since it's a real, reproducible defect with a straightforward fix (append `.order_by(User.id)` or similar as a secondary key), not merely cosmetic.

details.title: list_users() search filter doesn't escape SQL LIKE wildcard characters
details.actual_behavior: The `search` term is lower-cased and wrapped as `f"%{search.lower()}%"` and passed straight into `.like()` without escaping `%` or `_`, which are SQL LIKE metacharacters. This is not a SQL-injection issue (the value is bound as a parameter), just an unescaped-wildcard correctness issue.
details.failure_scenario: An admin searches for a full_name/email substring that happens to contain a literal `_` (e.g. searching for the literal text "a_c"). Because `_` means 'any single character' in LIKE, this also matches unrelated names like "abc" or "a1c", returning imprecise results the admin didn't intend and giving no way to search for a literal `%`/`_` character.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading backend/app/core/users.py lines 109-123. The `search` parameter is lower-cased and interpolated directly into a Python f-string `f"%{search.lower()}%"` (line 112), which is then passed to SQLAlchemy's `.like()` on both `User.email` and `User.full_name` (line 113). There is no escaping of the LIKE metacharacters `%` and `_` before building the pattern. A grep across the backend confirms this is the only `.like()`/`ilike()` call site in the codebase, so there's no shared escaping helper being bypassed elsewhere — this is simply unescaped.

This is not SQL injection (the pattern is still passed as a bound parameter via SQLAlchemy, not string-concatenated into raw SQL), consistent with the reviewer's own characterization. It is a genuine, narrow correctness bug: if an admin searches for a literal substring containing `_` (e.g. "a_c"), the `_` is interpreted as a single-character wildcard, so the query over-matches (e.g. also matches "abc", "a1c"), and there is no way to search for a literal `%` or `_` character. This doesn't map to any of the 8 documented intentional-design patterns for this codebase — it's a plain missing-escape bug in an admin user-search filter.

Severity: I agree with the original P4 rating. Real-world impact is very low — this only affects an internal admin-facing user list search feature, causes over-broad (not under-broad or data-leaking) results, requires the somewhat unusual precondition of searching for a substring containing `_` or `%`, and has no security implication (parameterized query, no injection, no privilege escalation, no data exposure beyond what admins can already see). It's a minor UX/precision annoyance at most, correctly placed at the lowest severity tier.

titles: update_user() unconditionally locks every ADMIN row even for edits that never touch a role or an admin account

details.title: update_user() unconditionally locks every ADMIN row even for edits that never touch a role or an admin account
details.actual_behavior: update_user() calls `locked_admins = await _lock_all_admin_rows(db)` (a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE over every ADMIN-role row) at the very top of the function, before checking whether the `role` parameter is even non-None. The module docstring describes this lock as scoped to 'update_user()'s role-demotion path', but the code actually takes it for every call, including a pure full_name-only edit of a non-admin user.
details.failure_scenario: Admin A calls update_user(userX, full_name="New Name") where userX is an ordinary analyst (no role change, no admin involved). Concurrently, Admin B calls update_user(userY, full_name="Other Name") for a different ordinary analyst userY. Because both calls unconditionally acquire the same admin-rows lock set first, B's call blocks until A's transaction commits, even though neither request touches a role field or an admin account -- every user-management write in the system serializes behind this lock regardless of relevance.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code reading. In backend/app/core/users.py, update_user() (lines 193-232) calls `locked_admins = await _lock_all_admin_rows(db)` unconditionally as the first statement inside the session (line 201), before checking `if role is not None` (line 211) or whether the target user is even an ADMIN (line 216). _lock_all_admin_rows() (lines 76-81) issues `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` over every ADMIN-role row. `locked_admins` is only consumed inside the nested role-change/demotion branch (line 217), so the lock could be scoped to just that branch with no behavior change for the cases where it matters -- confirming it's truly superfluous for full_name-only edits and non-admin targets. Since Postgres FOR UPDATE row locks block other transactions trying to lock the same rows until commit, any two concurrent update_user() calls (even both plain full_name edits on ordinary analysts) will serialize against each other on the shared ADMIN row-lock set, exactly as the finding describes. This also contradicts the module's own docstring (lines 18-26), which describes the lock as scoped to "update_user()'s role-demotion path." Not an instance of any of the 8 listed intentional patterns. However, this is a performance/concurrency inefficiency, not a correctness, data-integrity, or security bug -- and the affected surface is an internal, admin-only user-management console that is realistically low-concurrency. I therefore downgrade the claimed P2 to P3: real and worth fixing, but not high-urgency.

titles: github.py search() loses already-fetched repo results when the second sub-search fails

details.title: github.py search() loses already-fetched repo results when the second sub-search fails
details.actual_behavior: search() awaits `_search_repositories()` then `_search_code()` sequentially with no isolation (lines 121-122). `_search_repositories`/`_search_code` re-raise `SourceRateLimitedError` on HTTP 403/429 (lines 52 and 88) instead of swallowing it. If the first call succeeds with real hits but the second raises (rate limit, or any exception escaping the unguarded item-building loop at lines 63-74/99-116), the exception propagates out of `search()` before `combined = repo_results + code_results` ever runs, so the already-successful repo_results are thrown away entirely. collector.py then records github as fully rate-limited/failed with 0 results for that IOC, even though valid repository hits existed.
details.failure_scenario: A query returns 200 with real hits from `/search/repositories`, then GitHub returns 403 on the immediately-following `/search/code` call (plausible once the per-process 6s limiter is exceeded, e.g. under multiple backend replicas each running their own instance of github_limiter, or GitHub tightening its unauthenticated threshold). collector.py's fetch() then reports github as rate-limited with source_count['github']=0, discarding the real repository results that were already fetched.
details.proposed_fix: Fetch repo and code results independently (e.g. asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) inside search(), or try/except around each call) and return whichever succeeded instead of letting one failure discard the other's results.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of backend/app/crawler/sources/github.py lines 119-124:

```
async def search(query: str, client: httpx.AsyncClient, limit: int) -> list[dict]:
    repo_results = await _search_repositories(query, client, limit)
    code_results = await _search_code(query, client, limit)
    combined = repo_results + code_results
    return combined[:limit]
```

Both `_search_repositories` (line 49-52) and `_search_code` (line 86-88) deliberately re-raise `SourceRateLimitedError` on HTTP 403/429 while swallowing every other exception internally (the `except Exception` catch-all, explicitly commented "best-effort source, never raise (except rate-limit, see above)"). `search()` itself has no try/except or isolation between the two awaited calls. So if `_search_repositories` succeeds and returns real hits, but the very next `_search_code` call raises `SourceRateLimitedError`, that exception propagates straight out of `search()` and `combined = repo_results + code_results` never executes — the already-fetched `repo_results` are silently discarded.

Cross-checked the actual downstream consumer, backend/app/crawler/collector.py: `fetch()` runs `github.search(...)` as one task inside `asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)` (line 66). It treats the *entire* task's outcome as a single unit (lines 73-83): if the outcome `isinstance(outcome, SourceRateLimitedError)`, it does `source_count['github'] = 0` and `continue` — there is no mechanism to recover partial results from within a task that raised, since the whole coroutine's return value is the exception object, not a partial list. This exactly matches the claimed downstream effect: a real, already-fetched set of repo results is thrown away and github is recorded as contributing 0 results for that IOC.

I also verified the rate-limiter (rate_limit.py): `github_limiter` spaces calls 6s apart specifically "to keep two calls (repo + code search) per crawl comfortably under" GitHub's 10 req/min unauthenticated cap for a single process. This makes the failure scenario a real edge case rather than the common path — it requires either multiple replicas each running an independent in-process limiter (explicitly not Redis-backed, confirmed in the same file's docstring: "correctness only requires bounding this process's own outbound request rate, not a global cross-replica limit"), request bursts across concurrent distinct-IOC lookups, or GitHub-side secondary rate limiting/abuse detection unrelated to the simple interval math — all plausible in production, not purely theoretical.

This is a genuine inconsistency with the module's own stated design intent (comments call it "best-effort," and each sub-function already isolates generic exceptions internally), but the composition in `search()` undoes that isolation for the one exception type it doesn't swallow. This is not one of the listed intentional patterns (it's not a ProviderStatus mapping decision, not the JWT/basket/pentest/nmap patterns) — it's a straightforward error-handling/composition bug.

Severity: I concur with P3. Impact is real but bounded — it only discards github-specific results in one of four OSINT sub-sources within one provider category, only triggers under a rate-limit edge case, doesn't crash anything, and doesn't fully null out the InternetIntelligenceCollector's overall result (other sources like reddit/rss_news/pastebin_search can still supply results and keep overall status OK) — so it's a data-completeness edge-case bug rather than a high-impact functional break, consistent with a Low/P3 rating rather than P0-P2.

titles: psbdmp query is interpolated unescaped into the URL path, letting reserved URL characters silently redirect/truncate the search

details.title: psbdmp query is interpolated unescaped into the URL path, letting reserved URL characters silently redirect/truncate the search
details.actual_behavior: `_SEARCH_URL_TEMPLATE.format(query=query)` (line 29, template at line 21) substitutes the raw IOC value directly into a URL path segment instead of using httpx's `params=` dict (as github.py and reddit.py both correctly do) or `urllib.parse.quote`. httpx.URL does auto-encode spaces, but it does NOT encode reserved characters like `/`, `?`, `#`, `&` since those are structurally significant in a URL. Verified directly: `httpx.URL('https://psbdmp.ws/api/v3/search/' + 'foo/bar?x=1')` parses to path `/api/v3/search/foo/bar` with query string `x=1` -- silently dropping everything after `?` from the actual search term and turning `/` into extra path segments, rather than searching psbdmp for the literal string.
details.failure_scenario: A campaign/threat-actor/malware-family free-text IOC value containing `/`, `?`, `#`, or `&` (e.g. a campaign alias like "Operation Aurora/Elderwood") is looked up. The request sent to psbdmp.ws is not a search for that literal string; it either 404s, hits an unrelated path, or gets its trailing segment truncated -- and the response (or lack thereof) is treated identically to 'this best-effort source genuinely found nothing', silently reporting wrong or missing intelligence instead of the value actually queried for.
details.proposed_fix: URL-encode the query segment, e.g. `_SEARCH_URL_TEMPLATE.format(query=urllib.parse.quote(query, safe=''))`.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading pastebin_search.py and empirically testing httpx directly. Line 29 builds the request URL via `_SEARCH_URL_TEMPLATE.format(query=query)` and passes the resulting raw string to client.get(), instead of using params={} (as github.py's _search_repositories/_search_code and reddit.py both correctly do -- verified github.py uses `params={"q": query, ...}`). Empirically verified with the installed httpx on this machine: httpx.Request('GET', 'https://psbdmp.ws/api/v3/search/' + 'Operation Aurora/Elderwood').url.raw_path == b'/api/v3/search/Operation%20Aurora/Elderwood' -- the space gets escaped but the literal '/' is sent unescaped as a path separator, turning one query into two path segments. Similarly 'foo?bar=1' produces raw_path b'/api/v3/search/foo?bar=1', i.e. everything after '?' is parsed as the query string and dropped from the actual search path/term. Applying the reviewer's proposed fix (urllib.parse.quote(query, safe='')) correctly produces raw_path b'/api/v3/search/Operation%20Aurora%2FElderwood', preserving the literal string as one segment -- confirming both the defect and the fix.

Cross-file check confirms this is reachable with real inputs, not just theoretical: app/crawler/collector.py's InternetIntelligenceCollector explicitly supports IOCType.CAMPAIGN, THREAT_ACTOR, and MALWARE_FAMILY (free-text types), and app/schemas/lookup.py's LookupCreateRequest.value has no character restriction (Field(min_length=1, max_length=2048)), with ioc_type_hint settable directly by the caller (app/api/routes/lookup.py line 85). So a user can submit a campaign/actor/malware name containing '/', '?', '#', or '&' (e.g. real-world aliased names like "Sandworm/Voodoo Bear") and it flows unmodified into pastebin_search.search's raw query. The malformed request then either 404s (silently absorbed by the `status_code != 200` branch at lines 33-35, returning []) or gets truncated at a reserved character -- in both cases indistinguishable from the documented "psbdmp genuinely found nothing" case, contradicting the module's own docstring intent that failure-collapse should reflect the third-party service's unreliability, not the caller's own request-construction bug.

This doesn't match any of the listed intentional design patterns (not graceful NOT_CONFIGURED degradation, not the AI-narration-only pattern, not a provider-status mislabeling issue, etc.) -- it's a genuine unescaped-interpolation defect distinct from those.

Severity: P3 is well-calibrated, matching the original reviewer. It's a real but narrow-scope correctness bug (URL-path corruption via unescaped query) affecting only one of four crawler sources, only for free-text IOC types, and only when the literal value contains a reserved URL character. There's no security/auth impact, no data corruption, no crash -- worst case is silently wrong/missing OSINT enrichment from an already low-trust, explicitly "no uptime/rate-limit guarantee" best-effort source, which the system already treats as an acceptable outcome (ProviderStatus.NO_DATA) for that source. That keeps it below P0/P1/P2 but above cosmetic P4.

titles: A single malformed/null 'data' field discards every already-parsed Reddit result instead of just that entry

details.title: A single malformed/null 'data' field discards every already-parsed Reddit result instead of just that entry
details.actual_behavior: `payload.get("data", {})` (line 54) and `child.get("data", {})` (line 56) only substitute the `{}` default when the key is *missing*; if the key is present with an explicit JSON `null`, `.get` returns `None` instead. `post.get("permalink", ...)` on that `None` then raises `AttributeError`, which is caught by the single try/except wrapping the *entire* for-loop (lines 53-73), causing the function to `return []` -- discarding every post already appended to `results` for prior, well-formed children in the same response, not just the offending one.
details.failure_scenario: Reddit's search.json response includes one child entry with `"data": null` (e.g. a removed/quarantined/promoted listing) among several normal posts. Parsing throws on that entry and the whole batch of otherwise-valid posts for that IOC lookup is thrown away, even though most of the response was parseable.
details.proposed_fix: Wrap the per-entry parsing in its own try/except inside the loop (continue on a bad entry) instead of one try/except around the whole loop, and treat an explicit `None` the same as a missing key (e.g. `post = child.get('data') or {}`).
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code reading. `child.get("data", {})` (line 56) and `payload.get("data", {})` (line 54) only apply the `{}` default when the key is missing; per standard Python dict semantics, an explicitly-present `None` value is returned as-is. If any child in the Reddit response has `data: null` (or is otherwise not a dict, or lacks expected fields in a way that raises), `post.get("permalink", ...)` on line 57 raises AttributeError. That exception is caught by the single try/except spanning the entire for-loop (lines 53-71), whose except clause does `return []` (line 73) rather than `return results` -- discarding every post already appended to `results` in prior loop iterations for the same response, not just the offending entry. The comment at line 71 ("malformed payload shouldn't break the collector") states an intent of per-entry resilience that the current control flow does not implement -- a single bad entry anywhere in the list zeroes out all otherwise-good parsed posts from that call. This is not covered by any of the listed intentional design patterns. The one caveat (matching the original reviewer's own low confidence) is that I could not independently confirm Reddit's live API ever actually emits `"data": null` for a child entry vs. some other malformed shape, but the code-level defect -- broad exception scope discarding already-good results on any single-entry parse failure -- is unambiguously present regardless of which specific malformed value triggers it. Severity: this is a best-effort, non-authenticated, non-security data source where the module docstring already documents that failures degrade to an empty list; worst-case impact is silently reduced recall for one Reddit-sourced batch in an IOC lookup, with no crash and no security exposure, so P3 (as originally claimed) is the right severity -- not higher, and not low enough to be dismissed as trivial since it is a real, reproducible data-loss defect relative to the code's own stated intent.

titles: _JA3_RE and _MUTEX_HINT_RE are compiled but never referenced; JA3/MUTEX (and several other IOCType enum members) are never produced by the detector

details.title: _JA3_RE and _MUTEX_HINT_RE are compiled but never referenced; JA3/MUTEX (and several other IOCType enum members) are never produced by the detector

This suggests an abandoned/incomplete feature rather than a deliberate design choice (unlike the MALWARE_FAMILY/THREAT_ACTOR/CAMPAIGN cases, which the code explicitly documents as intentionally left ambiguous at lines 150-158).

titles: /metrics is exposed unconditionally, unlike /docs/openapi.json which the file explicitly environment-gates for the same recon-value reasoning

details.title: /metrics is exposed unconditionally, unlike /docs/openapi.json which the file explicitly environment-gates for the same recon-value reasoning
details.actual_behavior: `Instrumentator().instrument(app).expose(app, endpoint="/metrics")` (line 231) registers /metrics with no environment gate and no auth dependency at all, unconditionally in every environment including production -- inconsistent with the threat model just articulated a few lines above for /docs.

details.proposed_fix: Gate /metrics the same way as /docs (e.g. only expose it when settings.environment != "production", or require a dependency/auth check), or explicitly document that operators must firewall it off in production.

Line 231 (`Instrumentator().instrument(app).expose(app, endpoint="/metrics")`) registers /metrics with zero environment gate and zero auth dependency -- a grep across the whole backend tree shows this is the only place /metrics is ever touched, so no auth/gating is applied anywhere else. So in a genuine production install with ENVIRONMENT=production (docs disabled per the file's own logic), the backend port is still reachable from the LAN and /metrics is fully open. BUG_TRIAGE.md already has a BUG-044 about /metrics, but it addresses a different angle (lack of per-incident/per-actor label granularity) and never addresses or dismisses the auth/environment-gating gap, so this isn't a duplicate of an already-adjudicated finding. prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator's default http_requests_total counters are labeled by handler (route template)/method/status (confirmed via BUG-044's own evidence, e.g. `http_requests_total{handler="/api/v1/lookup/stream",method="POST",status="4xx"}`), which does enumerate real route paths (including admin/pentest-exploit routes) plus relative traffic/error-rate signal -- a real, if narrower, subset of the same recon value the /docs gate exists to deny.

titles: MSF RPC placeholder-password check only matches the code-level default, not the literal value .env.example actually ships -- the exact gap the JWT-secret check next to it was already fixed for

details.title: MSF RPC placeholder-password check only matches the code-level default, not the literal value .env.example actually ships -- the exact gap the JWT-secret check next to it was already fixed for
details.actual_behavior: `if settings.msf_rpc_password == "horizon-grid-msf-rpc-local":` (line 290) checks only against config.py's Python-level Field default. .env.example line 16 ships `MSF_RPC_PASSWORD=replace-with-a-long-random-string` -- a different literal string (in fact the same placeholder text used for JWT_SECRET_KEY). The backend starts with a known, publicly-documented placeholder RPC password and never warns the operator, unlike the JWT check right above it which was specifically fixed for this exact pattern. Real-world impact is limited by msfrpcd's 127.0.0.1-only binding (per the function's own comment), but the warning mechanism itself silently fails for the realistic case it exists to catch.
details.proposed_fix: Check against a set of known placeholders the same way _KNOWN_PLACEHOLDER_JWT_SECRETS does, e.g. `{"horizon-grid-msf-rpc-local", "replace-with-a-long-random-string"}`.
