titles: Error banner is never cleared after a later successful action
refreshAll silently swallows failures for the page's own primary provider lists
Overlapping refreshAll() calls have no response-ordering guard

details.title: Error banner is never cleared after a later successful action
details.actual_behavior: `setError` is only ever invoked inside `catch` blocks (lines 128, 142, 161, 178). No code path -- not the try blocks, not refreshAll -- ever calls `setError(null)`. Once any single action fails, the error banner is permanently displayed for the rest of the page's life, even after the exact same operation later succeeds.
details.failure_scenario: User expands the Anthropic row, types an invalid API key, clicks Save -> configureAIProvider rejects -> banner shows e.g. 'Invalid credential value'. User then types the correct key and clicks Save again -> the save succeeds and the row flips to 'Configured', but the old 'Invalid credential value' banner is still shown at the top of the page, falsely suggesting the just-completed save also failed.
details.proposed_fix: Call setError(null) at the start of each onSave/onTest/onToggleEnabled/onSetActive handler, mirroring the pattern already used in app/pentest/page.tsx's and app/cases/page.tsx's handleCreate (setError(null) before the try block).
details.reasoning: Read frontend/app/providers/page.tsx directly. The page-level `error` state (declared line 60) drives the red banner at lines 92-96. Grepping every `setError` call site in the file confirms there are exactly four, at lines 128, 142, 161, 178, and all four are inside `catch` blocks setting an error message -- none is `setError(null)`. The `onSave` (AI, 122-130), `onSetActive` (137-144), `onSave` (IOC, 155-163), and `onToggleEnabled` (170-180) handlers all follow the same shape: try { ...await api call...; update local list state; refreshAll(); } catch (err) { setError(...) }. The success branch never clears a previously-set error, and `refreshAll` (62-66) swallows its own errors via `.catch(() => {})` without touching `error` either. So once any action fails and the banner appears, it is never cleared by any subsequent action, including a later successful retry of the exact same operation -- exactly the scenario described (invalid API key -> error banner -> correct key -> save succeeds, row flips to Configured, but the old 'Invalid credential value' banner remains). I also cross-checked the codebase's own convention: grepping `setError(null)` across frontend/app shows app/cases/page.tsx:68, app/pentest/page.tsx:68, app/pentest/[id]/page.tsx (8 occurrences), app/basket/page.tsx:75, app/login/page.tsx:22, and app/register/page.tsx:21 all clear the error at the start of their handler before the try block -- confirming this is an established, intentional pattern elsewhere in the app that providers/page.tsx simply omits. This does not match any of the 8 documented intentional design patterns (it's not about role-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED status, AI-narration-only scoring, basket visibility, security-toolkit/pentest-suite overlap, exploit gating, nmap flag restrictions, or per-call provider status semantics). Impact-wise, it's a real, reproducible, user-facing UX correctness bug (misleading stale error banner) but causes no data loss, no security exposure, and does not block the underlying action from succeeding -- the row's own state still updates correctly. That keeps it at low severity; P3 as originally claimed is appropriate, not an over- or under-statement.

details.title: refreshAll silently swallows failures for the page's own primary provider lists
details.actual_behavior: All three calls in refreshAll -- listAIProviders, listIOCProviders, and getAuditLog -- use `.catch(() => {})`, discarding any error with zero state update. This mirrors app/admin/page.tsx's refreshAll, but on that page the swallowed calls (getUserStats/getRoles/getAuditLog) are genuinely secondary panels while the real primary content (the user table) is a separate component with its own handling; here there is no such separation, so the page's actual primary lists get the same throwaway treatment as the audit log.
details.failure_scenario: Backend is mid-restart or briefly 500s on GET /api/v1/runtime/ai-providers exactly when a user loads /providers (or immediately after any Save/Toggle/Set-Active, since refreshAll re-runs after every one of those). listAIProviders() rejects, the catch discards it, aiProviders keeps its previous (initially empty) value, and the AI Providers tab renders with zero rows and no error message -- indistinguishable from 'you have no AI providers configured', even though the built-in AI_BACKENDS entries always exist server-side. The user cannot tell 'the fetch failed' from 'nothing is configured'.
details.proposed_fix: Give listAIProviders()/listIOCProviders() an explicit `.catch(err => setError(...))` (leaving getAuditLog's swallow as-is, since that one is genuinely secondary), consistent with how every mutating handler on the same page already surfaces its own errors.

details.title: Overlapping refreshAll() calls have no response-ordering guard
details.actual_behavior: refreshAll() (lines 62-66) is invoked, unawaited, after every mutating handler and simply chains `listAIProviders().then(setAiProviders)` with no request token, AbortController, or sequence check. If two refreshAll() calls overlap and their GET responses arrive out of issue-order (ordinary network jitter), the later-issued (more current) response can be overwritten by an earlier-issued response's `.then(setAiProviders)` resolving after it.
details.failure_scenario: User clicks 'Set Active' on provider B, then immediately clicks 'Save' on provider A with new credentials. Both handlers call refreshAll(), starting two concurrent listAIProviders() requests. If the first request's response is delayed and lands after the second's, the first (now-stale) response's setAiProviders call runs last, and the UI can show provider B as not-yet-active or provider A's pre-save config until some later action happens to trigger another refresh.
details.proposed_fix: Track a monotonically increasing request id (or use an AbortController per refreshAll invocation) and ignore a response if a newer request has since been issued.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct reading of frontend/app/providers/page.tsx lines 62-66: refreshAll() is exactly as described -- three independent fire-and-forget `.then(setState)` chains with no AbortController, request token, or sequence guard, invoked unawaited after every mutating handler (onSave, onTest, onSetActive, onToggleEnabled). Cross-checked ProviderConfigRow.tsx: Save/Test buttons are only disabled per-row for their own in-flight action; Set Active and Enable/Disable have no pending guard at all, and nothing disables buttons across different provider rows -- so a user really can trigger two overlapping refreshAll() calls in quick succession (e.g. Set Active on one row immediately followed by Save on another). Cross-checked lib/api.ts: listAIProviders/listIOCProviders/getAuditLog are plain authedFetch calls with no dedup or cancellation logic. So if the two GETs resolve out of issue-order due to ordinary network jitter, the stale (earlier-issued) response's setState can run after and overwrite the fresher one -- a genuine, unguarded race condition, not one of the documented intentional patterns. Impact is limited to a transient, self-healing UI staleness on an authenticated admin settings page; server state is never corrupted, and any subsequent action or reload corrects the display. This matches a P4 (trivial/cosmetic, no security or data-integrity impact) severity, consistent with the original reviewer's claim -- no adjustment needed.

titles: "firstOther" default-selection filter never actually filters anything

details.title: "firstOther" default-selection filter never actually filters anything
details.actual_behavior: `list.find((p) => p.provider_id)` uses a predicate that is truthy for every entry, since `RuntimeProviderConfig.provider_id` (frontend/lib/types.ts:103) is a required, always-non-empty string. The `.find` therefore always returns `list[0]` regardless of whether that provider already produced the original assessment — it is functionally `list[0]`, not "first other [than something]". No comparison against `records`/`alreadyRunBackends` (computed separately at line 68) is performed at all when picking the default.
details.failure_scenario: A lookup's original assessment was produced with backend "anthropic" (is_primary=true), and `listAIProviders()` returns ["anthropic", "groq", "ollama"] in that order. On panel load, `selected` defaults to "anthropic" — the option shows "(already run)" next to it, but the Analyze button is pre-armed to re-run the exact same backend that already produced the original result, contrary to the feature's stated purpose of comparing against a different backend.
details.proposed_fix: Filter candidates against `alreadyRunBackends` (or the primary record's `ai_backend`) before picking the default, e.g. `list.find((p) => !records.some((r) => r.ai_backend === p.provider_id))`.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the file directly. `list.find((p) => p.provider_id)` at line 47 uses a predicate that tests truthiness of `provider_id`, which per frontend/lib/types.ts:103 is a required (non-optional, non-nullable) string, and per backend/app/core/runtime_config.py is always populated from a fixed non-empty backend-name constant for every row returned by the /ai-providers endpoint. Therefore the predicate is truthy for every element in the list without exception, making `.find` equivalent to `list[0]` -- it never filters anything. The code never references `alreadyRunBackends` (computed separately at line 68 from `records`) inside this effect, so the default selection has no awareness of which backend already produced the original/a prior assessment for this lookup. This contradicts both the variable name `firstOther` and the feature's own stated purpose (re-run against a genuinely different backend for comparison). This does not match any of the 8 known intentional design patterns. Real-world impact is real but modest: it only affects the pre-selected dropdown default (user can still manually pick a different provider), and the UI already annotates the already-run option with "(already run)" as a passive cue, and no data is corrupted or mislabeled -- just a potential redundant re-run if the analyst doesn't change the default. This matches a P3 (minor logic/UX defect, not functionality-breaking) severity, consistent with the original reviewer's rating; no correction needed.

titles: Tabs' defaultValue goes stale when detectionRules changes without a remount, leaving no active tab

details.title: Tabs' defaultValue goes stale when detectionRules changes without a remount, leaving no active tab
details.actual_behavior: `<TabsPrimitive.Root defaultValue={formats[0]}>` (line 75) only seeds Radix's internal uncontrolled active-tab state once, at mount. `formats` itself is correctly recomputed via useMemo whenever `detectionRules` changes (lines 30-35), but the Tabs primitive's own selection state does not follow it. Both consumer pages (`/app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx`, `/app/lookup/new/page.tsx`) reuse the same DetectionRulesPanel/page component instance across a `lookupId` change (no `key` prop; confirmed via grep), so once this branch of the ternary (line 74-onward) is already mounted, a subsequent prop change doesn't remount TabsPrimitive.Root.
details.failure_scenario: Viewing /lookup/AAA, detectionRules = [{format:"Sigma"},{format:"YARA"}], "Sigma" tab active by default. Analyst client-navigates (e.g. via a pivot link) to /lookup/BBB whose detectionRules = [{format:"Suricata"},{format:"Snort"}]. `formats` recomputes to ["Suricata","Snort"] and both tab triggers render, but Radix's internal state still points at "Sigma", which matches none of the new `TabsPrimitive.Content value=`. Result: two tab buttons are shown, neither highlighted as active, and no rule content renders at all despite detectionRules.length > 0 -- until the analyst manually clicks one of the tabs.
details.proposed_fix: Either pass a `value`/`onValueChange` pair (controlled Tabs) synced to a React state that's reset via a `useEffect` on `detectionRules`/formats change, or force a remount by keying the whole `<TabsPrimitive.Root>` (or the panel) on `formats.join(',')`/lookupId.
details.reasoning:
Verified the core technical mechanism directly against source, and it is real:

1. DetectionRulesPanel.tsx:30-35 recomputes `formats` via useMemo whenever `detectionRules` changes, but line 75 passes it only as `defaultValue={formats[0]}` (uncontrolled, no `value`/`onValueChange`).
2. Read @radix-ui/react-use-controllable-state's actual source (node_modules): the uncontrolled branch is `React.useState(defaultProp)` — React only reads that initial value on first mount; later re-renders with a different `defaultValue` prop do not reset the internal state. Confirmed.
3. Read @radix-ui/react-tabs' actual source: `TabsContent` only renders via `Presence present={forceMount || isSelected}` where `isSelected = value === context.value`; DetectionRulesPanel passes no `forceMount`. So if the stale internal `value` (e.g. "Sigma") matches none of the newly rendered formats (e.g. ["Suricata","Snort"]), no Trigger shows `data-state=active` and no Content renders — exactly as claimed.

So the code-level defect described in the finding is genuine and I reproduced the mechanism by reading both files, not just trusting the description.

However, the claimed reachability is overstated and needed correction:
- I read both consumer pages in full. `/app/lookup/new/page.tsx` explicitly guards against exactly this class of bug: `LookupNewPageKeyed` does `<LookupNewPageInner key={rawValue} />` (lines 264-273), with a comment stating this is precisely to force a full remount when the IOC value changes so stale state isn't reused. The reviewer's claim that "both consumer pages reuse the same instance... no key prop; confirmed via grep" is factually wrong for this page.
- The claimed trigger ("pivot link" causing navigation from /lookup/AAA to /lookup/BBB) does not exist in this app. I grepped every navigation call in the frontend (PivotPanel, RelationshipGraph, basket page, cases/[id] page, TopSearchBar, home page) — every single "investigate this IOC" action routes to `/lookup/new?value=...` (which is key-protected), never to `/lookup/[id]`. There is no Link/router.push anywhere in the codebase that transitions client-side from one `/lookup/[id]` URL to a different `/lookup/[id]` URL; the only way to view a completed lookup by id is a direct/typed URL (a hard navigation, which fully remounts everything, avoiding the bug).
- The one genuinely unprotected page is `/app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx` (no key), but it has no in-app-triggered soft transition to another id. The realistic way to hit the bug is a browser back/forward between two independently (hard-)loaded `/lookup/{id}` pages, since Next.js App Router intercepts popstate for client-side transitions once hydrated, reusing the mounted page component across the same dynamic route pattern. This is a plausible but narrower and more incidental trigger than "pivoting via a link," and it is trivially recoverable (one click on a tab restores full functionality), and it only affects a secondary display panel (detection rules), not verdict/scoring/security-critical data.

Given the defect is real and verified at the source level, but the claimed severity assumed a broader, incorrect reachability (both pages, pivot-link-triggered) that doesn't hold up, I downgrade from P2 to P3: a real, narrow-scope, easily-worked-around UI staleness bug rather than a significant functional break in a primary workflow.

titles: Severity stat tile colored with verdictColor(), whose switch cases never match a severity value

titles: OSINT finding URLs are rendered as anchor hrefs with no scheme validation

details.title: OSINT finding URLs are rendered as anchor hrefs with no scheme validation
details.actual_behavior: Line 169 does `<a href={finding.url} target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">`, and line 285 does the same for `result.source_url`, with no scheme check anywhere in this component (or, as far as this file shows, upstream). `rel="noopener noreferrer"` protects against reverse-tabnabbing via `window.opener` but does not prevent a `javascript:`-scheme href from executing script in the page's origin when the link is clicked.
details.failure_scenario: backend/app/crawler/collector.py only checks `if not url or url in seen_urls: continue` (collector.py line 87) before using a source module's returned `url` value verbatim -- it never validates the scheme. If any crawler source module (or a compromised/malicious upstream search result) ever returns a `url` value using the `javascript:` scheme instead of `http(s):`, `OsintFindingsList` will render it as a normal-looking link (`finding.title || finding.url` as the visible text) that executes arbitrary script in the analyst's authenticated session when clicked, instead of navigating away.
details.proposed_fix: Validate/allowlist the URL scheme (e.g. only render as a clickable `<a>` when `new URL(url).protocol` is `http:` or `https:`, otherwise render as plain text) before using `finding.url` / `result.source_url` as an href.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct code reading. frontend/components/dashboard/ProviderCard.tsx line 169 does `<a href={finding.url} target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">` inside OsintFindingsList, and line 285 does the identical pattern for `result.source_url` in the CardHeader — neither performs any scheme check (no allowlist, no `new URL(...).protocol` guard, nothing). `rel="noopener noreferrer"` only stops reverse-tabnabbing via window.opener; it does nothing to stop a `javascript:`-scheme href from executing script in the page's own origin when clicked, and no CSP was found anywhere under frontend/ that would mitigate this.

Traced the call chain into backend/app/crawler/collector.py: line 87 (`if not url or url in seen_urls: continue`) is indeed the only check applied to a source module's returned `url` before it's placed into `merged` (used for `osint_findings`) and also copied verbatim into `source_url` (line 133: `source_url=merged[0]["url"] if merged else None`) — confirming both hrefs named in the finding trace back to the same unsanitized value. No scheme validation exists anywhere in this path.

I read all four source modules to check real-world exploitability of the claimed `javascript:` scenario:
- pastebin_search.py always builds the URL from a hardcoded template `f"https://pastebin.com/{dump_id}"` — scheme is fixed, not attacker-controllable.
- github.py uses GitHub's own API `item.get("html_url", "")` — GitHub-controlled, not directly attacker-settable via search content.
- rss_news.py pulls `entry.get("link", "")` from a small fixed list of trusted security-news RSS feeds (BleepingComputer, Krebs, Talos, MSFT, CrowdStrike, Unit42, etc.) — low realistic risk absent a compromised trusted feed.
- reddit.py is the one genuinely attacker-influenceable path: for link-type posts it uses `post.get("url", "")` directly from Reddit's API with no scheme check. This is user-submitted content on a public platform; whether Reddit's own submission pipeline rejects non-http(s) schemes is not verified in this codebase and cannot be assumed as a safety net the app is relying on (and clearly isn't, since the app does no check of its own).

So this is a real, narrow, defense-in-depth gap: untrusted externally-sourced URLs are placed directly into `href` with no scheme allowlist, and at least one crawler source (Reddit) plausibly carries attacker-influenceable URL content end-to-end to that href with zero validation anywhere in the chain. This is not one of the documented intentional design patterns. Exploitation requires several chained conditions (malicious/compromised source content, that content ranking for the analyst's specific IOC query, and the analyst clicking the link), which keeps real-world likelihood low — consistent with the original P3 rating. details.title: Inconsistent fallback value for a missing/falsy `confidence` between text paths (0) and render paths (0.5)
details.actual_behavior: `link.confidence ?? 0` is used for the tooltip (line 111) and the list view (line 153), but `link.confidence ?? 0.5` is used for link color opacity (line 285) and link width (line 293) -- two different defensive fallbacks for the exact same field on the same object.

- Line 293 (linkWidth): `0.6 + ((link as GraphLinkDatum).confidence ?? 0.5) * 1.5`

Severity: real-world impact is very low — it only manifests when confidence is missing/null despite the type declaring it required (a defensive-only path that, per current backend code, is not known to actually occur), and even when triggered it's a purely cosmetic/visual disagreement (percentage text vs. opacity/width), not a data-integrity, security, or crash issue. details.title: Link `id` used as React list key is not guaranteed unique across edges the backend can legitimately emit
details.actual_behavior: The link `id` is derived only from `${edge.source}->${edge.target}:${edge.relationship}` (lines 202-205), ignoring `confidence`/`provenance`, and that id is used directly as the React `key` in GraphListView's `<tr key={link.id}>` (line 149). The backend does not guarantee (source,target,relationship) uniqueness in the payload sent to this component: `merge_correlation_results()` in backend/app/correlation/engine.py explicitly documents that it does NOT re-run corroboration/dedup merge across an already-persisted correlation and a freshly computed one, so 'an edge asserted identically by both an original threat-intel provider and a new security-assessment tool will appear twice rather than being merged'. `_correlation_payload()` in backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py (which builds the exact JSON GET /lookup/{id} returns to this component) confirms this in practice: it emits one edge dict per persisted CorrelationEdgeRecord row with zero deduplication across rows from different runs.
details.failure_scenario: Initial provider pass finds `evil.com resolves_to 1.2.3.4` (edge A: confidence 0.9, provenance "virustotal"). A later Security Assessment Toolkit run independently observes and persists the same relationship as a second CorrelationEdgeRecord row (edge B: confidence 1.0, provenance "dns_tool"). Both rows come back in the same `edges` array. RelationshipGraph.tsx computes the identical id `domain:evil.com->ipv4:1.2.3.4:resolves_to` for both, so GraphListView renders two `<tr>` with the same React key. React logs a duplicate-key warning, and its reconciliation guarantee is broken for that pair: on any subsequent re-render where the edges array order/count changes (switching lookups, a later live update), React can reuse the wrong DOM node for the wrong row, displaying an incorrect confidence/provenance pairing to the analyst for a security-relevant relationship.
details.proposed_fix: Include provenance (and/or a backend-supplied edge id) in the derived id, e.g. `${edge.source}->${edge.target}:${edge.relationship}:${edge.provenance}`, or fall back to the array index as a tiebreaker.
details.reasoning: Verified by reading the actual code. frontend/components/dashboard/RelationshipGraph.tsx lines 202-205 derive link.id as `${edge.source}->${edge.target}:${edge.relationship}` (no confidence/provenance), and line 149 uses that id directly as the React key in GraphListView's <tr>. On the backend, merge_correlation_results() in backend/app/correlation/engine.py (lines 199-229) explicitly documents that it does not dedupe/merge an already-persisted correlation against a freshly computed one, so an edge asserted by both an original provider and a later security-assessment tool run will appear twice. Confirmed the actual persistence paths: backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py (lines 178-192) and backend/app/core/security_assessment.py (lines 576-627) each independently call correlate() and insert new CorrelationEdgeRecord rows with no check against existing rows for the same lookup_id, so two rows with identical (source,target,relationship) but different confidence/provenance can and do coexist in the DB. _correlation_payload() in lookup.py (lines 804-843) then emits one edge dict per row with zero cross-row dedup, confirming duplicate ids reach the frontend. This is a real, verified bug -- not one of the documented intentional design patterns. I lowered severity from the claimed P2 to P3 because: (1) it only affects the secondary 'View as list' table, not the primary force-directed graph (react-force-graph-2d doesn't use the link id for node/link identity the way it does nodeId); (2) the triggering backend condition is explicitly documented in-repo as 'rare in practice'; (3) duplicate keys don't corrupt displayed content on the very first render (React only mis-reconciles on a later re-render while the collision persists and the list changes), so the full 'analyst sees wrong confidence/provenance' failure mode requires stacking two independently narrow conditions. It's still a cheap, worthwhile fix (add provenance to the id, as the reviewer proposed) but not P2-level impact.

details.title: `isEmpty` collapses 'no data yet' (data === null) and 'confirmed zero relationships' (data.edges.length === 0) into the identical UI, defeating the backend's explicit design to keep them distinguishable
details.actual_behavior: `const isEmpty = !data || data.edges.length === 0;` treats a null `data` prop (correlation not yet received) exactly the same as a real payload with zero edges (correlation received, genuinely no relationships found) -- both render the identical `EmptyState` message 'No relationships discovered yet' (lines 163-173, 251-252). backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py's `_correlation_payload()` docstring states this distinction is intentional and load-bearing: 'Always includes the seed IOC as a node even with zero edges... otherwise "no relationships found" would look identical to "graph data unavailable" instead of being distinguishable.' The frontend re-merges the two states the backend went out of its way to keep apart.
details.failure_scenario: On /lookup/new, `correlation` state starts as `null` and is only set once the backend's SSE `correlation` event fires (see frontend/app/lookup/new/page.tsx `onCorrelation` handler) -- which happens only after providers have run and correlation has executed, i.e. noticeably later than page load. During that whole window, RelationshipGraph shows 'No relationships discovered yet', identical to what it will show later if the run genuinely finds no relationships. An analyst watching the live investigation can read the early, still-loading state as 'the investigation already checked and found nothing,' when in fact no correlation attempt has completed yet.
details.proposed_fix: Distinguish the two states, e.g. render a loading/pending placeholder when `data === null` and only show 'No relationships discovered yet' once a real payload with `edges.length === 0` has arrived.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading the actual code.

1. frontend/components/dashboard/RelationshipGraph.tsx:231 — `const isEmpty = !data || data.edges.length === 0;` — and lines 251-252 render the identical `EmptyState` ("No relationships discovered yet") for both branches of that OR. There is no code path anywhere in this component that treats `data === null` differently from a real zero-edge payload.

2. backend/app/api/routes/lookup.py `_correlation_payload()` (lines 804-834) has a docstring that explicitly states: "Always includes the seed IOC as a node even with zero edges, matching the live event's behavior (confirmed live: a lookup with no discovered relationships still streams a single-node, zero-edge `correlation` event, not a missing one) — otherwise 'no relationships found' would look identical to 'graph data unavailable' instead of being distinguishable." This confirms the backend deliberately engineered a real, non-null payload (with a seed node, zero edges) specifically so it could be told apart from "no payload at all." The frontend's `isEmpty` check throws that distinction away by keying only off `data.edges.length` (or `!data`), never off whether `data`/`data.nodes` exists at all.

3. frontend/app/lookup/new/page.tsx: `correlation` state is initialized to `null` (line 65) and only populated by the SSE `onCorrelation` handler (line 120-122), which fires only once the backend actually completes correlation — i.e., strictly later than page load, confirming the "not yet available" window claimed in the finding is real, not hypothetical. Also telling: sibling panels on the same page (`ThreatScoreGauge`, `MitreMatrix`, `DetectionRulesPanel`) all take an explicit `loading={!isDone}` prop to distinguish "still running" from "ran and found nothing," but `RelationshipGraph` (line 202) is passed only `data={correlation}` with no loading prop and no such distinction inside the component — an inconsistency with the rest of the page's own pattern for exactly this problem.

This is a real, verified defect, not one of the documented intentional patterns (it doesn't match any of the 8 listed design patterns). Severity: it's a purely cosmetic/UX state-conflation bug — it doesn't corrupt data, break functionality, or affect security, and it self-corrects once the SSE event fires (it's not a permanent misrepresentation). It could plausibly mislead an analyst who looks only at this one card mid-investigation, but the rest of the page (ProviderProgressTracker, ThreatScoreGauge's own loading spinner state, event log) gives strong contextual cues that the investigation is still in progress, which somewhat mitigates real-world impact. P3 (minor, transient, UX-only misleading state, easy fix) matches the actual impact — I see no basis to upgrade to P2/P1 or downgrade to P4.

titles: No effect resets selectedTools/selectedProfile/authorizationConfirmed/activeFinding when the lookupId/iocValue props change, so the authorization checkbox can carry over stale consent from a previous investigation

details.title: No effect resets selectedTools/selectedProfile/authorizationConfirmed/activeFinding when the lookupId/iocValue props change, so the authorization checkbox can carry over stale consent from a previous investigation
details.actual_behavior: `selectedTools`, `selectedProfile`, `authorizationConfirmed`, and `activeFinding` are plain `useState` (lines 71-76) with no `useEffect` keyed on `lookupId` (or `iocValue`) that resets them. The only lookupId-reactive logic in this component is `refreshRuns`/the mount effect (lines 78-89), which only refreshes `runs`/`profiles`/`toolHealth`/`canRun`. Because React does not unmount/remount a component merely because a parent passes it new prop values at the same JSX position, if the parent (`app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx`) re-renders with a different `lookupId`/`iocValue` for an already-mounted `SecurityAssessmentPanel` (that page's own pattern of manually re-fetching lookup data inside a `useEffect([lookupId])`, at lines 96-147 of that file, rather than relying on remount, shows this exact page is not assumed to remount on lookupId change), this panel's local state -- including the `authorizationConfirmed` checkbox -- survives across the switch to a different investigation/target.
details.failure_scenario: User views investigation A, checks "I am authorized..." for target A, then navigates away (e.g. via browser back/forward between two previously-visited /lookup/[id] history entries, which Next's client-side router handles without a full reload/remount) to investigation B while this component instance persists. On landing on B, `iocValue`/`lookupId` props update to B's target, but `authorizationConfirmed` is still `true` and `selectedTools`/`selectedProfile` may still be non-empty/valid, so `canSubmit` is already true; the very next click of "Run Security Assessment" fires an active scan against B's target using a consent checkbox the user only ever ticked for A.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed directly in the source. SecurityAssessmentPanel.tsx lines 71-76 declare selectedTools, selectedProfile, authorizationConfirmed, and activeFinding as plain useState with no initializer tied to lookupId/iocValue. The only lookupId-reactive logic (lines 78-97) is refreshRuns/the mount effect, which refreshes runs/profiles/toolHealth/canRun but never touches those four pieces of state. There is no useEffect keyed on lookupId or iocValue anywhere in the file that resets them, and the parent (`app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx` line 234) renders `<SecurityAssessmentPanel lookupId={lookupId} iocValue={iocValue} iocType={iocType} />` with no `key` prop, so React will reuse the same component instance (and its state) across a lookupId/iocValue prop change rather than remounting.

That the parent itself does NOT rely on remount for its own state is independently verifiable: its own `useEffect([lookupId])` (lines 96-150) manually re-fetches and resets iocValue/iocType/providerResults/etc. on every lookupId change, which would be pointless if the page remounted automatically. Stronger corroboration comes from a sibling file in the same codebase: `TopSearchBar.tsx`'s docstring explicitly states "Next.js won't remount LookupNewPageInner on its own" when navigating within the same route with a new param, which is exactly why `/lookup/new/page.tsx` deliberately keys its root element on `?value=` to force a remount. No equivalent `key` or reset effect was applied to `SecurityAssessmentPanel` or its parent's rendering of it. I also checked the backend's `_validate_scope` (core/security_assessment.py) — it only checks that `target_confirmation` (the frontend's currently-displayed `iocValue`) matches `lookup.ioc_value` and that `authorization_confirmed` is `true`; it does not verify the checkbox was ticked specifically for the currently active target. So a stale `authorizationConfirmed=true` left over from a previous target would sail through server-side validation since the frontend always sends the current (correct) iocValue alongside the stale boolean. This is a genuine violation of the "fresh per-target confirmation" invariant promised by the checkbox copy and module docstring, and it isn't covered by any of the listed intentional-design exclusions.

However, I downgrade the severity from the claimed P2 to P3: after searching the whole frontend for any `href`/`router.push` that navigates directly from one `/lookup/[id]` URL to a different `/lookup/[id]` URL, I found none. Every cross-investigation pivot in the shipped app (PivotPanel, RelationshipGraph, cases/[id] "Investigate" button, basket page, TopSearchBar) routes through `/lookup/new?value=...`, a structurally different Next.js route/page module from `/lookup/[id]`; transitioning through it forces a full unmount of the previous page tree (including SecurityAssessmentPanel), which incidentally clears the stale state before a fresh `/lookup/[id]` instance for the new target is ever mounted. The reviewer's specific "browser back/forward between two previously-visited /lookup/[id] entries" trigger also doesn't actually reproduce the bug on inspection: reaching that scenario via Next's client router requires an original direct soft push from A's URL straight to B's URL (which doesn't exist in this app), and a plain hard/typed-URL navigation between A and B either forces a fresh mount or, if browser bfcache applies, restores each page's own separate, internally-consistent snapshot rather than mixing state across them. So the code-level defect is real and worth fixing defensively (a one-line `useEffect(() => {...reset...}, [lookupId])` would close it), but it is currently a latent gap rather than an actively exploitable path in the shipped product, which is why P3 (not P2) is the more accurate severity today.

details.title: cancellingRunId is a single scalar, so cancelling two runs in quick succession loses the in-flight state of the first one
details.actual_behavior: `cancellingRunId` (line 75) is a single `string | null`, not a set/map of in-flight run ids. `handleCancel` (159-170) sets it to the clicked run's id before the await and clears it to `null` in `finally`. Now A's button re-renders as enabled (since `cancellingRunId !== "A"`) even though A's original cancel request is still in flight; if the user clicks Cancel on A again, a second, duplicate cancel request is fired for the same run while the first is still pending.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code read: cancellingRunId (line 75) is a single string|null, set/cleared only in handleCancel (159-170), and both the disabled state and label at lines 281/284 compare it against each row's run.id. Since the panel allows multiple concurrent pending/running runs, clicking Cancel on run B while run A's cancel is still in flight overwrites cancellingRunId, causing A's button to incorrectly re-enable/relabel while A's original request is still pending -- exactly as claimed. This is a genuine per-run state bug, not one of the listed intentional patterns. However, cross-checking backend/app/core/security_assessment.py's cancel_run shows the backend deliberately treats a duplicate cancel() call on an already-cancelling task as a harmless no-op with no double-audit-write, specifically to handle concurrent cancel races -- so the dominant real-world consequence of this frontend bug is absorbed safely server-side. A narrower timing window could produce a spurious 'already cancelled' error banner, but that requires precise double-clicking across two different runs. Given the bug is real but low-impact/edge-case with backend-side mitigation, P3 (as originally claimed) is an appropriate severity -- not P0-P2 (no security/data-integrity impact) and not mere P4 cosmetic noise (it can produce a real duplicate network call or a confusing user-visible error).

titles: Cancel Scan button is shown to users without security_assessment:create (viewers), contradicting the file's own stated no-403-UI design goal

details.title: Cancel Scan button is shown to users without security_assessment:create (viewers), contradicting the file's own stated no-403-UI design goal
details.actual_behavior: The per-run "Cancel Scan" button (lines 277-286) is rendered unconditionally for any run in `pending`/`running` status, inside the runs list block (lines 255-321) that is NOT gated by `canRun`. `canRun` (line 65, set at line 84) only gates the run-creation form (line 193). The backend's cancel endpoint (`backend/app/api/routes/security_assessment.py` line 104-106) requires `security_assessment:create`, the SAME permission used to gate run creation -- not `security_assessment:read`, which is all a viewer role has (per `ROLE_PERMISSIONS[Role.VIEWER]` in `backend/app/models/user.py`, which grants only `security_assessment:read`). Runs are visible to viewers because listing only needs `security_assessment:read`.
details.failure_scenario: A user with the `viewer` role opens an investigation that has an admin's or analyst's security-assessment run still `pending`/`running`. The viewer sees and can click "Cancel Scan"; `handleCancel` (lines 159-170) calls `cancelSecurityAssessmentRun`, the backend returns 403, and the viewer sees a raw "Failed to cancel security assessment run" error banner for an action the UI should never have offered them, exactly the situation the file's own docstring says it exists to prevent.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of both files.

Frontend (SecurityAssessmentPanel.tsx):
- `canRun` (state at line 65, set at line 84) is `true` only for `user.role === "admin" || user.role === "analyst"`.
- `canRun` gates only the run-creation form block, `{canRun && (...)}` at line 193-253.
- The runs-list block (lines 255-321), which is NOT inside the `canRun` gate, renders unconditionally for anyone who can load the panel (including viewers, who can list runs via `security_assessment:read`).
- Inside that ungated block, lines 277-286 render a "Cancel Scan" button unconditionally whenever `run.status` is `pending`/`running`, with no additional role/permission check.
- `handleCancel` (159-170) calls `cancelSecurityAssessmentRun` and on failure sets `error` to the raw exception message ("Failed to cancel security assessment run"), displayed verbatim in the error banner (lines 187-191).

Backend (security_assessment.py):
- `POST /runs/{run_id}/cancel` (lines 103-119) is gated by `require_permission("security_assessment:create")` — the identical permission required by the run-creation endpoint (line 75), confirmed by the route's own docstring ("Gated on security_assessment:create (the same permission required to start one)").

Role permissions (models/user.py, lines 48-76):
- `Role.VIEWER` (71-75) has only `security_assessment:read`, `lookup:read`, `evidence:read`, `case:read`, `dashboard:read`, `pentest:read` — it does NOT have `security_assessment:create`.
- `Role.ADMIN`/`Role.ANALYST` both have `security_assessment:create`.

So a viewer who opens an investigation with another user's pending/running scan will see and can click "Cancel Scan," triggering a 403 from the backend surfaced as a raw error banner — exactly as claimed. This isn't covered by any of the eight documented intentional patterns. It also directly contradicts the module's own docstring (lines 4-15, "this panel only avoids showing a viewer a run form that would 403"), which the code fails to honor for the per-run cancel control specifically.

Severity: this is a genuine RBAC/UX gating inconsistency, but it is NOT a security bypass — the backend correctly enforces `security_assessment:create` and blocks the viewer's cancel attempt server-side. The real-world impact is confined to a confusing/unpolished error UX for viewer-role users who happen to try cancelling someone else's active scan, not any actual unauthorized action succeeding. That matches a low-severity/UI-polish bug rather than a high-impact security flaw, so P3 (as originally claimed) is an appropriate rating — not P0/P1/P2, since no privileged action is actually achievable, but not P4 either since it's a concrete, reproducible violation of the file's own documented design goal.

titles: refresh() has no request-ordering/cancellation guard, so a slower in-flight fetch can overwrite a newer one
