details.title: refresh() has no request-ordering/cancellation guard, so a slower in-flight fetch can overwrite a newer one
details.actual_behavior: `refresh()` (lines 53-71) is invoked from a `useEffect` on every change to `page`/`sortBy`/`sortDir`/`roleFilter`/`activeFilter`/`appliedSearch` (lines 73-76), and again directly from each mutation dialog's success callback. Each call fires a fresh `listUsers(...)` promise and unconditionally calls `setUsers`/`setTotal` in `.then` with no AbortController, request-id, or 'is this still the latest request' check.
details.failure_scenario: An admin clicks 'Next' twice in quick succession (page 2, then page 3). If the page-2 request's server round trip happens to complete after the page-3 request (plausible under normal network/backend latency variance), the resolved page-2 `items`/`total` overwrite the table state after the page-3 request already rendered, so the UI ends up showing 'page 3 of N' in the footer while displaying page 2's rows.
details.reasoning: Read frontend/components/dashboard/UsersManagementPanel.tsx directly. Confirmed: `refresh()` (lines 53-71) calls `listUsers(...)` and unconditionally applies `.then`/`.catch` results to `setUsers`/`setTotal`/`setError` with no AbortController, request-id, or staleness/ordering check (grepped the whole file for AbortController/requestId/cancelled/latest/abort — zero matches). The useEffect at 73-76 re-fires refresh on page/sortBy/sortDir/roleFilter/activeFilter/appliedSearch changes, and dialog success callbacks (onCreated/onSaved/onReset/onToggled, e.g. line 241+) also call refresh directly, matching the reviewer's description. Crucially, the pagination buttons (lines 232-238) are disabled only via `page<=1`/`page>=totalPages`, NOT via the `loading` state, so nothing stops an admin from clicking Next/Previous multiple times while a prior request is in flight — making the described out-of-order-response race practically triggerable rather than purely theoretical. This is a genuine, unguarded last-write-wins race condition; last resolved promise always overwrites state regardless of which page it was requested for. This does not match any of the 8 documented intentional patterns (none relate to frontend fetch ordering). Impact assessment for severity: the panel is an admin-only Users management UI; the failure mode is a transient, self-correcting display mismatch (footer page number vs. displayed rows) until the next successful fetch. Row-level actions (Edit/Reset/Disable) are bound to the specific User object rendered in that row, not to page position, so a stale/out-of-order render does not cause an admin to act on the wrong user or leak any permission boundary — no data corruption or security impact. That impact profile is consistent with a low-severity UX/correctness bug, matching the originally claimed P3 (not an over- or under-statement).

details.title: page is never re-clamped after a mutation shrinks total below the current page
details.actual_behavior: `page` is reset to 1 on every filter/sort change (lines 87, 105, 123, 139), but the four mutation success callbacks (`onCreated`, `onSaved`, `onReset`, `onToggled`) just call `refresh()` directly with no page adjustment. `totalPages` is recomputed from the new `total` (line 78), but `page` itself is untouched.
details.failure_scenario: An admin filters by isActive=true, lands on the last page (e.g. page 2, 1 remaining active user), and disables that one remaining user via ToggleActiveDialog. `refresh()` re-fetches page=2 against a now-smaller filtered result set that only has 1 page; the table shows 'No users match these filters' (line 179-185) even though a matching user exists on page 1, and the 'Previous' button (still enabled since page=2>1) is the only way to discover it.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading frontend/components/dashboard/UsersManagementPanel.tsx and backend/app/core/users.py.

Frontend: `page` state (line 38) is only reset to 1 in the four filter/sort handlers — toggleSort (line 87), search submit (line 105), role-filter onChange (line 123), active-filter onChange (line 139). The four mutation dialogs (CreateUserDialog.onCreated, EditUserDialog.onSaved, ResetPasswordDialog.onReset, ToggleActiveDialog.onToggled — lines 241/247/254/261) all wire directly to `refresh` with no page adjustment. `refresh()` (lines 53-71) calls `listUsers` with whatever `page` currently is, and `totalPages` (line 78) is derived from the freshly returned `total`, but nothing ever compares the current `page` against the new `totalPages` and clamps it down.

Backend: core/users.py `list_users` (lines 88-131) only clamps `page = max(page, 1)` (line 97) — it never clamps against the number of available pages — and computes `offset((page-1)*page_size).limit(page_size)` (line 120). So requesting a page beyond the new total simply returns an empty `items` list with the correct (smaller) `total`.

Putting the two together: an admin filtered to a small result set, sitting on the last page, who disables/enables/edits/resets the last remaining row on that page via one of the four dialogs, will have `refresh()` re-query the same stale `page` against a now-smaller filtered set, get zero items back, and see "No users match these filters" (lines 179-185) with the Previous button still enabled (page > 1) as the only way to discover the real data on an earlier page. This is a genuine, reproducible logic error, not one of the documented intentional patterns.

Severity: this is UI-only (admin console pagination state), does not lose or corrupt any data, does not cross a security boundary, and is fully recoverable by clicking "Previous" — the total count shown ("Showing page 2 of 1...") is even a visible clue that something is off. It only manifests in the narrow edge case of being on a non-first page whose filtered set shrinks to fit in fewer pages. That matches a cosmetic/trivial-impact classification. P4 as originally claimed is appropriate; I would not raise it.

titles: Early return on !isLoggedIn() never resets isAdmin/basketCount, leaving stale privileged nav state after session invalidation
listBasket()/getCurrentUser() fetches in the pathname-keyed effect have no cancellation/staleness guard, unlike the sibling SystemStatusIndicator's established pattern

details.title: Early return on !isLoggedIn() never resets isAdmin/basketCount, leaving stale privileged nav state after session invalidation
details.actual_behavior: The effect (`React.useEffect(() => { if (!isLoggedIn()) return; ... }, [pathname])`) only *skips fetching new data* when logged out; it never calls `setIsAdmin(false)` / `setBasketCount(null)` in that branch. Because WorkspaceNav is embedded directly in each page.tsx (no shared layout) and there is currently no in-app 'sign out' control on any page that renders it, this state can only go stale via an external event -- most concretely, `localStorage` is shared across same-origin tabs, so calling `logout()` (lib/api.ts) in one tab clears `access_token`/`refresh_token` for every tab. A second tab that already has `isAdmin=true`/`basketCount>0` and stays on a dynamic sub-route (e.g. `/cases/[id]`, `/pentest/[id]`, `/lookup/[id]`) does NOT remount WorkspaceNav when only the `[id]` segment changes (same page.tsx, React reuses the instance) -- it just re-renders with a new `pathname`, re-running this effect. `isLoggedIn()` now reads false (tokens gone), the effect returns early, and the previously-fetched `isAdmin`/`basketCount` are left untouched.
details.failure_scenario: Tab A: admin user signs out via the home page's 'Sign out' button (app/page.tsx calls `logout()`, clearing both tokens from localStorage). Tab B: same browser, still open on /cases/CASE-1 with WorkspaceNav showing the Administration 'Manage' dropdown and a basket badge from before sign-out. User in Tab B clicks a same-page link to /cases/CASE-2 (pathname changes, component does not remount). The effect re-runs, `isLoggedIn()` is now false, returns early -- the Administration dropdown and the stale basket count keep rendering in Tab B indefinitely (until a full page reload), even though the session was just invalidated (the code's own `logout()` comment says it bumps token_version to invalidate all outstanding tokens).
details.proposed_fix: In the effect, when `!isLoggedIn()`, explicitly reset both `setIsAdmin(false)` and `setBasketCount(null)` before returning, instead of only skipping the fetch.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading WorkspaceNav.tsx lines 130-142: the useEffect's `if (!isLoggedIn()) return;` early-return genuinely never calls setIsAdmin(false)/setBasketCount(null), so previously-fetched privileged nav state (Administration dropdown, basket count) survives a subsequent effect re-run after logout, as long as the component isn't remounted. The claimed mechanism checks out: lib/api.ts's isLoggedIn()/logout() operate on localStorage tokens shared across same-origin tabs, and WorkspaceNav is embedded via BrandHeader directly in each page.tsx (app/cases/[id]/page.tsx, app/pentest/[id]/page.tsx, app/lookup/[id]/page.tsx, etc.) with no shared layout.tsx, consistent with Next.js App Router's known behavior of not remounting the page component on dynamic-segment-only navigation.

However, the P2 severity is overstated. I checked the actual privileged destination pages (app/admin/page.tsx, app/providers/page.tsx, app/basket/page.tsx) and each independently guards itself: on mount, they call isLoggedIn() and router.replace('/login?next=...') if false, before rendering any privileged content or fetching privileged data. The code's own comment at lines 135-138 explicitly frames isAdmin here as display-only, with real enforcement server-side (require_permission on every /api/v1/admin/* route). So in the exact failure scenario described (Tab B stays stale after Tab A logs out), the impact is purely cosmetic — a stale Administration menu/basket badge that, if clicked, immediately redirects to /login with zero data exposure or privilege escalation. This is a real bug worth fixing (the proposed fix — resetting state in the early-return branch — is correct and cheap) but it's a minor cosmetic staleness issue in a narrow multi-tab scenario, not a P2 state-management/security issue.

details.title: listBasket()/getCurrentUser() fetches in the pathname-keyed effect have no cancellation/staleness guard, unlike the sibling SystemStatusIndicator's established pattern
details.actual_behavior: WorkspaceNav's effect fires `listBasket()` and `getCurrentUser()` on every `pathname` change with no `cancelled`/AbortController guard. Since WorkspaceNav lives directly inside dynamic-segment pages (e.g. `app/cases/[id]/page.tsx`) that do not remount on an id-only navigation, consecutive pathname changes reuse the same component instance and can have two in-flight requests whose responses can resolve out of order.
details.failure_scenario: User navigates quickly from /cases/A to /cases/B (e.g. via a 'next case' link) before the /cases/A-triggered `listBasket()`/`getCurrentUser()` calls resolve. If the A-triggered response arrives after the B-triggered one (plausible under normal network jitter/load-balancing), `setBasketCount`/`setIsAdmin` are overwritten with the older (A) response's data, and nothing further corrects it until the next pathname change -- the nav can briefly (or, if no further navigation occurs, indefinitely) show a stale/incorrect basket count or admin state relative to the page actually being viewed.
details.proposed_fix: Add the same `let cancelled = false` guard used in BrandHeader.tsx's SystemStatusIndicator (or an AbortController) and skip the `setState` calls if a newer effect run has since started.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading WorkspaceNav.tsx lines 130-142: the effect is keyed only on [pathname], fires listBasket() and getCurrentUser() unconditionally on every pathname change, and neither .then() callback checks any cancellation/staleness flag before calling setBasketCount/setIsAdmin -- last-resolved-wins regardless of which request was fired first. This is a real gap relative to the codebase's own established convention: BrandHeader.tsx's SystemStatusIndicator (lines 33-56) explicitly uses a `let cancelled = false` flag checked before every setState inside its async .then()/.catch() callbacks, precisely to prevent a stale response from clobbering fresher state.

The causal chain also checks out: BrandHeader (and therefore WorkspaceNav) is invoked directly inside each dynamic-segment page.tsx (e.g. app/cases/[id]/page.tsx line 76), not inside a shared layout.tsx. Under Next.js App Router, client components rendered at a stable tree position are reconciled by position/type, not by route-param identity, so navigating between /cases/A and /cases/B via client-side Link does not unmount/remount WorkspaceNav -- it's the same instance, and pathname simply changes, re-firing the effect while a prior in-flight request may still be outstanding. I verified lib/api.ts's listBasket()/getCurrentUser() are plain authedFetch wrappers with no AbortController, de-dup, or caching that would otherwise neutralize the race.

Whether this is exploitable in practice: it's a genuine, if narrow, race -- most plausibly triggered not by exotic network reordering but by the first-fired request simply taking longer to complete than the second (e.g. transient backend latency variance) during rapid sequential navigation (e.g. a 'next case' triage workflow). It doesn't match any of the documented intentional patterns (JWT role re-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED, AI narration-only scoring, basket privacy, toolkit/suite overlap, nmap flag safety, provider status semantics).

Severity: the code's own comment (lines 135-138) states isAdmin here only gates whether the Administration link is shown, with the real authorization boundary always re-enforced server-side via require_permission -- so a stale isAdmin can only cause a transient, self-correcting (next pathname change re-fires and overwrites) display glitch: a wrong basket badge count or an admin link briefly shown/hidden incorrectly. No security bypass, no data corruption, no persistent user-visible failure. That matches a low-priority, edge-case, cosmetic-but-real correctness bug -- P3 as originally claimed is appropriate; I don't see grounds to elevate it (no security/data-integrity impact) or fully dismiss it as a P4 nit (it's a concrete logic gap with a clear, already-established fix pattern in the same file's sibling component, not a style preference).

titles: destructive Button variant hardcodes 'text-white' instead of the 'text-destructive-foreground' token every other variant/component uses

details.title: destructive Button variant hardcodes 'text-white' instead of the 'text-destructive-foreground' token every other variant/component uses
details.actual_behavior: Line 17 uses the literal 'text-white' instead of 'text-destructive-foreground', even though tailwind.config.ts defines 'destructive-foreground' as hsl(var(--destructive-foreground)) and globals.css currently sets it to an off-white 40 15% 96% (not pure #fff).
details.failure_scenario: When a future '.light' theme (explicitly anticipated in globals.css's own comment) redefines --destructive-foreground to a darker color appropriate for a lighter destructive-red background, every other themed element updates automatically, but Button variant='destructive' text stays pure white regardless, producing a low-contrast/inconsistent destructive button in that theme while nothing else in the app needs a code change.
details.proposed_fix: Change 'text-white' to 'text-destructive-foreground' to match the token-driven pattern used by every other variant.
details.reasoning:
Verified directly against the files.

- button.tsx line 17: `destructive: "bg-destructive text-white hover:bg-destructive/90"` — confirmed literal `text-white`, while the sibling `default` variant on line 14 uses `text-primary-foreground` (a token), establishing the intra-file pattern the finding describes.
- tailwind.config.ts confirms `destructive-foreground` IS a defined Tailwind color mapped to `hsl(var(--destructive-foreground))`, so the token exists and is directly substitutable for `text-white`.
- globals.css confirms `--destructive-foreground: 40 15% 96%` (an off-white, not pure white) and contains the explicit design-contract comment: "a light variant can be added under `.light` later without touching component code, since everything reads these variables." Only `:root` (dark) is currently defined — no `.light` block exists yet anywhere in the codebase (grep for `.light` only hits this comment itself).
- StatusBadge.tsx's `critical` state independently confirms the established cross-component convention: `text-destructive-foreground` (token), not a literal, for the exact same brick-red destructive/critical semantic.
- A repo-wide grep of components/ for `text-white` returns exactly one hit — this line — confirming it is the sole outlier violating the token-driven theming contract that every other color usage in this file and in StatusBadge.tsx follows.

This is a genuine, verifiable design-system inconsistency, not one of the eight documented intentional patterns (none of which concern frontend theming). It doesn't match any listed intentional-pattern exception. Today it's visually near-invisible (off-white 96% lightness vs. pure white 100% lightness are nearly indistinguishable), so there is no live user-facing bug yet — the failure mode is latent and only activates if/when a `.light` theme variant is added, exactly as the codebase's own comment anticipates. That makes it correctly scoped as a low-severity, forward-looking maintainability defect rather than a functional break today, matching the reviewer's own claimed P3 rather than something higher. Fix is a trivial one-token swap (`text-white` → `text-destructive-foreground`) with no downside risk.

titles: login() discards the backend's specific error detail (rate-limit / disabled-account message)
login() discards the backend's distinguishing error detail (429 rate-limited / 403 disabled) and frontend always shows a generic 'Invalid email or password'
register() stringifies FastAPI's 422 `detail` array into a literal "[object Object]" error message

details.title: login() discards the backend's specific error detail (rate-limit / disabled-account message)
details.actual_behavior: `if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Login failed");` -- every non-2xx status (401 wrong password, 403 disabled account, 429 rate-limited) produces the exact same static string, with the response body never even read.
details.failure_scenario: A user is rate-limited by the backend's per-account login limiter after several failed attempts within the configured window; the backend returns 429 with 'Try again in under 900 seconds', but login() only ever produces 'Login failed', giving the user zero indication they're being throttled or for how long. Same for a disabled account: they see the identical generic message as a wrong password.
details.proposed_fix: Mirror register()'s pattern: `const body = await res.json().catch(() => null); throw new Error(body?.detail ?? "Login failed");`
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by direct reading of both files.

frontend/lib/api.ts lines 81-92: `login()` does `if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Login failed");` — it never reads res.json() on the error path, so every non-2xx status collapses to the identical static string. Immediately below it (lines 94-105), `register()` does `const body = await res.json().catch(() => null); throw new Error(body?.detail ?? "Registration failed");`. A grep across the whole file shows every other one of ~27 mutating API functions (register, compareIOCs, configureAIProvider, createUser, resetPassword, pentest actions, exploit actions, etc.) follows the `body?.detail ?? "..."` pattern — `login()` is the sole outlier that never reads the body at all.

backend/app/api/routes/auth.py confirms the backend genuinely emits distinct, useful, non-enumerating details for login specifically: 429 "Too many login attempts for this account. Try again in under N seconds." (line 107-111), 403 "Account disabled" (line 123-124), vs. 401 "Invalid email or password" which already collapses no-such-user and wrong-password server-side (line 120-122) — so unlike register()'s deliberate collapsing (which exists specifically to prevent an email-enumeration oracle across two different failure modes), there is no enumeration rationale for also collapsing 403/429 into the same bucket as 401. The reviewer's rejection of the register()-analogy concern is correct.

One nuance the original reviewer didn't mention: frontend/app/login/page.tsx's catch block is `catch { setError("Invalid email or password."); }` — it doesn't even reference the caught error object, unlike register/page.tsx's `catch (err) { setError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : "..."); }`. This means fixing api.ts's login() alone (per the proposed fix) would not yet surface anything to the user until login/page.tsx's catch block is also updated to use err.message. This doesn't invalidate the finding (the specific claim — that api.ts:81-92 discards the backend's detail — is verifiably true, and is one of two components of the full fix needed), but it means the proposed one-line fix is incomplete on its own.

Severity: this is a real but minor UX/error-handling gap — no security bypass, no data loss, no functional break in the core login path (users still get correctly denied/rate-limited/blocked; they just get a confusing generic message instead of "try again in 900 seconds" or "account disabled"). This matches P3 (minor, non-security, UX-quality issue) and I would not adjust it up or down from the original reviewer's rating.

details.title: login() discards the backend's distinguishing error detail (429 rate-limited / 403 disabled) and frontend always shows a generic 'Invalid email or password'
details.actual_behavior: login() (api.ts lines 81-92) throws a bare `new Error("Login failed")` on any non-2xx response without reading `res.json()`'s `detail` field, even though the backend (auth.py's login()) returns three genuinely distinct, actionable statuses: 401 'Invalid email or password', 403 'Account disabled', and 429 'Too many login attempts...'. frontend/app/login/page.tsx's handleSubmit (lines 20-32) then catches with a bare `catch {}` and unconditionally sets `setError("Invalid email or password.")` regardless of which of the three actually occurred. This is the same class of bug the codebase's own comments explicitly call out and fixed elsewhere in this file (streamLookup's res.clone().json() detail-surfacing) and in register()'s own error handling two functions above -- login() was never given the equivalent fix.
details.failure_scenario: An administrator disables a user's account (POST /admin/users/{id}/active with is_active=false) or the user trips the 10-attempts/60-second login rate limiter after a few mistyped passwords. On their next login attempt the user sees only 'Invalid email or password' and has no way to know their account was disabled by an admin or that they are being rate-limited, so they are likely to keep retrying with password guesses (compounding the rate-limit lockout) instead of contacting an administrator.
details.proposed_fix: In login(), parse `await res.json().catch(() => null)` and throw an Error carrying `body?.detail`, matching register()'s existing pattern; in login/page.tsx's catch block, surface `err instanceof Error ? err.message : ...` instead of a hardcoded string, matching RegisterPage's own handleSubmit.
details.reasoning: Verified directly against both files. frontend/lib/api.ts lines 81-92: login() does `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(\"Login failed\");` with no res.json() read at all -- confirmed via Read tool, exact line match. This is inconsistent with register() two functions below (lines 94-105) which does `const body = await res.json().catch(() => null); throw new Error(body?.detail ?? \"Registration failed\");`, and with the file's own explicit comment on streamLookup describing the identical bug class as previously fixed there. Backend confirmed via backend/app/api/routes/auth.py lines 87-129: login() genuinely raises three distinguishable HTTPExceptions with actionable `detail` strings -- 429 \"Too many login attempts for this account. Try again in under N seconds.\" (rate limiter), 401 \"Invalid email or password\", 403 \"Account disabled\" -- so the detail being discarded is real, distinct, actionable information, not redundant boilerplate. Also verified frontend/app/login/page.tsx lines 20-32: handleSubmit has a bare `catch { setError(\"Invalid email or password.\"); }`, discarding any thrown message regardless of source, confirming the second half of the claim. This does not match any of the 8 listed intentional-design exceptions (JWT role re-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED, AI-narration-only scoring, basket visibility, security-assessment/pentest-suite overlap, destructive-pentest-action absence, nmap flag safety boundary, provider status enum) -- none apply to a login error-message pipeline. The bug is real: an admin-disabled or rate-limited user sees only a generic \"Invalid email or password\" and has no way to distinguish their situation, plausibly leading to repeated guessing that compounds a rate-limit lockout. On severity: reviewer proposed P3. This is UX-only (no auth bypass, no data loss, no security boundary crossed), self-resolving for the rate-limit case after the window elapses, and for the disabled-account case the required remedial action (contact an admin) is the same regardless of whether the user understands why -- so P3 (minor confusing-UX papercut, not blocking, not rare-but-plausible-security-impact) is the right severity; I don't see grounds to escalate to P2 since no functional workflow is broken, nor downgrade to P4 since the trigger conditions (rate limiting, admin deactivation) are realistic and recurring in normal operation.

details.title: register() stringifies FastAPI's 422 `detail` array into a literal "[object Object]" error message
details.actual_behavior: On a non-ok response, `register()` does `throw new Error(body?.detail ?? "Registration failed")`. FastAPI's 422 validation-error bodies always return `detail` as an ARRAY of `{loc, msg, type}` objects (never a string), so `body?.detail` is a truthy array and gets passed straight to `Error()`. `Error()` stringifies its argument via `Array.prototype.toString`, which joins each element through the default `Object.prototype.toString`, yielding the literal text `"[object Object]"`.
details.failure_scenario: On frontend/app/register/page.tsx, the password `<input>` has `minLength={8}` but no client-side max length, while backend/app/schemas/auth.py caps `password` at `max_length=72`. A user types a 73+ character passphrase and submits; the backend 422s with `detail: [{"type": "string_too_long", ...}]`; register/page.tsx's `setError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : ...)` then renders the useless string "[object Object]" instead of any actionable message. The same happens for an over-long full name (backend caps at 255 chars, frontend enforces no limit) or any other 422.
details.proposed_fix: When `body.detail` is not a string (FastAPI's list-of-errors shape), map over it and join the individual `msg` fields instead of passing the raw array to `Error()`.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading frontend/lib/api.ts lines 94-105 verbatim: register() does `throw new Error(body?.detail ?? "Registration failed")` with no check for detail's shape. Confirmed backend/app/schemas/auth.py has `password: Field(min_length=8, max_length=72)` and `full_name: Field(default="", max_length=255)`, and backend/app/main.py has no custom exception_handler for RequestValidationError (only one for DBAPIError, unrelated) -- so FastAPI's default pydantic-validation 422 handler applies, which always returns `detail` as a list of {loc, msg, type} dicts, never a string. Verified in a Node REPL that `new Error([{a:1}]).message` really does become the literal string "[object Object]" (and "[object Object],[object Object]" for multiple errors), because the Error constructor coerces its argument via ToString, and Array.prototype.toString joins elements via their own (Object.prototype) toString. Confirmed frontend/app/register/page.tsx has no maxLength on the password (only minLength={8}) and no maxLength on the full-name input, and renders the caught error verbatim via `setError(err instanceof Error ? err.message : ...)` / `{error &&

{error}

}`. So the exact reproduction the reviewer described (73+ char password, or an over-255-char full name, or actually any 422 at all e.g. a malformed email) really does surface literally "[object Object]" to the user instead of any actionable message. This isn't one of the documented intentional patterns (JWT role re-derivation, provider NOT_CONFIGURED, AI narration-only, basket privacy, toolkit/pentest overlap, nmap flag safety, provider status semantics) -- it's a genuine, previously-undetected error-handling gap. Severity: matches the original P3 -- it's a real, easily-reproducible, purely-cosmetic UX bug (confusing error message) confined to the registration form, with no security, data-integrity, or availability impact, and the page itself already documents that self-registration is a narrow bootstrap-only path. Not P0-P2 since nothing breaks functionally and no security boundary is crossed; not P4 since it fully defeats the purpose of surfacing a validation error to the user during initial account setup.

titles: authedFetch has no signal analogous to streamLookup's onAuthExpired for the ~50 other functions built on it

details.title: authedFetch has no signal analogous to streamLookup's onAuthExpired for the ~50 other functions built on it
details.actual_behavior: authedFetch just returns the still-401 Response after a failed refresh attempt, with no way for any of the ~50 functions built on top of it (getLookup, listCases, listUsers, etc.) to know the failure was specifically an expired/invalidated session rather than an ordinary error. Each wrapper then throws only a generic 'Failed to fetch X' message.
details.failure_scenario: A user's refresh token expires (7 days idle) or an admin resets their password (bumping token_version) while they are sitting on /cases. listCases() -> authedFetch -> 401 -> refreshAccessToken() fails and internally calls logout() (clearing localStorage) -> returns false -> the stale 401 Response is returned -> listCases() throws Error('Failed to fetch cases'). The page (app/cases/page.tsx) just shows that bare generic string in an error banner; nothing redirects the user to /login even though their tokens have already been wiped underneath them, so they're stuck looking at a broken page.
details.proposed_fix: Have authedFetch (or a thin wrapper around it) accept/invoke an optional onAuthExpired-style callback, or throw a distinguishable error subclass on a post-refresh-failure 401 so calling pages can redirect, instead of duplicating that logic only in streamLookup.
details.reasoning: Confirmed by reading lib/api.ts directly. authedFetch (lines 172-183) retries once on 401 via refreshAccessToken(), and on failure just returns the still-401 Response with no signal. refreshAccessToken() (112-129) calls logout() on failure, which clears both tokens from localStorage. Grepped all ~50 authedFetch call sites: every one does a bare `if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Failed to fetch X")`, losing the distinction between an ordinary error and an unrecoverable session expiry. Confirmed via app/cases/page.tsx that isLoggedIn() is only checked once on mount before the call, not re-checked in the .catch() handler, so a mid-call session death just produces a generic error banner with no redirect. Grepped the whole app/ tree for any other 401/onAuthExpired handling and found only one wiring: app/lookup/new/page.tsx's use of streamLookup's bespoke onAuthExpired callback (the one place this is handled). No global interceptor, middleware.ts, or shared auth-guard hook exists to compensate. This matches the finding's claimed call chain and failure scenario exactly, and is not one of the 8 documented intentional patterns. Severity: real but mild — not a security or data-loss issue (tokens are correctly wiped), and the user isn't permanently stuck since any subsequent navigation/reload re-triggers the mount-time isLoggedIn() check and redirects correctly; the concrete harm is limited to a confusing generic error message instead of an immediate redirect on the current page. This supports the original P3 rating rather than something higher.

titles: streamLookup()'s SSE parser silently discards a trailing partial event if the connection ends before its closing blank line arrives

details.title: streamLookup()'s SSE parser silently discards a trailing partial event if the connection ends before its closing blank line arrives
details.actual_behavior: The read loop does `if (done) break;` as soon as reader.read() reports the stream finished, without first flushing/processing whatever is still sitting in `buffer`. Any event whose bytes were received but which never got its trailing '\n\n' delimiter before the underlying connection closed (e.g. truncated by a proxy/timeout, or the server process being killed mid-write) is left in `buffer` and never dispatched to any handler -- there is no warning, error, or partial-completion signal for this case.
details.failure_scenario: If the connection is cut by an intermediary (reverse proxy idle timeout, load balancer, or the backend process being restarted) at the exact moment the final `final_assessment` or `done` event's bytes have been partially delivered but not yet terminated by a blank line, that event is silently dropped: the frontend never calls onFinalAssessment/onDone for it and never surfaces any error either, leaving the investigation UI stuck showing pre-completion state with no explanation, indistinguishable from the pipeline simply still running.

titles: recordAITestResult/recordIOCTestResult never check response status, silently discarding backend failures

details.title: recordAITestResult/recordIOCTestResult never check response status, silently discarding backend failures
details.actual_behavior: Both functions do `await authedFetch(...)` and return void with no check of `res.ok` at all -- a 403 (e.g. caller's role no longer has provider:manage), 404, 500, or an unrecoverable 401 (refresh also failed) is completely swallowed. The promise resolves successfully either way.
details.failure_scenario: In app/providers/page.tsx's onTest handler, `await recordAITestResult(p.provider_id, result.ok, result.message)` is called with no surrounding try/catch (unlike the sibling onSave/onSetActive handlers, which do wrap in try/catch and call setError). If this call 403s/500s/401s, the function returns normally, `refreshAll()` runs, and the UI shows no error -- the analyst believes the 'last tested' state was saved when the backend never persisted it (ProviderRuntimeConfig.last_test_at/last_test_ok/last_test_message are left stale).
details.proposed_fix: Check res.ok and throw (or at least log/surface) on failure, matching the pattern used by setIOCProviderEnabled a few lines below.
details.reasoning:
Verified directly in frontend/lib/api.ts (lines 553-559 and 607-613): both recordAITestResult and recordIOCTestResult call `await authedFetch(...)` and return void with zero inspection of `res.ok` or the response body. This is a real inconsistency in the file -- every other mutating function nearby (configureAIProvider, setActiveAIBackend, configureIOCProvider, setIOCProviderEnabled, addCaseNote, reanalyzeLookup, etc.) either does `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...)` or additionally surfaces `body.detail`. setIOCProviderEnabled sits literally one function above recordIOCTestResult and does check `res.ok` -- the asymmetry is exactly as described.

I also traced authedFetch (line 172-183): it never throws or normalizes on non-2xx status itself (only retries once on a 401 via refresh) -- it just returns the raw Response. So a non-2xx from record-test can only ever be surfaced if the caller checks `res.ok`, which these two functions don't.

I checked the actual caller, app/providers/page.tsx (lines 122-169): onSave/onSetActive/onToggleEnabled all wrap their awaited calls in try/catch + setError, but onTest does not wrap the `recordAITestResult`/`recordIOCTestResult` call site in its own try/catch at the page level, exactly as claimed. I also checked one level down, ProviderConfigRow.tsx's handleTest (lines 91-107), which does wrap the whole `onTest(...)` call in a try/catch -- this is a detail the original reviewer's "no surrounding try/catch" phrasing missed. However this doesn't rescue the bug: since recordAITestResult/recordIOCTestResult never throw regardless of status code, that catch block can never fire for a record-test failure -- it only catches a failure from the initial testAIBackend/testIOCProvider call. So the underlying defect (silently swallowed non-2xx from record-test) is real and un-caught at every level, confirming the reviewer's core claim even though one supporting detail (which layer lacks a catch) was slightly off.

I confirmed a real failure mode exists on the backend: backend/app/api/routes/runtime.py's record_ai_test/record_ioc_test endpoints are gated by `Depends(require_permission("provider:manage"))`, which per this codebase's documented pattern re-derives the caller's role from the DB on every request -- so a role downgrade mid-session while the Manage Providers page is still open would legitimately produce a 403 here that is completely swallowed today.

I checked whether last_test_at/last_test_ok/last_test_message drive any other logic (grep across backend+frontend) -- they are purely a display-only "last tested: ok, N minutes ago" field in the admin panel, never read for authorization, provider selection, or any other functional gating. The foreground "did the test succeed" feedback to the analyst is accurate regardless (it comes from testAIBackend/testIOCProvider's own return value, not from the record-test call), so this bug's blast radius is confined to a stale/incorrect informational timestamp behind an admin-only permission, with no security or data-integrity consequence and no misleading of the actual test-pass/fail signal. That confirms P3 (silent-failure error-handling gap, real but low real-world impact) is the right severity -- not higher, not lower.

titles: RiskAssessment interface is missing scoring_engine_version and scoring_breakdown, which the backend actually returns and persists
