titles: Sync-ComposeEnvFile has a brief window where the copied .env is not yet ACL-restricted

details.title: Sync-ComposeEnvFile has a brief window where the copied .env is not yet ACL-restricted
details.actual_behavior: Copy-Item (line 288) writes the real .env (API keys, DB password, JWT secret) into {app}\app\.env first, and only calls icacls (line 289) to restrict it to Administrators+SYSTEM afterward -- between those two lines the file briefly exists under whatever ACL it inherited from the parent (potentially the default, broader Program Files ACL).
details.failure_scenario: Invoke-DockerCompose calls Sync-ComposeEnvFile unconditionally on every single docker-compose invocation (up, down, restart, ps, logs, ...), recreating this window each time; a low-privileged local process or user actively polling {app}\app\.env at the right instant during any of those routine operations can read the plaintext secrets before icacls re-applies the restrictive ACL milliseconds later.
details.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading Common.ps1 directly: Sync-ComposeEnvFile (lines 286-290) does Copy-Item into $script:AppRepoDir ("C:\Program Files\IOC Intelligence Platform\app", confirmed at line 44) followed by a separate icacls call, with no atomic create-with-ACL step in between. I verified live that C:\Program Files really does carry an inheritable BUILTIN\Users:(RX) ACE ((OI)(CI), i.e. it propagates to new files/subfolders), matching the code's own header comment. So the core claim -- a brief window exists between Copy-Item and icacls during which the copied .env can carry a broader, inherited ACL instead of the intended Administrators+SYSTEM-only one -- is technically correct.

However, the reviewer's failure scenario is overstated. I empirically tested Copy-Item -Force's Windows semantics: when the destination file does NOT yet exist, the new file inherits the parent folder's ACL (reproducing the broad-ACL window); but when the destination file ALREADY exists (as it will after the very first successful sync + icacls lockdown), Copy-Item -Force overwriting it PRESERVES the existing (locked-down) ACL rather than reverting to the parent's inherited permissions -- confirmed with a direct before/after icacls comparison across two successive Copy-Item calls onto the same destination. Since Invoke-DockerCompose (line 188) calls Sync-ComposeEnvFile on every docker-compose invocation, but Setup-Wizard.ps1 only ever creates {app}\app\.env fresh once (line 1583, the initial `up -d --build` during first-time setup, run under an elevated token per Assert-Elevated), every later call (Service-Start/Stop/Restart, Watchdog, Open-Platform, Restore-Database, etc.) is overwriting an already-locked-down file and does NOT reopen the broad-ACL window. So this is not a recurring, ongoing exposure on "every single docker-compose invocation" as the reviewer claims -- it is a one-time (or, in the rare event the app folder/file is later deleted and recreated, occasional) sub-millisecond window during initial installation only.

Given that: (1) the actual exposure is a single narrow race at first-time setup rather than a continuously recreated window, (2) exploiting it requires an attacker who already has unprivileged local code execution on the machine and who happens to be polling that exact path in a tight loop at the precise moment an elevated setup wizard writes the file for the first time, and (3) such an attacker already has many easier/higher-value avenues on a machine they can already execute code on -- the real-world risk is materially lower than the claimed P3. I'm downgrading it to P4 (a genuine but very low-probability, single-occurrence, hard-to-exploit TOCTOU gap) rather than rejecting it outright, since the underlying non-atomic write-then-lock-down sequence is a real and fixable gap (e.g., pre-creating the destination file with the restrictive ACL before writing content into it, which per my test would avoid the window entirely since overwrite preserves existing ACLs).

titles: Email validation regex blocks consecutive/trailing dots in the local part but not in the domain part

details.title: Email validation regex blocks consecutive/trailing dots in the local part but not in the domain part
details.actual_behavior: The local-part group `[A-Za-z0-9...]+(\.[A-Za-z0-9...]+)*` correctly rejects consecutive/leading/trailing dots before the @, but the domain group `[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$` only requires at least one dot somewhere and otherwise allows any non-@/non-whitespace character, including further dots -- so addresses like 'user@domain..com' or 'user@domain.com.' (trailing dot) pass this client-side check even though they are likely still rejected by the backend's real validator, reproducing the exact 'Account creation failed' surfaced-too-late failure mode this fix was written to close, just for the domain side instead of the local side.
details.failure_scenario: Administrator enters 'admin@corp..example.com' on the Administrator Account page. The page-level check passes (no error shown), but registration at Start Installation may still fail with a raw Pydantic email-validation error, which is exactly the confusing-late-failure this validation was added to prevent for the local-part case.
details.reasoning: Confirmed genuine bug by direct testing, not just code reading. (1) Read Setup-Wizard.ps1 lines 493-533: the Validate block for the Administrator Account page uses regex '^[A-Za-z0-9!#$%&\'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+(\.[A-Za-z0-9!#$%&\'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+)*@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$'. The local-part group requires an atext-run, then zero-or-more (dot + atext-run) groups -- this structurally forbids leading/trailing/consecutive dots before the @. The domain group '[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$' merely requires 'one or more non-@/non-space chars, a dot, one or more non-@/non-space chars' -- crucially, '.' is NOT excluded from the [^@\s] character classes, so it can absorb extra dots via backtracking. (2) I actually ran this exact regex through real PowerShell (pwsh) via -match: 'admin@corp..example.com' -> True (passes), 'admin@corp.example.com.' -> True (passes), while 'double..dot@email.com' -> False (correctly rejected). This directly confirms the domain/local asymmetry claimed by the finding. (3) I ran the real backend email_validator library (found installed in backend/.venv_test) against the same domain-side strings: 'admin@corp..example.com' -> INVALID ('cannot have two periods in a row'), 'admin@corp.example.com.' -> INVALID ('cannot end with a period'). So the backend genuinely rejects exactly what this client-side regex lets through. (4) I traced the call chain: Start Installation's install handler (lines 1617-1663) calls POST /api/v1/auth/register with $State.AdminEmail, and on failure logs 'Account creation failed: ...' at line 1661 -- the exact late/confusing failure mode the comment at lines 496-509 explicitly says this validation was added to eliminate. So the fix is incomplete: it closes the loophole for local-part dot placement but leaves an identical loophole open for domain-part dot placement, reproducing the same class of bug it was written to fix. This is not any of the listed intentional design patterns. Severity: this is a real but very low-impact bug -- it's a one-time setup-wizard UX validation gap (admin enters a mistyped domain, gets a generic error at the final Start Installation step instead of immediately on the Administrator page, and must go Back and retype), with no security impact, no data loss, and an easy, obvious recovery path. This matches the P4 the original reviewer assigned; I see no basis to raise or lower it.
